一句话：误差高可能是物理不对，也可能只是画面难预测；三步框架把这两件事分开。

要点：

  • 常见误读：视频世界模型的预测误差经常被直接当成「物理惊讶」，但误差也可能来自外观差异、静态内容、运动复杂度，或只是普通难预测
  • 作者给出一个三步评测框架：分离「冻结表示里含有什么」「它如何组织外观与物理差异」「什么会改变模型自身的预测误差」
  • 在 IntPhys2（物理可能 / 不可能事件的基准）上，对来自不同训练的表示做系统对比

为什么值得看：用世界模型做决策时，最怕把「画面难预测」当成「物理违规」。这套三步拆解提供了一个可操作的口径：先验表示里有没有物理信息、再用误差判断，而不是看一个数字就下结论。

中文摘要：视频世界模型的预测误差常被直接解读为「物理惊讶」，但作者指出误差还有别的来源：外观差异、静态内容、运动复杂度，或者仅仅是这一帧本来就难预测。为此他们提出一个三步评测框架：先看冻结的表示里到底包含什么，再看这种表示如何组织外观差异与物理差异，最后看究竟是什么在改变模型自身的预测误差。在 IntPhys2（由物理上可能/不可能事件构成的基准）上，作者对比了来自不同训练的表示。对用世界模型做决策或验收的系统，这套拆法能把「物理不对」与「画面难预测」分开，避免被单一误差数字误导。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

Abstract

Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model’s own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

1 Introduction

Video world models are expected to capture regularities that make visual futures predictable. Prediction errors and related scores are consequently used to assess physical plausibility and identify unexpected events [(Smith et al., 2019; Piloto et al., 2022; Riochet et al., 2018; Dai et al., 2023; Garrido et al., 2025; Bordes et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026)]. Such scores also guide the selection of physically plausible generated videos [(Baldassarre et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026)]. Understanding what they measure matters when errors are used to locate events, compare videos, or reward trajectories.

Let f_C and f_T construct context and target latent representations, also called features, from observations x. Both functions include the model’s encoding and token-selection steps. For a predictor p, optional actions a, and a scoring distance d, the prediction-error score is

S(x,a)=d (p(f_C(x),a), f_T(x)).

This score measures prediction difficulty in the chosen representation. A large value may reflect physical inconsistency, appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary model error. Physical information may also be accessible to a classifier even when the predictor’s error responds primarily to other properties of the video.

We first test whether linear classifiers can distinguish physically possible from impossible events using frozen representations. We also test how well appearance information can be recovered from the same representations. IntPhys2 is a synthetic video benchmark pairing physically possible events with violations such as an object passing through a solid obstacle [(Bordes et al., 2025)]. We compare V-JEPA2-G, trained to predict latent representations, with VideoMAE2-G, trained to reconstruct masked pixels, and simple visual statistics. Linear classifiers readily recover appearance labels from all three. V-JEPA2-G provides a modest advantage when classifying events as possible or impossible.

We then examine how appearance and physical differences are organized across network depth. Changes in hue, brightness, and object color let us measure how far representations move, how consistently they move in the same direction across scenes, and how much those directions overlap with differences between possible and impossible events. In both V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G, appearance shifts become smaller relative to distances between unrelated videos. At deeper layers, the shifts line up more than those from randomly paired videos and overlap less with physical changes, though these trends sometimes reverse between layers. Appearance labels nevertheless remain easy to recover at the evaluated probe layers. We also test whether representation distances help predict changes in V-JEPA2-G’s prediction error. In a regression analysis, they add little beyond scene conditions and simple visual statistics.

Finally, we test prediction error under controlled changes to actions, appearance, motion, and physical validity. Across three action-conditioned world models, incorrect actions raise error while the observed frames are held fixed. Color changes also alter error without changing the simulated physical state. In Physion++ videos of physical interactions, repeating a single frame can increase error, whereas changing color throughout a clip can lower it [(Tung et al., 2023)]. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we test stopping and falling with and without support beneath an object [(Greff et al., 2022)]. Mean error is higher for stopping in both settings, even though stopping is lawful only when support is present. A fixed error threshold also flags many lawful events as impossible. These results show why recoverable physical information and action sensitivity alone are insufficient to interpret prediction error as physical surprise.

2 Related work

Predictive video representations.

Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting latent representations rather than pixels [(LeCun, 2022; Bardes et al., 2024)]. V-JEPA2 extends this approach to video understanding, prediction, and planning [(Assran et al., 2025)], while VideoMAE and VideoMAE2 learn representations through masked pixel reconstruction [(Tong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023)]. Action-conditioned models such as LeWorldModel, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WM predict visual representations from observations and actions [(Maes et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2024; Terver et al., 2026)]. These objectives provide different representations and native error scales. Our comparisons retain each released pipeline and test the meaning of its error through controlled interventions.

Physical information and latent geometry.

Inverse-dynamics probes recover actions from video representations [(Yeom et al., 2026)]; robotic evaluations distinguish representations useful for reconstruction from those useful for planning [(Nilaksh et al., 2026)]. Layerwise probes and subspace analyses reveal physics-related structure in V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE2 [(Joseph et al., 2026; Punzo et al., 2026)]. Geometry regularization can improve multistep prediction [(Xia et al., 2026)], and PhyLatent studies physical invariance and identifiability under appearance and dynamics changes [(Zeng et al., 2026)]. We connect this representation-level evidence to a separate question: whether measured geometry predicts native-error differences in the same model and setting.

Physical prediction and violation of expectation.

IntPhys and IntPhys2 evaluate possible versus impossible events [(Riochet et al., 2018; Bordes et al., 2025)]; Physion and Physion++ evaluate physical-outcome prediction and inference of latent physical properties [(Bear et al., 2021; Tung et al., 2023)]. Violation-of-expectation models use predicted-versus-observed discrepancies to identify unexpected physical events [(Smith et al., 2019; Piloto et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2023; Garrido et al., 2025)]. Related evaluations address counterfactual consistency and physical plausibility in generated videos [(Begiristain et al., 2026; Baldassarre et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026)]. We focus on the specificity and transfer of a fixed native score: whether physical violations increase error across controlled changes in motion, appearance, and context.

3 Evaluation framework

We retain each evaluated pipeline’s encoders, token selection, normalization, and native distance. Context-only prediction and encoding a full clip before selecting context tokens are distinct computations (Section 4.2). Native score magnitudes are compared only within a model.

Table 1 separates evidence about representations from evidence about the score. Readout and geometry characterize encoded information; the remaining checks test predictive sensitivity and physical decisions. For threshold-based detection, a lawful clip above the threshold is a false alarm, and an impossible clip below it is a missed violation.

We evaluate V-JEPA2-G on controlled Kubric videos and IntPhys2, V-JEPA2-L on Physion++ Mass, and released action-conditioned models on TwoRoom and PushT. The IntPhys2 comparison includes VideoMAE2-G and low-level visual statistics. DINO-WM and JEPA-WM share a frozen DINOv2 encoder [(Oquab et al., 2024)], so their comparison varies only the predictor.

Uncertainty is estimated by bootstrap over independent configurations, Physion++ matched pairs within scenarios, IntPhys2 scenes, or action-test episodes. All conditions belonging to one unit remain together. Bonferroni-adjusted intervals are used for the specified families of contrasts. Thresholds and regression coefficients are fitted on data separate from evaluation. Full protocols, fitting and split histories, and reproducibility records are in the appendices. Code and numeric experiment records are available at https://github.com/3-ml/jepa-surprise (Appendix G).

4 Results

4.1 Physical-violation ordering and threshold transfer

To separate physical validity from trajectory identity, we render a falling sphere above either a solid platform or an opening. Each setting has two continuations: the sphere stops at platform height or falls below it. Stopping is lawful on the solid platform and unsupported over the opening; falling is lawful through the opening and violates solidity when it passes through the platform. Figure 8 in the appendix shows the rendered construction. The 256 configurations cross these four cases with the original appearance, a 30^∘ hue shift throughout the clip (persistent), or the same shift starting at the target interval (abrupt), giving 3,072 clips. Stopping trajectories match across settings, as do falling trajectories. Within each setting and appearance, the two continuations share context frames and predictor outputs. Support appearance, shadows, and occlusion differ across settings. The predictor observes the first 12 of 48 frames; native error is mean absolute difference from normalized EMA-target tokens for the remaining 36 frames.

V-JEPA2-G gives stopping higher mean error in both settings. Consequently, impossible-minus-possible error is negative on solid support and positive over the gap (Figure 1). The native score’s ordering follows the trajectory across this reversal of physical validity (Appendix Figure 9).

The reversal holds under both clean and persistent-hue appearance; all four adjusted intervals exclude zero in their respective directions. Averaging the two settings would conceal the opposite orderings. Appendix E.2 reports the complete margins and intervals.

A single threshold fitted on 24 separate clean calibration configurations yields 53.9% balanced accuracy [52.1, 55.8] on clean evaluation clips, with equal weight to both support settings. Performance differs sharply by setting: 80.7% over gaps versus 27.1% on solid support. The threshold falsely flags about 69% of lawful clips, including every lawful solid-support continuation (Appendix Figure 10). Thus the above-chance average coexists with a large false-alarm rate. Figure 1 also shows transfer under persistent and abrupt hue; Appendix E.2 gives all per-setting rates and the threshold definition.

4.2 Static-content and persistent-appearance controls

We evaluate V-JEPA2-L’s full-clip masked-prediction score on the 192 official Physion++ Mass videos. The encoder processes each 16-frame window before context tokens are selected, so target frames can influence the predictor. The static diagnostic compares every complete, nonoverlapping window with versions repeating its first, middle, or last frame. These still-frame controls have higher mean error than the original videos. Across videos, the mean share of windows scoring no higher than their average static baseline is approximately 84%. The mean original-minus-static difference is negative in every scenario, and the layout-cluster sensitivity check agrees. Uncertainty is based on scenario-stratified matched pairs, with windows averaged within videos, not treated as independent observations. Repeating frames changes both content and history, so this comparison neither isolates motion’s causal effect nor supplies a universal score correction.

Persistent appearance changes can also lower error. This separate experiment uses one fixed middle 16-frame window per video. Hue shifts and pixel darkening applied throughout the window both lower mean error relative to the original and to their target-only counterparts (Table 2). Changes restricted to the final four frames have uncertain original-relative effects: their adjusted intervals include zero. The persistent-versus-target-only hue ordering reverses in Collision, so the overall mean does not describe every scenario.

The normalized L1 score averages spatial-token errors over the two target frame-pairs (temporal tubelets). Because the encoder sees the full window, target-only edits can affect the predictor despite unchanged context pixels. These are diagnostics of the evaluated masked-prediction implementation. Appendix D.1 gives the complete counts, intervals, and scoring details.

4.3 Physical-label and appearance readouts

Linear probes readily recover appearance labels. For V-JEPA2-G, physical-label accuracy under these probes is only modestly above chance: approximately 58% for possible versus impossible events, against 50% chance (Table 3). Its four-class appearance accuracy is approximately 98%, but the two tasks do not provide a common scale for the amount of information encoded. The physics result shows that label information is accessible. Whether native prediction error detects violations is a separate question, which the later experiments test.

IntPhys2 tests object permanence, continuous motion, solidity, and constant object properties [(Bordes et al., 2025)]. For example, a solidity pair contrasts a solid object stopping at an obstacle with one passing through it. We compare V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G with PixelSummary (RGB statistics, color histograms, and frame differences). Five-fold scene cross-fitting keeps each scene’s pairs and appearances together, with class-balanced linear probes and training-only feature scaling. Appendix B.1 documents layer selection and the post-hoc split correction.

For the all-appearance physics task, V-JEPA2-G’s paired advantage over each comparator has an interval above zero. The clean-only comparison with PixelSummary remains uncertain. Table 3 and Appendix B.2 give the full comparisons. Architecture and training differ across models, so the comparison covers the released representations as a whole and does not isolate the JEPA objective.

4.4 Layerwise representation geometry

Both models show smaller final-layer appearance shifts relative to between-video differences than at the first layer (Figure 2A). Relative magnitude divides each shift by the median unrelated-video distance at that layer. V-JEPA2-G’s hue ratio falls from approximately 57% to 8%. The measures compare V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G on the same 57 IntPhys2 scenes.

Directional coherence measures alignment across videos. At later depths, appearance shifts are more aligned relative to shuffled source-transform pairings, whereas physical-change directions remain closer to that reference (Figure 2B).

Subspace overlap measures the fraction of squared physical-feature change projected into an appearance subspace fitted on other scenes. Final overlap is lower than initial overlap, but the trajectory is not monotonic. V-JEPA2-G’s final overlap is approximately 6%, above the roughly 0.28% dimension-matched random reference (Figure 2C).

Appendix B.3 gives the complete geometry and source-video retrieval results.

4.5 Predicting native-error differences from geometry

We next test whether geometric measurements predict native-error differences in the crossed-support setting. Ordinary least squares (OLS) models fitted on 24 separate configurations predict physical margins (impossible minus lawful error) and appearance-induced score changes on the 256-configuration evaluation population. The baseline uses condition labels and static, motion, and shuffled-frame statistics; the expanded model adds relative representation distances and interactions with support or appearance timing. This compares geometry with information already available from the experimental conditions and visible changes.

Adding final-encoder geometry changes physical-margin R² from approximately 0.771 to 0.774, but the adjusted improvement interval includes both gains and losses. Some earlier locations worsen prediction. Here R² uses the error of predicting the fitting-set mean as its denominator, rather than the evaluation-set mean. For appearance-score differences, both models perform worse than that reference. Across all five locations and both tasks, no improvement interval lies entirely above zero (Appendix Tables 23–24).

This post-hoc analysis gives limited evidence of added predictive value from the tested geometry features and linear models. Native prediction error is the world model’s discrepancy between predicted and observed representations; the regression error here measures how well a separate model predicts differences in that discrepancy. Configuration-bootstrap intervals condition on the fitted regressions. Appendix F.1 (Figure 12) gives the full protocol and analysis history.

4.6 Action and appearance sensitivity

All three action-conditioned models use the supplied action: incorrect actions increase prediction error when the observed outcome is held fixed. We test 256 episodes per task or scorer under correct, zero, and reversed actions. LeWorldModel (LeWM) uses task-specific released checkpoints; DINO-WM and JEPA-WM reuse the PushT target frames and action interventions with their own preprocessing and predictors. Table 4 reports positive reversed-minus-correct contrasts for every model.

Color changes also raise error while simulator state is held fixed. Figure 3 measures each hue change relative to the unchanged static target, and each action mismatch relative to the lawful prediction of the same moving target. Both interventions affect LeWM, with larger hue-induced increases at the two higher rendered-effect matches.

The DINO-based models likewise have larger mean hue-induced than action-mismatch increases at the 60^∘/0.75 PushT match: 0.04977 versus 0.00307 for DINO-WM, and 0.01738 versus 0.00284 for JEPA-WM, each relative to its respective lawful baseline. These are descriptive means. Comparing absolute hue and opposite-action scores instead gives the reverse ordering because the moving lawful targets already have higher error. Appendix C.1.2 (Figure 6) decomposes that baseline difference and retains the absolute contrasts with their original intervals. These models therefore use the action and also respond to color. Matching the rendered RGB change of a hue edit to that of an action change does not make the two equally predictable to the model.

4.7 Task-associated color controls

In a separate PushT study with simulator state fixed and RGB change matched, LeWM’s error still depends on color choice. Agent-blue blocks score higher than novel-orange blocks; block-gray agents likewise exceed matched purple. The target-only blue/orange gap is positive in 233 of 256 episodes. Persistent changes reduce the mean gaps but retain both orderings (Appendix C.2).

For target-only edits, the prediction is unchanged and differences in target-encoder shifts account for almost all of the score gaps algebraically. Role colors can carry task information. These controls therefore show that the score depends on color. They leave open whether that color information helps predict physical outcomes and whether LeWorldModel encodes task roles.

5 Discussion

Physical labels can be read out of V-JEPA2-G representations (about 58% accuracy against 50% chance), yet its native prediction error does not consistently track physical validity in the crossed-support test. Appearance remains decodable even as its relative displacement decreases across depth, while physical labels are modestly accessible under the evaluated probes. These findings describe the representation, but do not determine which video changes produce large native errors. The same-model regression makes that connection explicit: the selected geometry features add little predictive value beyond visual statistics and experimental conditions.

The native-error controls identify several sources of discrepancy. A score can remain high when motion is removed, or decrease after a persistent color change. In the crossed-support test, a stable trajectory ordering produces opposite physical-violation orderings and poor shared-threshold performance. Abrupt recoloring asks a different question: an unexpected color transition may itself violate object-property constancy. Persistent transformations remove that transition, allowing sensitivity to a stable appearance change to be examined separately. In PushT, the moving lawful targets already have higher error than the static ones. Comparing absolute scores can therefore rank the action change above the hue change, even though the hue increase over its own baseline is larger.

Table 5 summarizes what each setting establishes. The evaluation framework turns the broad question of physical understanding into testable claims about a particular score. For a physical-surprise application, the decisive checks are violation ordering within relevant conditions and false-alarm and miss rates when a fixed decision rule transfers across them. These measurements connect the interpretation of prediction error to the decisions it is intended to support.

6 Limitations

The controlled support experiment samples one procedural family with restricted cameras, colors, and lighting. It tests transfer across those conditions only; real-world and material generalization are untested. Material appearance can convey mass or friction cues, and greater training diversity may change appearance sensitivity. Those questions require additional data and controlled model comparisons.

The IntPhys2 readout and geometry-to-error transfer are post-hoc analyses. Their intervals condition on fitted models and omit refitting uncertainty; the readout also conditions on fold assignments. The tested linear geometry models do not establish a mechanism or the effect of removing appearance directions. Physion++ provides contact labels and no physical-violation labels, and its full-clip scoring implementation permits target information to affect context tokens. These distinctions constrain the interpretation of each result.

Model comparisons also vary architecture, pretraining, capacity, and native score. We do not estimate a general limit on planning or anomaly-detection performance. Application-specific acceptable error rates were not specified. Detailed split histories, failed compatibility checks, and excluded follow-ups are retained in the appendix.

Broader impact.

Prediction errors can serve as measures of physical surprise when controlled tests establish what they respond to. Their use as rewards or safety signals requires validation in the intended task and environment.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Evidence map and interpretation

The experiments deliberately answer different questions. Table 6 records the independent unit, evidential status, supported inference, and stopping point for each block. The main conclusion depends on their separation: representation accessibility, representation geometry, action-conditioned sensitivity, and error specificity are not interchangeable.

Criteria for the main-text evidence table.

In Table 5, support refers to the inference named in Table 1. IntPhys2 readout support is post-hoc, and geometry support concerns measured representation structure. The separate crossed-support geometry-to-error regression is not a second test of that structural criterion. Its result is discussed in Section 4.5. The physical-validity check fails in the crossed-support experiment because violation margins have opposite signs across support conditions. Calibration remains insufficient: the fixed threshold makes frequent errors and no application-specific acceptable-error margin was specified. D records measured score dependence under appearance or static controls, without treating every such response as a failed physical judgment. The Physion++ entry concerns the full-clip score; the action-model entries use the historical controls and the baseline decomposition in Appendix C.1.2. Action support comes from same-target action contrasts, with JEPA-WM marked post-hoc. The excluded later two-model PushT continuation contributes no verdict.

Appendix B Representation readouts and geometry

B.1 IntPhys2 readout protocol and uncertainty

The corrected IntPhys2 sealed test contains 114 matched possible/impossible pairs from 57 held-out scenes, 228 source videos, and 912 appearance-conditioned samples. Each sample uses exactly 64 decoded source frames sampled by rounded linear spacing. The four appearance conditions are clean, 90-degree hue rotation, brightness multiplier 0.45, and 180-degree selective recoloring. V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G are extracted at five frozen depths (block_00, block_10, block_20, block_30, final); PixelSummary is a 100-dimensional low-level baseline of RGB summary, color-histogram, and frame-difference statistics. The probe is StandardScaler plus balanced logistic regression with C=1.0 and at most 2000 iterations. The post-hoc correction reported here sorts scenes by hash (seed 0) and splits them into five folds. The fold index (0 to 4) is also the classifier’s random state. Fold k is test, fold (k+1)\bmod5 is validation, and the remaining folds are training. Sealed test folds contain 12, 12, 11, 11, and 11 scenes; development test folds contain 8, 8, 8, 7, and 7, with all pair IDs and appearance variants from one scene held together. Primary layers preserve the original development choices: V-JEPA2-G block_20 for appearance and block_30 for physics, VideoMAE2-G block_30 for appearance, block_00 for all-appearance physics, and block_30 for clean-only physics, with PixelSummary using its only layer. The cross-fit development check retains V-JEPA2-G block_20 for appearance and block_30 for physics_all; its all-appearance comparator deltas include zero. Table 7 summarizes the model-specific input and temporal pipelines.

Both neural pipelines receive the same decoded frames, use ImageNet RGB normalization, and expose 1408-dimensional pooled features at matched relative depths. V-JEPA2-G resizes without cropping; VideoMAE2-G uses its pinned short-side resize and center crop. The shared coarse token grid is 4×4×4, obtained by mean pooling native spatiotemporal tokens.

For physics, correctness is averaged over samples within each out-of-fold pair and then over both pairs in each unique scene. Each of 10,000 bootstrap draws samples all 57 sealed scene values globally with replacement. Model deltas preserve fold, scene, and pair alignment before scene aggregation and paired resampling. These intervals reflect resampling of scenes with the trained probes held fixed. They do not include variation from refitting the probes or from a different fold assignment. Near- or below-chance comparator estimates are not interpreted as meaningful anti-physics signals.

B.2 Linear-probe results

The main text reports all three classification tasks and paired model differences in Table 3. Figure 4 visualizes the same physics-readout estimates; it is not an additional experiment or an independent confirmation.

B.3 Geometry estimands and complete results

Geometry estimands and nulls.

Let ẑᵢ^(ℓ)=zᵢ^(ℓ)/\lVertzᵢ^(ℓ)\rVert₂ and d(x,y)=1-\cos(x,y). The unrelated clean scale and relative displacement magnitude are

G_ℓ=\mathopmedian_i,j: sᵢ≠sⱼd(ẑᵢᶜˡᵉᵃⁿ,ẑⱼᶜˡᵉᵃⁿ), R_ℓ(T;i)=(d(ẑᵢᶜˡᵉᵃⁿ,ẑᵢᵀ))/(G_ℓ),

with the same G_ℓ used for matched physical pairs. For Δᵢᵀ=ẑᵢᵀ-ẑᵢᶜˡᵉᵃⁿ and non-negligible uᵢᵀ=Δᵢᵀ/\lVertΔᵢᵀ\rVert₂, directional coherence is the standard mean resultant length [Mardia and Jupp, 1999],

MRL_ℓ(T)=\lVertN⁻¹∑ᵢuᵢᵀ\rVert₂, ΔMRL=MRL_obs-𝔼[MRL_shuffle].

Our operational control shuffles source-transform correspondence only across scenes, retaining the factor, model, and layer. An orthonormal appearance basis U_app,k^(ℓ) is obtained by standard SVD/PCA [Jolliffe and Cadima, 2016] on training-scene displacements. For held-out Δᵢᵖʰʸˢ=ẑᵢⁱᵐᵖᵒˢˢⁱᵇˡᵉ-ẑᵢᵖᵒˢˢⁱᵇˡᵉ,

P_app,k^(ℓ)(i)=(\lVert(U_app,k^(ℓ))^⊤Δᵢᵖʰʸˢ\rVert₂²)/(\lVertΔᵢᵖʰʸˢ\rVert₂²).

Five-fold scene cross-fitting excludes evaluation scenes when fitting U_app,k; dimension-matched Haar-random subspaces provide the reference. The primary k=4 was retained from development before sealed effects were observed. Every unrelated pair uses different scenes, possible-to-impossible orientation is fixed, and the reported intervals use 10,000 scene-bootstrap draws. Shuffled-correspondence and random-subspace references each use 10,000 draws. Principal-angle diagnostics follow standard subspace comparison [Björck and Golub, 1973]; tiny-displacement, raw-feature, local-normalization, and anisotropy checks remain supplementary.

Directional robustness.

Raw MRL is insufficient: the shuffled V-JEPA2-G block-00 brightness population has first-PC energy 0.886, showing strong background anisotropy. Figure 2 therefore reports ΔMRL; Table 11 gives full curves. Major observed MRL effects are not driven by one scene: leave-one-scene-out ranges are [0.781, 0.797] for V-JEPA2-G hue at block 30 (full 0.784), [0.953, 0.961] for brightness at block 30 (0.954), and [0.708, 0.720] for recoloring at block 30 (0.712). Final projection is likewise stable at 0.060 with leave-one-scene-out range [0.057, 0.060].

The final-layer transformed-to-clean nearest-feature retrieval rates are 65.6% for V-JEPA2-G and 44.6% for VideoMAE2-G. These measure recovery of source-video identity under the evaluated transformations. Appearance accessibility is evaluated separately by the linear probes.

B.4 Exploratory transformation trajectories (run after the sealed test)

Status: exploratory, run after the sealed test. This analysis does not change the sealed geometry result. It applies the exact paper V-JEPA2-G checkpoint to corrected development (38 scenes, 76 pairs, 152 source videos) at the five reported depths. Each source has clean video plus hue rotations of 15^∘, 45^∘, and 90^∘; brightness multipliers 0.85, 0.65, and 0.45; and selective recoloring rotations of 45^∘, 90^∘, and 180^∘. Brightness strength is 1-b. Scene is the independent unit and intervals use 10,000 bootstrap draws. We use these trajectories to probe transformation geometry and local equivariance descriptively [Lenc and Vedaldi, 2015].

For an ordered trajectory z(a₀),…,z(aₘ), straightness is endpoint distance divided by path length, \lVertz(aₘ)-z(a₀)\rVert₂/∑ⱼ\lVertz(aⱼ₊₁)-z(aⱼ)\rVert₂. Displacement dimensionality uses entropy effective rank, \exp[-∑ⱼpⱼ\logpⱼ], where pⱼ is normalized squared singular-value energy. These quantities describe ray-likeness and dimensionality; neither identifies a semantic axis.

Figure 5 shows that at final, brightness is the most ray-like evaluated factor: straightness is 0.907 [0.899, 0.914], versus 0.692 [0.673, 0.710] for hue and 0.553 [0.520, 0.587] for selective recoloring. Final effective ranks are 5.43, 9.83, and 13.72, respectively. Thus selective recoloring is higher-dimensional than the other evaluated factors, while brightness remains only relatively ray-like and has more than one effective dimension.

For hue, held-out relative error is 0.798 for a shared-ray model and 0.747 for a harmonic curved model. This is modest evidence that the observed 0^∘–90^∘ arc is better represented by a curved model than one common ray, but the final effective rank of 9.83 makes the low-dimensional part of the hypothesis only partial. Three nonzero doses spanning at most 90^∘ cannot test closure, periodicity, circularity, or a latent color wheel.

The main exploratory result compares a local appearance basis with an endpoint basis of the same dimension. At final and k=4, held-out physical projection is 0.0416 [0.0297, 0.0559] into the strongest-endpoint appearance space, 0.0414 [0.0295, 0.0564] into the all-dose space, and 0.0668 [0.0448, 0.0932] into the local appearance-tangent space; the random reference is approximately 0.00284. The paired tangent-minus-endpoint difference is 0.0252 [0.0072, 0.0450]. The advantage is not universal across depth: at block 20, tangent projection (0.037) is below endpoint projection (0.043). The final result therefore says only that a matched-k local appearance-tangent basis captures more held-out physical-displacement energy than the strongest-endpoint basis at that layer; it does not establish entanglement, causal factorization, or physical understanding.

Table 12 gives the qualitative classifications: factor-specific geometry replicated; brightness as the most ray-like factor replicated; recoloring as higher-dimensional replicated; hue as curved and low-dimensional replicated only partially; and final tangent projection exceeding endpoint projection replicated. Table 13 reports direction by dose. These labels are a cross-check and say nothing about the effect of model scale.

Appendix C Action and appearance controls

C.1 Action mismatch and hue controls

C.1.1 LeWorldModel, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WM controls

The TwoRoom and PushT studies strict-load the released LeWorldModel checkpoints, preserve the official four-frame, frame-skip-five preprocessing and action normalization, and use 256 fresh independent episodes per task. LeWorldModel combines latent prediction with the SIGReg regularizer introduced in LeJEPA [Balestriero and LeCun, 2025]. For each episode we simulate lawful targets from the third context state under scaled five-action blocks ca for c∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}, render the lawful target once, and reuse the exact same target bytes under lawful ca, zero, and opposite -ca action blocks. The LeWM native score is mean squared error between predicted and encoded target latents. The DINO-WM PushT extension uses the same 256 PushT episodes, target bytes, action blocks, and rendered-effect matches; it normalizes actions and proprioception with the released DINO-WM PushT statistics and scores final-step visual-latent MSE between the predictor output and encoded target. The JEPA-WM PushT extension uses the same controlled construction and three-frame teacher-forcing context with the released 224-pixel preprocessing, action and proprioception statistics, AdaLN plus RoPE predictor, and final one-step visual embedding MSE over DINOv2 patch tokens. The visual score excludes proprioceptive prediction loss, and the analysis is post-hoc exploratory. Action contrasts are same-target differences relative to the lawful-action baseline. The reported hue-minus-opposite contrasts instead subtract the opposite-action score for a moving target from the hue-modified static-target score. They are absolute score comparisons across different target baselines, with predeclared rendered-effect matches. Episode-level 95% intervals use 10,000 bootstrap draws over episodes. Appendix Sections C.2.1–C.2.3 separately test matched color directions and decompose their latent source.

C.1.2 Separating target difficulty from intervention effects

Let S₀ denote the static lawful score, Sₕ the hue-modified static score, Sₗ the moving lawful score, and Sₒ the score for that same moving target under the opposite action. The reported cross-target contrast decomposes as

Sₕ-Sₒ=(Sₕ-S₀)-(Sₒ-Sₗ)-(Sₗ-S₀).

The first two terms are the hue and action increments relative to their respective lawful baselines. The third is the difference in lawful target difficulty. Table 15 gives the stored condition means at the higher PushT rendered-effect match. It clarifies the existing score comparison without introducing a new inferential test.

The mean hue increment exceeds the mean action increment for all three models at this match. For the DINO-based models, however, the moving lawful baseline is much higher than the static baseline, producing a negative absolute Sₕ-Sₒ contrast. The sign of that contrast therefore cannot identify which intervention changes the score more. Neither contrast makes the two interventions equally predictable, equally relevant to the task, or equally far from the training distribution. The shared DINOv2 encoder and differing training pipelines also prevent attributing the result to color augmentation alone.

C.2 PushT role-color decomposition

C.2.1 Question and matched design

PushT uses blue for the agent, gray for the block, and green for the goal. Color is a potentially task-relevant cue in PushT. We test whether native LeWorldModel prediction MSE depends only on the amount of rendered change or also on color direction. The frozen confirmatory run uses 256 independent episodes excluded from all earlier PushT pilots, the released checkpoint, official four-frame and frame-skip-five preprocessing, and the installed Pymunk/Pygame renderer. Because the installed renderer is close but not byte-identical to stored observations, every contrast uses the paired current-renderer output as its baseline.

The block is recolored to agent blue and compared with a novel orange selected to match rendered magnitude; the agent is recolored to block gray and compared with a matched novel purple. Figure 7 illustrates these paired recolorings. Each condition is applied either only to the target or persistently to all four frames. Across colors, the maximum realized simulator-state difference is zero. In target-only conditions, context pixels, actions, and predictor outputs are exactly identical; only the target-encoder representation changes. Table 16 summarizes the matched rendered changes.

C.2.2 Matched contrasts

For each object and scope, the contrast, declared before the run, is the score with the role color minus the score with the matched novel color. Episode-level 95% intervals use 10,000 paired-bootstrap draws. All four directional contrasts are positive in the mean (Table 17), including substantially matched target RGB change and affected-pixel fraction.

C.2.3 Exact latent decomposition

Let r₀=p₀-z₀ be the baseline residual and q=Δp-Δz the intervention-induced residual shift. Because the native score is mean squared latent error,

ΔS=2 mean(r₀⊙q)+mean(q²).

Reconstructing every intervention score from this identity has maximum absolute error 2.38×10⁻⁷. In target-only conditions Δp=0 exactly, and the role-minus-novel score gaps nearly equal the corresponding target-encoder shift gaps (Table 18). This locates the abrupt effect primarily in target-encoder color-direction sensitivity.

Persistent predictor and target shifts point in similar directions, especially for block recoloring, but not identically (cosines 0.71 to 0.93 across the four conditions). The experiment therefore supports color-direction sensitivity and partial agreement between predictor and target shifts under persistent changes.

Appendix D Physion++ static and appearance diagnostics

D.1 Full-population controls

The fixed official Mass manifests contain 192 videos / 96 pairs: 32 pairs each in Mass-Collision, Mass-Dominoes, and Mass-Waterpush. Additional directory files do not enlarge this cohort. Every complete nonoverlapping 16-frame window is used for the static study (5,177 windows); incomplete tails are recorded and left unpadded. Each window is scored as original and with frame 0, 8, or 15 repeated throughout. The appearance study selects window ⌊n/2⌋ from each video’s n complete windows, without using scores, and evaluates original, persistent hue, target-only hue, persistent darkening, and target-only darkening. Hue adds 21 PIL HSV bins modulo 256; darkening applies ⌊4 RGB/5⌋. Persistent transformations affect all 16 frames and target-only transformations frames 12-15. Paired future pixels/tensors match exactly; target-only context pixels/tensors match original.

The exact archived scoring body uses FP16 CUDA batch-one evaluation, 12 selected context frames / four target frames, FP32 layer normalization of both operands, and mean L1 over 512 target tokens.

The Transformers implementation encodes all 16 frames before selecting context tokens. Thus even target-only image changes can alter the predictor; identical future pixels under persistent/target-only transformations need not yield identical target embeddings. This diagnostic concerns the released full-clip scoring implementation, not a causal forecast conditioned only on the first 12 frames. We kept this implementation after seeing the results and did not replace it.

For static results, let d_vw be original minus the mean of the three static scores in window w of video v. We first average d_vw, or 1[d_vw≤0], within each video, then average the two videos within each matched pair. This is not an independent-window prevalence estimate. We use 50,000 scenario-stratified pair-bootstrap draws, seed 2026102601; layout-cluster sensitivity uses seed 2026102701 and 13/10/19 layout clusters. The mean residual is -0.028264 with pair 95% interval [-0.028999,-0.027525] and layout 95% interval [-0.029265,-0.027421]. Scenario means are -0.032012, -0.031993, and -0.020788, respectively. Mean within-video nonpositive fractions are 89.20%, 88.01%, and 76.17%; their overall mean is 84.46% [pair 95% interval 83.67%, 85.24%], not a physical-violation false-positive rate.

Appearance contrasts also average the two videos within each pair. We use 50,000 scenario-stratified draws, seed 2026102602, and 99.1667% intervals for the six fixed contrasts (familywise Bonferroni level 0.05); layout sensitivity uses seed 2026102702. Main Table 2 reports all six. Layout-adjusted intervals retain negative persistent effects and negative persistent-minus-target-only effects; target-only hue is sensitive to the resampling unit (layout interval [-0.001676,-0.000012], while the primary pair interval crosses zero). Table 19 gives every scenario mean, including sign reversals; none was used to select the population or transformation.

For normalized predictor p and target t, define Eᵢⱼ=mean|pᵢ-tⱼ| for original (0) and transformed (1) clips. Descriptive contributions are

Cₜ=\tfrac12[(E₀₁-E₀₀)+(E₁₁-E₁₀)], Cₚ=\tfrac12[(E₁₀-E₀₀)+(E₁₁-E₀₁)].

They sum algebraically to E₁₁-E₀₀. FP64 hybrid checks use 10⁻¹⁰ identity tolerance and 10⁻⁶ native reconstruction tolerance; no intervention fixes one operand in the actual network. Table 20 is therefore bookkeeping, not causal mediation. In particular, target-only predictor contributions need not vanish. Pixel darkening is not physical relighting, and contact labels do not label violations.

D.2 Historical static-audit selection and scoring

The checkpoint identity is recorded in the online checkpoint table. Ten additional Physion++ Mass test videos were selected deterministically as evenly spaced files after excluding the earlier single-video debug example. Every complete 16-frame segment was scored, yielding 273 segments. For each segment we record the native latent residual, mean consecutive absolute RGB difference on the 0-255 scale, and the fraction of pixels whose consecutive-frame change exceeds 5.

For static calibration, the first, middle, or last decoded frame is repeated across all 16 input positions and rescored. The first-frame event residual is the original score minus the corresponding frozen-frame score. This control does not estimate a universal corrected surprise score; it asks only whether a local raw peak requires temporal change.

D.3 Motion association and static candidates

Across all segments, raw score and mean consecutive RGB change have Pearson correlation r=0.596. Each video’s highest raw-score segment contains substantial motion; their mean pixel-motion value is 3.712 and their first-frame residuals are positive, from 0.0165 to 0.0492. However, 6 of 10 videos also contain a high-scoring near-static segment with mean RGB change below 0.01. Table 21 shows that all six have nonpositive frozen-frame residuals.

The mean first-frame residual over these six candidates is -0.0350. The threshold and highest-candidate rule were diagnostic choices, so 6/10 is not a population false-positive rate. Raw V-JEPA2-L error partially tracks visible motion but also admits high-error static-content candidates. This motivates the main paper’s pixel-motion and static baselines; it is not evidence about V-JEPA2-G benchmark accuracy or a general event detector.

Appendix E Physical-validity tests with Kubric

E.1 Population, rendering, and native score

After development on 24 configurations (288 clips), we froze 256 candidates with seeds 2026102700–2026102955 before rendering or scoring. Each candidate independently samples sphere radius in [0.60,0.70], nominal contact time in [1.18,1.24], initial horizontal position in [-0.035,0.035], one of four camera positions, and one of four development colors. Initial height follows the specified free-fall contact time. The manifest fixes all draws. Each configuration crosses solid/gap support with lawful/inconsistent stopping or falling and clean/persistent/abrupt 30^∘ hue, giving 12 clips. Appearance does not change the simulated trajectory. Abrupt hue begins at frame 12; persistent hue applies throughout. Support is simulator-fixed. Across worlds the stop trajectories match, as do the fall trajectories, but support appearance, shadows, and occlusion differ.

Clips contain 48 frames at 12 fps, with 240-Hz simulation and 256×256 rendering (Cycles CUDA, 64 samples/pixel, no denoising). The scorer uses 12 context frames and 36 future frames (18 target tubelets), FP32 weights, bfloat16 compute/subtraction, and FP32 mean absolute error against normalized EMA-target tokens.

This context-only predictor path is distinct from the full-clip V-JEPA2-L path in Appendix D.1.

E.2 Estimands, threshold, and audit disposition

The primary family comprises four means of inconsistent minus lawful error: solid/gap under clean/persistent hue. We resample all conditions within complete configurations together, with 50,000 draws (seed 202610256) and 98.75% percentile intervals, Bonferroni-adjusted for four means. Bootstrap coverage is approximate. A consistently positive ordering would require all four intervals to lie above zero. The two solid-support intervals lie below zero instead. The 0.001 planning target denotes reporting resolution, not an equivalence or useful-effect margin.

The four inconsistent-minus-lawful means and their 98.75% intervals are: clean solid -0.006734 [-0.007421, -0.006045]; clean gap +0.006908 [+0.006189, +0.007632]; persistent solid -0.007839 [-0.008446, -0.007233]; and persistent gap +0.007495 [+0.006897, +0.008095]. These are the complete numerical counterparts of Figure 1’s ordering panel.

The threshold 0.4858863055706024 was fitted on the 24 clean development configurations by maximum balanced accuracy with largest-threshold tie breaking; flagging uses ≥. No final refit, score inversion, or world-specific threshold is allowed. Secondary rates and AUROC use 10,000 configuration-bootstrap draws and descriptive 95% intervals. Table 22 reports both worlds separately. The balanced rows average the two worlds; they are not an independent sample or an equivalence result.

E.3 Kubric exact rerendering

The Kubric pilot uses V-JEPA2-G with eight accepted MOVi-A scenes rendered from saved simulator trajectories (Figure 11). The first 12 frames are identical context bytes across all conditions, and the target is the remaining 36 frames represented as 18 two-frame tubelets. Appearance conditions rotate only the target object’s post-event base color; physical conditions apply a persistent target-object +z displacement of 0.25, 0.50, 1.00, or 1.50 object diameters while preserving non-target states. The scalar score is mean absolute error between predictor output and layer-normalized EMA-target-encoder tokens. We report scene-level paired differences from clean with 10,000 bootstrap draws; with eight scenes, the matched hue-versus-displacement contrasts are exploratory and used only to test scalar specificity under exact state and rendering controls. The two predeclared physical minus appearance contrasts are 0.000259 [-0.000632, 0.001145] for a 120^∘ hue change versus a displacement of 0.25 object diameters, and 0.000201 [-0.000791, 0.001035] for a 180^∘ hue change versus a displacement of 0.50 object diameters. Both intervals include zero.

Appendix F Geometry-to-error regression

F.1 Development-only geometry fit, evaluated post-hoc

We extract FP32 target-token means from all 3,072 original final inputs at block_09, block_19, block_29, final encoder, and native target: a (3072,5,1408) matrix. Two tables retain six physical-margin cells or eight appearance-change cells per configuration. The physical baseline uses gap, persistent, and abrupt indicators; the appearance baseline uses gap, falling-trajectory, and abrupt indicators. Both add differences in static, motion, and shuffled-frame statistics. Geometry-only models retain the same three indicators and add relative feature distance ∥zₐ-z_b∥/∥z_b∥ and its gap (physical) or abrupt (appearance) interaction. Combined models add those two terms to the full baseline. All models include an intercept and use development-only ordinary least squares (lstsq, rcond=None), with no selected regularization or layer. Coefficients were frozen before final extraction, but after final outcomes had been inspected: this is post-hoc, not an untouched confirmation.

We report MSE and R²=1-MSE(ŷ,y)/MSE(ȳ_\rmdev,y), which uses the development training mean rather than the final mean. Negative values are retained. All 50,000 configuration-bootstrap draws (seed 2026102801) preserve conditions and layers. Coefficients stay fixed, so intervals omit development-fit uncertainty. The ten incremental-R² contrasts use 99.5% intervals (Bonferroni family of ten); zero-crossing intervals do not demonstrate equivalence.

The shuffle diagnostic uses 1,000 whole-configuration permutations (seed 2026102803+j), identical across conditions, locations, and tasks, retaining baseline features. Its combined-model R² distribution is descriptive, not a causal or confirmatory randomization test. Extrapolation counts flag rows with any design value outside its development range; rows are not discarded or refitted. No result demonstrates that removing appearance improves native error or that the model lacks physical information.

Appendix G Reproducibility resources

Code and numeric experiment records are available at https://github.com/3-ml/jepa-surprise/tree/local-launchers-2026-10-31.

  • •

    Representation and action studies: historical/results/.

  • •

    Crossed-support experiment: release/final256/.

  • •

    Physion++ controls: release/physion-static/ and release/physion-appearance/.

  • •

    Geometry-to-error regression: release/geometry-transfer/.

  • •

    Hardware, software, and recorded runtimes: docs/reproducibility.pdf.

  • •

    Checkpoint identities: docs/reproducibility.md.

  • •

    Execution instructions and required inputs: docs/LOCAL_EXECUTION.md and release/DEPENDENCIES.md.

  • •

    File hashes and verification: release-manifest.json and tools/check_release.py.

    • Datasets, model weights, rendered videos, and large feature caches must be obtained separately. The execution instructions specify the required input files, software versions, and hardware.

item.title: 把 agent 当第一用户重做引擎：ForgeAX 是 TypeScript + WebGPU，CLI 全部返回 JSON、能逐 draw 逐像素验收 ｜ ForgeAX Engine — AI-native TypeScript game engine for AI agents
item.description:
一句话：数据、生命周期、API、工具围绕「AI 能理解、能操作、能自查」设计，而不是事后加个插件。

要点：

  • 定位写在第一行：AI 原生 TypeScript 游戏引擎，**以 AI agent 为第一用户**——数据、生命周期、API 与工具都围绕同一目标设计，让 AI 理解系统、准确操作、检查结果并完成修复
  • 能效口径很具体：目标是让 AI 用更少上下文、更少试错、更短反馈完成更多**经过验证**的游戏开发工作；对应的是 CLI 的 `--json` 输出（观察结果带 `revision`）与「查询活实体 / 录制重放渲染帧 / 逐 draw 逐像素检查」这套 AI 优先调试能力
  • 引擎本体：WebGPU 渲染（材质/光照/阴影/后处理/GPU 粒子/trail 与 beam）、ECS World、2D/3D 物理（Rapier）、动画、输入、音频与网络同步；资产管线支持 glTF/FBX/图像导入，也能用 TypeScript 生成资产并参数化派生变体；已有多款上线游戏与微信小游戏/Steam/Switch 等目标平台

为什么值得看：这是目前少数把「agent 一等公民」落到**每一层接口**的实现：CLI 输出结构化 JSON、状态带 revision、渲染帧可录制重放并逐 draw 检查。对比只在编辑器里加个聊天框的做法，这套接口才让 agent 能真正自查与修复。

中文摘要：ForgeAX 是一个 AI 原生的 TypeScript 游戏引擎，明确把 AI agent 当作第一用户：数据、生命周期、API 与工具都围绕「让 AI 理解系统、准确操作、检查结果并完成修复」来设计。它追求的是「AI 能效」——让 agent 用更少上下文、更少试错、更短反馈，完成更多经过验证的开发工作；落到工程上就是 CLI 全量 `--json` 输出、观察结果带 `revision`，以及「查询活实体 / 录制与重放渲染帧 / 逐 draw 逐像素检查」这套 AI 优先调试能力。引擎本体基于 WebGPU（材质、灯光、阴影、后处理、GPU 粒子），玩法侧是 ECS World 加 Rapier 物理、动画、输入、音频与网络同步，资产管线支持 glTF/FBX/图像导入，也能用 TypeScript 生成资产并派生参数化变体；官方展示了多款基于它上线的游戏，目标平台覆盖微信小游戏、Steam、Switch 等。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：GitHub·ForgeAX（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

（正文为仓库 README 节选，去掉徽章与安装细节。）

Language: 简体中文 · [English](README.en.md)

ForgeAX Engine

AI 原生的 TypeScript 游戏引擎 —— 把想法变成可玩的游戏。

以 AI agent 为第一用户：数据、生命周期、API 与工具围绕同一目标设计，

让 AI 理解系统、准确操作、检查结果并完成修复。

游戏展示 ·

特性 ·

开始使用 ·

AI 能效 ·

引擎架构 ·

深入阅读

[!IMPORTANT]
能效是目标，设计是方法。 让 AI 用更少上下文、更少试错和更短反馈时间，完成更多经过验证的游戏开发工作。

用 ForgeAX 制作

这些游戏都基于本引擎，通过 forgeax CLI 与 AI 优先的工作流创作。

天工战甲 · 机甲动作 / 3D

我的 AI 队友不可能是上古器灵！ · ARPG / 3D

萌宠卡丁车 · 竞速 / 3D

腐坏农场

查看完整游戏展示 →

特性

  • 渲染 — 材质、灯光、阴影、后处理、GPU 粒子、trail 与 beam，基于 WebGPU
  • 玩法 — ECS World、2D/3D 物理（Rapier）、动画、输入、音频与网络同步
  • 资产管线 — 导入 glTF / FBX / 图像，或用 TypeScript 生成资产并参数化派生变体
  • AI 优先调试 — 查询活实体、录制 / 重放渲染帧，逐 draw 逐像素检查
  • CLI 工作流 — 用 forgeax 命令创建、运行、检查与打包游戏
  • 多平台 — 造化工坊、微信小游戏、Steam、Steam Deck、Switch 与 Kubee

开始使用

把引擎和它的 AI 工具链装进你的编辑器：

npx -y @forgeax/game install

支持：Claude Code · Cursor · ChatGPT · Kimi Code · DeepSeek · VS Code。

或直接用引擎新建工程：

pnpm dlx @forgeax/engine project new my-game --template game-3d

cd my-game

pnpm exec forgeax dev start --headless false

game-3d 是第三人称参考工程，empty 是最小起点。先读生成的 README 与技能，再看 [Engine](packages/engine/README.md) 与 [CLI 使用指南](skills/forgeax-engine-cli/SKILL.md)。

运行与验证

pnpm exec forgeax help --tree --json

pnpm exec forgeax project check

pnpm exec forgeax dev status --json

pnpm exec forgeax dev capture --json

pnpm exec forgeax dev stop --json

pnpm exec forgeax project test

pnpm exec forgeax project package --format web-zip

观察结果携带 revision，截图返回 PNG 与报告引用。实体查找、摄像机控制和实例身份约束见 [持久运行实例](packages/devkit/README.md#persistent-live-control)。

从引擎源码 / SDK 构建

工具链版本以 [.nvmrc](.nvmrc)、[.pnpm-version](.pnpm-version)、[.bun-version](.bun-version) 为准。

pnpm install

pnpm build:engine

pnpm test
  • 场景 ｜ 入口
  • 获取 SDK ｜ pnpm dlx @forgeax/engine sdk install ./forgeax-sdk
  • SDK 的 source/engine/ ｜ 独立公开源码面，带 .forgeax-public-distribution 标记与预构建 WASM；运行上述 install / build，无需私有子模块
  • 完整贡献者 checkout ｜ 首次 clone 使用 --recurse-submodules 获取有权限访问的私有资产；完整应用构建运行 pnpm build
  • 单个示例迭代 ｜ pnpm build:app hello/triangle；更大范围验收遵循 Smoke gate

SDK 包含构建产物、模板、技能与 Engine 源码。详见 [SDK 指南](skills/forgeax-engine-sdk/SKILL.md)。

环境要求

  • Node.js ≥ 22.13.0 —— [.nvmrc](.nvmrc) 锁定 22.22.3
  • pnpm 12.10.1，通过 Corepack 启用（corepack enable）
  • Bun ≥ 1.2.0
  • 支持 WebGPU 的浏览器（最新版 Chrome / Edge）

AI 能效

能效关注经过验证的结果，同时考虑错误定位与返工、上下文和工具往返成本。

  • 能力 ｜ 如何提高 AI 能效
  • 渲染透明 ｜ [RHI-debug](packages/rhi-debug/README.md) 录制并重放自包含帧，检查 draw/dispatch、binding、资源与像素，定位异常输入
  • 运行时逻辑与数据透明 ｜ [ECS](packages/ecs/README.md) 显式描述组件、查询和调度；[Remote](packages/remote/README.md) 查询活实例，依据真实状态定位逻辑错误
  • 资产可编写、可溯源 ｜ [ScriptablePack / Pack](packages/pack/README.md) 以 TypeScript 生成或 JSON 声明内容；稳定 GUID 连接源与产物，修复沿 producer 返回源输入
  • 插件变更可撤销 ｜ [原生 Cordis](packages/plugin/README.md) 统一依赖、激活与清理；配置更新失败可回到上一个工作的 Fiber
  • 性能与结果可验证 ｜ [Profiler](packages/profiler/README.md) 提供有界 CPU capture 与离线比较；[Preview](packages/preview/README.md)、浏览器截图和项目测试提供运行证据
  • CLI 优先操作 ｜ [DevKit](packages/devkit/README.md) 统一 forgeax 命令发现、JSON 输入输出和持久实例，使操作可组合、可重复
  • 按需获取上下文 ｜ [Skills](skills/)、包契约与工具描述逐层展开，只加载当前任务需要的知识
  • 结构化失败与恢复 ｜ [Result 与闭合错误 union](packages/types/README.md) 提供 code、预期、提示与详情；能力、执行层级和恢复状态显式可查
[!NOTE]
截图、结构检查和真实 GPU 执行回答不同问题；CPU capture 也不能替代 GPU 性能测量。

设计原则

压缩即智能：减少理解局部行为所需的概念数。 避免重复状态源、额外生命周期和隐式分支。

  • 设计原则 ｜ 在 ForgeAX 中的落实
  • AI 是第一用户 ｜ 优先机器可发现、可调用、可验证的契约；与人类使用习惯冲突时，优先服务 AI
  • 单一事实来源 ｜ World 拥有游戏状态，Renderer 拥有渲染投影，源资产与 Meta 拥有作者事实；其他层读取或推导
  • 从声明推导，避免手动同步 ｜ 材质 paramSchema 推导布局；RenderGraph 从访问声明推导资源依赖与生命周期；Catalog 从项目声明生成
  • 组合能力，保持领域边界 ｜ 物理、渲染、资产、音频各自拥有执行数据；插件负责装配，ECS 负责帧内逻辑
  • 原生生命周期，统一撤销 ｜ Cordis 的 Context / Entry / Fiber 管理能力存在性，inject / provide / effect 表达依赖、服务与清理
  • 显式状态与失败 ｜ 闭合 union、结构化错误、明确的能力缺失与 fallback 报告，减少隐藏分支
  • 构建期准备，运行时消费 ｜ 导入、WGSL 组合与反射、VFX 编译在构建期完成；运行时加载已发布内容

完整约束见 AI-first 设计公理 与 模块职责地图。

架构

一个权威 World。 Runtime 装配服务，Render 维护渲染投影，构建工具生产资源。

flowchart TB

    PROJECT["游戏工程forge.json · 代码 · 资产源"]

    DEVKIT["DevKit / CLI项目操作 · 构建 · 检查"]

    COOK["构建期生产导入 · cook · shader / VFX 编译"]

    ASSETS["AssetRegistryGUID → 已发布内容"]

    APP["App + 原生 Cordisrealm 装配 · 输入 · 帧节奏 · 生命周期"]

    WORLD["ECS World状态 · 时间 · Update / FixedUpdate"]

    DOMAINS["领域系统场景 · 动画 · 物理 · 音频意图 · 网络"]

    RUNTIME["Runtime选择后端与服务 · 装配 Renderer"]

    RENDER["Render持久投影 · extract / prepare / record"]

    GRAPH["RenderGraph资源访问 · pass 依赖 · 生命周期"]

    RHI["RHI不透明句柄 · capabilities"]

    GPU["rhi-webgpu / rhi-wgpu浏览器 WebGPU / wgpu WASM"]

    NULL["rhi-null结构验证"]

    DEBUG["RHI-debugcapture · replay · inspect"]

    PROJECT --> DEVKIT

    DEVKIT --> COOK

    COOK --> ASSETS

    DEVKIT --> APP

    APP --> WORLD

    APP --> RUNTIME

    WORLD  DOMAINS

    RUNTIME --> RENDER

    WORLD -->|"变化证据与场景数据"| RENDER

    ASSETS --> RENDER

    RENDER --> GRAPH

    GRAPH --> RHI

    RHI --> GPU

    RHI --> NULL

    RHI -.->|"可选录制"| DEBUG

渲染与 GPU

  • 子系统 ｜ 关键设计与职责 ｜ 深入阅读
  • Render / RenderGraph ｜ 持久 CPU 投影与能力门控的 GPU Scene；可编程管线与 RenderFeature；图推导依赖、资源使用与生命周期，按声明顺序执行 raster / compute / copy pass ｜ [Render](packages/render/README.md) · [RenderGraph](packages/render-graph/README.md)
  • Shader / Material ｜ 材质 schema 推导参数和绑定布局；WGSL 组合、Naga 验证与反射；运行时查询内容寻址的已编译产物 ｜ [Shader](packages/shader/README.md) · [Compiler](packages/shader-compiler/README.md)
  • GPU VFX ｜ GPU 模拟与间接绘制；代码定义、构建期编译；粒子、ribbon、trail、beam、billboard 与 mesh 效果 ｜ [VFX](packages/vfx/README.md) · [VFX render](packages/vfx-render/README.md)
  • RHI / 后端 ｜ 按 capability 统一浏览器 WebGPU、wgpu WASM 与 null 后端；接口规范对齐，采用不透明句柄且无数学依赖 ｜ [RHI](packages/rhi/README.md) · [wgpu](packages/rhi-wgpu/README.md)

ECS 与多 Worker

[ECS World](packages/ecs/README.md) 统一管理实体、组件、关系、资源和时间；Update / FixedUpdate 系统声明访问与调度。[Scene](packages/scene/README.md) 管理层级与变换，[State](packages/state/README.md) 管理状态所属实体；Renderer 消费 World 变化，维护持久渲染投影。

flowchart LR

    HOST["HostDOM / UI · 输入 · Web Audio · 帧 credit"]

    ENGINE["Engine WorkerWorld + Renderer + Assets + 游戏插件"]

    KERNEL["Kernel Worker 池共享数值列上的 QuerySpan 分片"]

    HOST -->|"输入与一帧执行许可"| ENGINE

    ENGINE -->|"结果与音频意图"| HOST

    ENGINE -->|"满足条件的数值任务"| KERNEL

    KERNEL -->|"完成屏障"| ENGINE
  • 执行层级 ｜ 放置方式 ｜ 约束与适用边界
  • shared ｜ Engine Worker 加持久 Kernel Worker 池 ｜ 需要跨源隔离、SharedArrayBuffer 等能力；仅符合条件的数值任务并行
  • engine-worker ｜ World、Renderer、资产与游戏插件共置于一个 Worker ｜ Host 保留 DOM、输入与音频；需要对应 Worker 渲染能力
  • main-serial ｜ World 与 Renderer 在主线程 ｜ 最直接的串行执行路径
  • auto ｜ 根据能力选择可用层级 ｜ 报告实际选择和原因；显式指定不可用层级则返回错误
[!NOTE]
多 Worker 保持一个逻辑 World，结构变更串行，不传递活对象或拆分 RenderGraph；共享写入部分失败须重建 World。详见 [App 执行契约](packages/app/README.md#execution-tiers) 与 [多线程示例](apps/hello/multithreaded-execution/README.md)。

文本化与脚本化资产

程序生成与参数复用，让内容创作进入代码工作流。 AI 能批量生成资产，也能直接编辑文本、审查 diff 和自动验证。

  • 创作形式 ｜ 用途

（其余章节见仓库 README。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：数据、生命周期、API、工具围绕「AI 能理解、能操作、能自查」设计，而不是事后加个插件。

要点：

  • 定位写在第一行：AI 原生 TypeScript 游戏引擎，**以 AI agent 为第一用户**——数据、生命周期、API 与工具都围绕同一目标设计，让 AI 理解系统、准确操作、检查结果并完成修复
  • 能效口径很具体：目标是让 AI 用更少上下文、更少试错、更短反馈完成更多**经过验证**的游戏开发工作；对应的是 CLI 的 `--json` 输出（观察结果带 `revision`）与「查询活实体 / 录制重放渲染帧 / 逐 draw 逐像素检查」这套 AI 优先调试能力
  • 引擎本体：WebGPU 渲染（材质/光照/阴影/后处理/GPU 粒子/trail 与 beam）、ECS World、2D/3D 物理（Rapier）、动画、输入、音频与网络同步；资产管线支持 glTF/FBX/图像导入，也能用 TypeScript 生成资产并参数化派生变体；已有多款上线游戏与微信小游戏/Steam/Switch 等目标平台

为什么值得看：这是目前少数把「agent 一等公民」落到**每一层接口**的实现：CLI 输出结构化 JSON、状态带 revision、渲染帧可录制重放并逐 draw 检查。对比只在编辑器里加个聊天框的做法，这套接口才让 agent 能真正自查与修复。

中文摘要：ForgeAX 是一个 AI 原生的 TypeScript 游戏引擎，明确把 AI agent 当作第一用户：数据、生命周期、API 与工具都围绕「让 AI 理解系统、准确操作、检查结果并完成修复」来设计。它追求的是「AI 能效」——让 agent 用更少上下文、更少试错、更短反馈，完成更多经过验证的开发工作；落到工程上就是 CLI 全量 `--json` 输出、观察结果带 `revision`，以及「查询活实体 / 录制与重放渲染帧 / 逐 draw 逐像素检查」这套 AI 优先调试能力。引擎本体基于 WebGPU（材质、灯光、阴影、后处理、GPU 粒子），玩法侧是 ECS World 加 Rapier 物理、动画、输入、音频与网络同步，资产管线支持 glTF/FBX/图像导入，也能用 TypeScript 生成资产并派生参数化变体；官方展示了多款基于它上线的游戏，目标平台覆盖微信小游戏、Steam、Switch 等。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：GitHub·ForgeAX（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

（正文为仓库 README 节选，去掉徽章与安装细节。）

Language: 简体中文 · [English](README.en.md)

ForgeAX Engine

AI 原生的 TypeScript 游戏引擎 —— 把想法变成可玩的游戏。

以 AI agent 为第一用户：数据、生命周期、API 与工具围绕同一目标设计，

让 AI 理解系统、准确操作、检查结果并完成修复。

游戏展示 ·

特性 ·

开始使用 ·

AI 能效 ·

引擎架构 ·

深入阅读

[!IMPORTANT]
能效是目标，设计是方法。 让 AI 用更少上下文、更少试错和更短反馈时间，完成更多经过验证的游戏开发工作。

用 ForgeAX 制作

这些游戏都基于本引擎，通过 forgeax CLI 与 AI 优先的工作流创作。

天工战甲 · 机甲动作 / 3D

我的 AI 队友不可能是上古器灵！ · ARPG / 3D

萌宠卡丁车 · 竞速 / 3D

腐坏农场

查看完整游戏展示 →

特性

  • 渲染 — 材质、灯光、阴影、后处理、GPU 粒子、trail 与 beam，基于 WebGPU
  • 玩法 — ECS World、2D/3D 物理（Rapier）、动画、输入、音频与网络同步
  • 资产管线 — 导入 glTF / FBX / 图像，或用 TypeScript 生成资产并参数化派生变体
  • AI 优先调试 — 查询活实体、录制 / 重放渲染帧，逐 draw 逐像素检查
  • CLI 工作流 — 用 forgeax 命令创建、运行、检查与打包游戏
  • 多平台 — 造化工坊、微信小游戏、Steam、Steam Deck、Switch 与 Kubee

开始使用

把引擎和它的 AI 工具链装进你的编辑器：

npx -y @forgeax/game install

支持：Claude Code · Cursor · ChatGPT · Kimi Code · DeepSeek · VS Code。

或直接用引擎新建工程：

pnpm dlx @forgeax/engine project new my-game --template game-3d

cd my-game

pnpm exec forgeax dev start --headless false

game-3d 是第三人称参考工程，empty 是最小起点。先读生成的 README 与技能，再看 [Engine](packages/engine/README.md) 与 [CLI 使用指南](skills/forgeax-engine-cli/SKILL.md)。

运行与验证

pnpm exec forgeax help --tree --json

pnpm exec forgeax project check

pnpm exec forgeax dev status --json

pnpm exec forgeax dev capture --json

pnpm exec forgeax dev stop --json

pnpm exec forgeax project test

pnpm exec forgeax project package --format web-zip

观察结果携带 revision，截图返回 PNG 与报告引用。实体查找、摄像机控制和实例身份约束见 [持久运行实例](packages/devkit/README.md#persistent-live-control)。

从引擎源码 / SDK 构建

工具链版本以 [.nvmrc](.nvmrc)、[.pnpm-version](.pnpm-version)、[.bun-version](.bun-version) 为准。

pnpm install

pnpm build:engine

pnpm test
  • 场景 ｜ 入口
  • 获取 SDK ｜ pnpm dlx @forgeax/engine sdk install ./forgeax-sdk
  • SDK 的 source/engine/ ｜ 独立公开源码面，带 .forgeax-public-distribution 标记与预构建 WASM；运行上述 install / build，无需私有子模块
  • 完整贡献者 checkout ｜ 首次 clone 使用 --recurse-submodules 获取有权限访问的私有资产；完整应用构建运行 pnpm build
  • 单个示例迭代 ｜ pnpm build:app hello/triangle；更大范围验收遵循 Smoke gate

SDK 包含构建产物、模板、技能与 Engine 源码。详见 [SDK 指南](skills/forgeax-engine-sdk/SKILL.md)。

环境要求

  • Node.js ≥ 22.13.0 —— [.nvmrc](.nvmrc) 锁定 22.22.3
  • pnpm 12.10.1，通过 Corepack 启用（corepack enable）
  • Bun ≥ 1.2.0
  • 支持 WebGPU 的浏览器（最新版 Chrome / Edge）

[ECS World](packages/ecs/README.md) 统一管理实体、组件、关系、资源和时间；Update / FixedUpdate 系统声明访问与调度。[Scene](packages/scene/README.md) 管理层级与变换，[State](packages/state/README.md) 管理状态所属实体；Renderer 消费 World 变化，维护持久渲染投影。

flowchart LR

    HOST["HostDOM / UI · 输入 · Web Audio · 帧 credit"]

    ENGINE["Engine WorkerWorld + Renderer + Assets + 游戏插件"]

    KERNEL["Kernel Worker 池共享数值列上的 QuerySpan 分片"]

    HOST -->|"输入与一帧执行许可"| ENGINE

    ENGINE -->|"结果与音频意图"| HOST

    ENGINE -->|"满足条件的数值任务"| KERNEL

    KERNEL -->|"完成屏障"| ENGINE
  • 执行层级 ｜ 放置方式 ｜ 约束与适用边界
  • shared ｜ Engine Worker 加持久 Kernel Worker 池 ｜ 需要跨源隔离、SharedArrayBuffer 等能力；仅符合条件的数值任务并行
  • engine-worker ｜ World、Renderer、资产与游戏插件共置于一个 Worker ｜ Host 保留 DOM、输入与音频；需要对应 Worker 渲染能力
  • main-serial ｜ World 与 Renderer 在主线程 ｜ 最直接的串行执行路径
  • auto ｜ 根据能力选择可用层级 ｜ 报告实际选择和原因；显式指定不可用层级则返回错误

item.title: 世界模型的历史不该整段塞回去：Compression Forcing 用分层历史 token 化，让上下文预算变成可调旋钮 ｜ Compression Forcing: Hierarchical History Tokenization Enables Flexible World Models
item.description:
一句话：世界模型借了视频生成的架构，但目标不同：要能按需压历史、按预算换精度。

要点：

  • 背景差异讲得清楚：世界模型借用视频生成的架构与训练范式，能力提升显著，但两者目标本质不同——视频生成追求观感，世界模型要在有限上下文里支持规划与决策
  • Compression Forcing 把历史做**分层 token 化**：不同时间尺度/重要度的历史用不同粒度表示，从而在推理时按预算选择读多少历史
  • 因此模型可以「灵活」：同一套权重在不同显存/时延条件下给出不同精度-成本折中，而不是固定上下文窗口

为什么值得看：长时程世界模型最实际的约束是上下文预算。把历史压成分层 token，等于把「记多久」从架构常数变成运行时参数——这对要同时上云端与端侧的系统很关键。

中文摘要：世界模型近年借用视频生成的架构与训练范式，生成与预测能力提升明显，但两类模型的目标其实不同：视频生成优化观感，世界模型要在有限上下文里支撑规划与决策。Compression Forcing 因此把「历史」当作可压缩的对象：用分层的方式对历史做 token 化，不同时间尺度或重要度的历史用不同粒度表示，推理时按预算选择读入多少历史。这样同一套权重可以在不同显存与时延条件下给出不同的精度—成本折中，把「能记多久」从架构常数变成运行时可变参数。对需要同时覆盖云端与端侧的长时程世界模型，这是很实用的一层。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

1 Introduction

World models [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; LeCun, 2022)] have emerged as a cornerstone of intelligent decision-making, enabling agents to plan and act by simulating future trajectories conditioned on past observations and actions [(Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2025)]. Recently, by adopting architectural designs and training paradigms from video generation models, world models have achieved unprecedented generative and predictive capabilities across diverse domains [(Huang et al., 2025a; Guo et al., 2025; Pai et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026)]. Despite remarkable progress, the objectives of the two paradigms are fundamentally distinct: video generation optimizes for perceptual fidelity and visual realism, whereas world modeling demands faithfully capturing environment dynamics to support accurate downstream prediction and planning. This distinction raises a natural question: From first principles, how should we design a sequential generative model specifically tailored to the requirements of world model applications?

The use of historical information (e.g. frames) is a central consideration. Standard autoregressive approaches treat history in a binary manner: frames within the context window are fully conditioned upon, while those outside are entirely discarded. Diffusion Forcing [(Chen et al., 2024; Song et al., 2025)] introduces a more flexible alternative by enabling conditioning on partially noised histories at inference time. By interpolating between isotropic Gaussian noise and clean observations, this essentially acts as a frequency-based low-pass filter [(Dieleman, 2024)] of history information, treating partial noising as partial masking. While this mechanism aligns well with perceptual objectives in video generation, where low-frequency structure dominates human sensitivity, it is less aligned with the predictive purposes of world modeling.

Instead, we introduce an alternative principle: partial compression as partial masking. Rather than relying on human-imposed prior for masking, we learn an ordered tokenization where hierarchy is induced by a task-specific objective. By conditioning on variable-length prefixes of this learned sequence, truncation naturally serves as a structured form of partial masking, aligning information decomposition in a data-centric fashion. As a concrete realization of this principle in the context of world modeling, we introduce Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a tokenization method compressing historical information into a hierarchical sequence ordered by dynamic saliency. Through training via a task-specific objective, DAT prioritizes dynamic motions in earlier tokens, whereas static visual information is encapsulated in later tokens.

Building upon this structured tokenization, we further introduce Compression Forcing (CF), a training and sampling framework that operationalizes partial compression as partial masking within diffusion-based world models. Specifically, CF trains a diffusion-based backbone to condition on variable-length prefixes of DAT tokens, enabling prediction under partial history compression (Figure1), used as a residual stream to make dynamics-relevant information accessible to network attention queries (Figure3, Section3.2). Crucially, this architectural design unlocks a novel inference-time capability: Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H, Section3.3). By composing score functions derived from the full history sequence and DAT’s leading subset, the model is equipped with the inference-time flexibility to selectively amplify dynamic-relevant history, effectively suppressing visual nuisances to ensure robust world modeling.

Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that Compression Forcing achieves high-fidelity future prediction across a diverse set of environments and action spaces, including dynamic video forecasting [(Carreira et al., 2018)], 3D game simulation [(Pearce and Zhu, 2022)], and real-world robotic manipulation [(Collaboration, 2023; Google, 2023)]. Moreover, beyond perceptual metrics, we show that our world model translates to stronger downstream policy evaluation [(Li et al., 2025)] performance, verifying Compression Forcing’s effectiveness in aiding downstream decision-making.

Our main contributions are as follows: (1) We propose partial compression as partial masking, a general principle that replaces noise-based history conditioning with learned, task-driven hierarchical compression, applicable beyond world modeling. (2) We instantiate this principle through Compression Forcing, a framework comprising Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT) for saliency-ordered history compression, a diffusion-based backbone for prefix-flexible conditioning, and Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H) for inference-time amplification of dynamics-critical information. (3) We validate the effectiveness of our approach across various domains, demonstrating improved prediction fidelity and effective downstream decision-making performance.

2 Preliminaries and Related Work

2.1 World Models

World Models [(LeCun, 2022; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018)] are predictive models learned by agents to capture the dynamics of the environment, commonly formulated as Partially-Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) [(Kaelbling et al., 1998)]. Concretely, a POMDP is specified by the tuple (S,O,Ω,A,T,r,γ), where the environment evolves over an underlying Markovian state sₜ∈S according to a transition function T:S×A→Δ(S). Since the states sₜ are inaccessible, agents rely on observations oₜ∼Ω(·|sₜ) to perceive the environment. Consequently, the primary objective of world models is to approximate the environment dynamics by estimating the distribution of future observations conditioned on history observations and actions: p_θ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,a_≤t). In this paper, we focus on pixel-space observations O≡\mdmathbbR^H×W×C, and denote each frame as xₜ, following conventions in diffusion-based generation.

2.2 Diffusion Models

Diffusion Models [(Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021)] generate high-fidelity samples by learning to reverse a gradual noise-injection process. Formally, the forward process gradually converts data x⁰∼q into noise x^K∼ℕ(0,I) through a Markov Chain, defined as

q(xᵏ|xᵏ⁻¹)=ℕ(√1-βᵏxᵏ⁻¹,βₖI),

(2.1)

where β_0:K is a pre-defined schedule of noise levels. Sampling is implemented via a reverse process, given by

p_θ(xᵏ⁻¹|xᵏ)=ℕ(μ_θ(xᵏ,k),ₖI).

(2.2)

Rather than explicitly modeling the transition densities, modern approaches often reparameterize this by learning to approximate the noise component added at each step εᵏ=(√1-ᾱₖ)⁻¹(xᵏ-√ᾱₖ x⁰), where αₖ=1-βₖ and ᾱₖ=∏ᵢ₌₁ᵏαᵢ. The training objective is then simplified to minimizing the mean square loss:

L(θ)=\mdmathbbE_k,ε,x⁰[||ε-ε_θ(xᵏ,k)||²].

(2.3)

Sampling is performed by iterative ancestral denoising:

xᵏ⁻¹←(1)/(√αₖ)(xᵏ-(1-αₖ)/(√1-ᾱₖ)ε_θ(xᵏ,k))+σₖw,wherew∼ℕ(0,I).

(2.4)

2.3 Sequential Video Generation and History Guidance

Sequential video generation predicts future frames x_G⁰ conditioned on history observations x_H⁰, enabling long-context video generation with flexible horizon [(Huang et al., 2025b; Cui et al., 2025)] and on-the-fly streaming [(Yin et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025)]. Beyond standard teacher forcing approaches [(Yan et al., 2021)], a prevailing paradigm utilizes Diffusion Forcing[(Chen et al., 2024)] to enable flexible history conditioning compatible with diffusion architectures. By sampling independent noise levels for each frame during training, it allows for diffusion-based auto-regressive rollouts conditioned on clean history. Building on this, DFoT [(Song et al., 2025)] proposes to treat the history sequence as an external control signal [(Ho and Salimans, 2022)], steering future generation by composing score functions conditioned on history interpolated with isotropic Gaussian noise of varying levels k_H:

∇\logpₖ(x_Gᵏ|x_H⁰)+ω[∇\logpₖ(x_Gᵏ|x_H^k_H)-∇\logpₖ(x_Gᵏ)].

(2.5)

By operationalizing guidance through noised history tokens x_H^k_H, this history-conditioning mechanism acts as a frequency-based low-pass filter to enforce conditioning on low-frequency components in history observations. While this frequency-based prior is well-suited for general video synthesis, it is less suited for world modeling, where context differentiation should be governed by predictive salience (i.e., dynamics) rather than spatial frequency.

2.4 Vision Tokenization

Visual tokenization serves as a foundational component of modern generative architectures, compressing high-dimensional observations into computationally tractable representations for backbone processing. Classical generative approaches, such as SD-VAE [(Rombach et al., 2022)] and VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2020)], focus on optimizing perceptual fidelity through continuous regularization or discrete codebooks. Concurrently, emerging research [(Zheng et al., 2025)] demonstrates that representation encoders commonly seen in VLMs [(Oquab et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025)], originally designed for semantic understanding, are also highly effective tokenizers for generative tasks. On the structural front, approaches like Semanticist [(Wen et al., 2025)] and ElasticTok [(Yan et al., 2024)] explore hierarchical tokenization via nested dropout, enabling adaptive reconstruction with variable token counts. However, while recent world models have shown impressive results [(Bar et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024)], they predominantly rely on tokenizers inherited from video generation models, allocating a fixed, uniform number of tokens per frame regardless of their predictive importance. The potential of vision tokenization methods specifically tailored for the predictive needs of world models remains largely unexplored.

3 Compression Forcing

In this section, we introduce Compression Forcing, a general framework for constructing flexible world models via hierarchical history tokenization. Departing from standard approaches [(Alonso et al., 2024; Bar et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a)] that employ history tokenization methods which allocates fixed, uniform budgets for each frame, Compression Forcing compresses history into sequences ordered by dynamic saliency, enabling world modeling with flexible amplification of dynamics-salient history information at inference time.

We first introduce Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses historical observations into hierarchical token sequences ordered by dynamic saliency (Section 3.1). Building on this structured representation, we detail the design of our Diffusion-based World Model Backbone, designed to condition on arbitrary-length prefixes of the DAT compressed token sequences (Section 3.2). Finally, we demonstrate that these designs unlock a novel inference-time capability: Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), a guidance mechanism that allows selective amplification of the role of dynamics-critical history information in generation guidance to facilitate flexible future prediction (Section 3.3).

3.1 Dynamics-Aware Tokenizer (DAT)

Standard vision tokenizers in video generation models [(van den Oord et al., 2017; Esser et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022)] are optimized for pixel-level reconstruction objectives, resulting in representations that allocate uniform budgets per frame. Especially combined with history guidance methods that interpolate between isotropic Gaussian noise and clean images, this creates a “frequency-based bias"[(Dieleman, 2024)] where guidance is performed by enforcing conditioning on low-frequency components, i.e. treating partial noising as partial masking. While this human-imposed prior aligns well with perceptual objectives in video generation, it is misaligned with the predictive demands of world modeling. We propose a more general alternative: partial compression as partial masking. Rather than relying on a fixed frequency-based decomposition, we learn a tokenization whose hierarchy is induced by dynamic saliency, so that truncating the token sequence naturally serves as a task-aligned form of partial masking that effectively retains dynamics-critical information.

Dynamics-Aware Objective.

To realize this principle, we design Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses history frames into a sequence ordered by dynamic saliency, disentangling dynamic motions from static visual nuisances. We achieve this through two complementary decoding objectives: static reconstruction and dynamic prediction, whose relative weighting across variable-length prefixes induces the desired hierarchy. Concretely, an encoder 𝔼 compresses the history frames x_t:t+τ into a latent sequence z_1:L=𝔼(x_t:t+τ),and a diffusion-based decoder D is trained to decode variable-length prefixes z_1:m (m≤L) under two distinct objectives:

  • (a)

    Static Reconstruction: Given only the prefix z_1:m and no external context, the decoder is trained to reconstruct the full clip \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008x_t:t+τ. Since the prefix alone must account for all visual content, this compels tokens to capture a lossless compression of information:

    \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008L_static=\mdmathbbE_k,ε[∥\color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008x_t:t+τ-D(z_1:m,\color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008xᵏ_t:t+τ,a_t:t+τ-1,k)∥²].

    		(3.1)
  • (b)

    Dynamic Prediction: Given the prefix z_1:m and the initial frame xₜ as additional context, the decoder is trained to predict target frames \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0x_t+1:t+τ given z_1:m. Essentially, xₜ allows the model to act as a residual learner, enabling the prefix to only focus on dynamic changes:

    \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0L_dyn=\mdmathbbE_k,ε[∥\color[rgb]0.6523,0,0x_t+1:t+τ-D(z_1:m,\color[rgb]0.6523,0,0xᵏ_t+1:t+τ,\color[rgb]0.5,0,0.5xₜ,a_t:t+τ-1,k)∥²].

    		(3.2)
