    • We enforce the desired hierarchy through a schedule-weighted combination of these two objectives. During training, we randomly sample prefix lengths m∈[1,L] and minimize:

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ=\mdmathbbEₘ[ω(m) \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008L_static+(1-ω(m)) \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0L_dyn],

    		(3.3)

    where ω(m) is a monotonic increasing function. When m is small, the objective is dominated by dynamic prediction \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008L_dyn, compelling leading tokens to prioritize motion dynamics; as m grows, \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0L_static takes over, shifting focus toward full visual reconstruction. This yields a naturally ordered sequence: earlier tokens encode dynamic changes, while later tokens progressively capture static visual details.

    Tokenizer Architecture.

    The tokenizer 𝔼 is built based on the Video Vision Transformer (ViViT) [(Arnab et al., 2021)] architecture. To produce the ordered sequence z_1:L, we append L learnable Slot Tokens at the end of the patchified video sequence. Information flow is regulated through a Hybrid Attention Mechanism: video patch tokens attend bidirectionally to each other but are masked from attending to slot tokens, whereas the i-th slot token zᵢ attends globally to all video patches but causally to preceding slots z_i, any prefix z_1:m remains a self-consistent representation regardless of the truncation point.

    For the diffusion decoder D, we adopt a video diffusion transformer architecture [(Ma et al., 2024)]. Notably, rather than maintaining separate networks for each objective, we implement the Static and Dynamic Decoders as a single model with shared parameters. The distinction between tasks is achieved through noise conditioning [(Chen et al., 2024)]: for Static Reconstruction, we apply identical noise levels to all frames; for Dynamic Prediction, we set the noise level of the condition frame xₜ to zero and identical noise levels to other frames.

    3.2 Prefix-Conditioned World Model Backbone

    Backbone Architecture.

    Building upon the hierarchical history representation produced by DAT, we instantiate the world model backbone W_θ as a conditional diffusion transformer [(Peebles and Xie, 2023; Bar et al., 2024)]. The backbone predicts the next frame xₜ₊₁ conditioned on the agent’s recent actions aₜ and observations x_t-n+1:t. Within each transformer block, we employ a dual-conditioning mechanism: the fine-grained history representation H is injected via cross-attention. Meanwhile, the low-dimensional conditions (action aₜ and diffusion noise level k) are projected into a joint embedding ξ=MLP_act(aₜ)+MLPₙₒᵢₛₑ(k), modulating intermediate features h via AdaLN [(Xu et al., 2019)]:

    AdaLN(h,ξ)=γ(ξ)⊙LayerNorm(h)+β(ξ),

    		(3.4)

    where γ(·) and β(·) are learned scale and shift parameters regressed from ξ.

    History Prefix Conditioning.

    Since DAT accepts a fixed-length input of τ frames, a discrepancy exists between its limited receptive field and the backbone’s need for broader history context (where n>τ). To bridge this gap, we encode the history context x_t-n+1:t using a sliding window approach with a temporal stride s. We extract I=⌊n-τ/s⌋+1 overlapping frame sequences. Each window x⁽ⁱ⁾is independently tokenized by the frozen DAT encoder, and the resulting latents are concatenated to form an encoded global history context Hᵉⁿᶜ:

    Hᵉⁿᶜ=Concat(𝔼(x⁽¹⁾),𝔼(x⁽²⁾),…,𝔼(x^(I)))∈\mdmathbbR^(I·L)×D.

    		(3.5)

    To fully leverage the saliency ordering within H, the world model backbone must learn to condition on variable-length prefixes of each history window. During training, for each encoded window 𝔼(x⁽ⁱ⁾), we independently sample a truncation budgetlₜ∼U[0,L] and construct a binary mask M_lᵢ that preserves the leading lᵢ tokens and masks out the rest. The training objective is defined as:

    L_backbone=\mdmathbbE_k,ε,l[∥ε-ε_θ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ,k,Hᵉⁿᶜ⊙Mₗ,aₜ)∥²],

    		(3.6)

    where l=[l₁,...,l_I] is the budget vector and Mₗ=Concat(M_l₁,...,M_l_I). This training objective equips the backbone with the ability to condition on any prefix length of the the DAT-encoded history, laying the foundation for controllable guidance of history information at inference time detailed in Section 3.3.

    3.3 Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H)

    Given the world model backbone’s flexibility to condition on arbitrary-length prefixes of the DAT-encoded history, we introduce Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), an inference-time guidance mechanism that amplifies dynamics-salient history information through score composition [(Ho and Salimans, 2022)].

    General Guidance Formulation.

    Let H⁽ˡ⁾ denote the encoded history context masked by a budget vector l. The diffusion backbone functions as a learned score estimator s_θ(xₜ₊₁,H⁽ˡ⁾,aₜ,k)≈∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁|H⁽ˡ⁾,aₜ). Given a set of budget vectors {lⱼ}^Jⱼ₌₁, we can guide generation via composing ∇̃\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁) as a weighted sum of conditional scores:

    ∇̃\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ)=∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|∅,aₜ)
    +∑ⱼ₌₁^Jωⱼ·[∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|H^(lⱼ),aₜ)-∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|∅,aₜ)],

    where ωⱼ controls the guidance strength for each component. Essentially, this formulation allows flexible amplification on specific historical information components based on their predictive utility.

    Hierarchical History Guidance.

    As the primary instantiation of this guidance formulation, we propose Hierarchical History Guidance(HG-H), prioritizing high-saliency dynamics over visual details. For every j∈{1,...,J}, we assign a uniform saliency budgetlⱼᵈʸⁿ=[mⱼ,…,mⱼ], where mⱼ≤L represents the truncation threshold across all history windows. The guidance objective simplifies to:

    ∇̃\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ)=∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|∅,aₜ)
    +∑ⱼ₌₁^J-1ωⱼ·[∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|H^lⱼ₊₁ᵈʸⁿ,aₜ)-∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|H^lⱼᵈʸⁿ,aₜ)].

    By guiding generation with truncated prefixes of each history window, HG-H amplifies the influence of motion dynamics encoded in the leading tokens, while suppressing stochastic visual nuances captured by later tokens. Essentially, this operationalizes the partial compression as partial masking principle: the saliency ordering imposed by DAT ensures that prefix truncation serves as a task-aligned form of partial masking, with ωⱼs controlling the degree of amplification at inference time.

    4 Experiments

    In this section, we evaluate Compression Forcing under three distinct world modeling environments, and compare their performance against state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate competitive performance against existing methods in a variety of tasks (Section 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4) and conduct in-depth analysis on tokenization and generation error distribution to understand the effects of DAT and HG-H (Section 4.5). Experimental Details can be found in Appendix C.

    4.1 Experimental Setting

    Environments.

    We evaluate Compression Forcing across three domains: general video prediction, game simulation, and robot manipulation. For video prediction, we use Kinetics-600 [(Carreira et al., 2018)], a large-scale benchmark with diverse, motion-rich videos, utilizing it for history-conditioned video prediction. For game simulation, we adopt Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO), using a 5.5M-frame online gameplay dataset [(Pearce and Zhu, 2022)]. For robot manipulation, we use RT-1 [(Collaboration, 2023)], comprising real-world manipulation tasks such as picking and placing. The action spaces differ across domains: Kinetics-600 is action-free; CS:GO involves discretized keyboard and mouse inputs; and RT-1 uses a 7D continuous end-effector action space. Together, these environments span a broad spectrum of dynamics complexity, action dependence, and visual diversity, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of Compression Forcing across both virtual and real-world settings. Further details can be found in Appendix C.1.

    Evaluation Metrics.

    We evaluate video prediction performance using a variety of widely-adopted metrics, measuring pixel-level fidelity and perceptual similarity. For pixel-level fidelity, we utilize PSNR [(Hore and Ziou, 2010)], and for perceptual similarity, we report SSIM[(Wang et al., 2004)], FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)], FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. Details are shown in Appendix C.2. Finally, we evaluate fidelity to physical dynamics through two downstream metrics deferred to Appendix D: (1) object tracking fidelity, where we sample query points within SAM-generated object masks, track them with CoTracker3 across ground-truth and predicted videos, and measure point-trajectory deviations and penalties for lost tracks, and (2) policy evaluation correlation via Real2Sim evaluation protocol of [Li et al. (2025)], capturing how reliable Compression Forcing is in predicting and ranking policy performance.

    Baselines.

    We compare Compression Forcing against two distinct sets of baselines. The first shares our backbone architecture but conditions on alternative latent spaces for history compression: SD-VAE [(Rombach et al., 2022)], which compresses each frame into a fix-budget representation, and ElasticTok [(Yan et al., 2024)], which compresses video segments into a 1D sequence with leading tokens prioritizing reconstruction fidelity, akin to a learned PCA. The second comprises strong existing world models, including DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)] in CS:GO and DreamerV4 [(Hafner et al., 2025)] in RT-1. Baseline details are shown in Appendix C.3.

    4.2 Compression Forcing for Dynamic Video Generation

    We first evaluate Compression Forcing on action-free video prediction using Kinetics-600 [(Carreira et al., 2018)], a large-scale benchmark featuring diverse, motion-rich natural videos. This setting is particularly informative as it isolates our DAT from action conditioning: the hierarchical structure must emerge purely from visual dynamics, instead of relying on actions to aid dynamic prediction. Across all baselines, we train the diffusion-based backbone for 160k gradient steps. We train the DAT tokenizer for 120k gradient steps and the ElasticTok tokenizer for 175k gradient steps. During inference, we condition our model on 16 history frames, and autoregressively rollout 8 frames. Further training and inference details are provided in Appendix C.5.

    As shown in Table 1, Compression Forcing consistently outperforms all existing baselines in all metrics evaluated. Even without guidance, where the model is exposed to all DAT tokens, the performance of our model consistently outperforms SD-VAE and ElasticTok, showcasing the efficacy of leveraging dynamics-aware tokenization for precise prediction. Performance gains yielded by HG-H further demonstrate that partial compression serves as an effective mechanism for targeted probability steering during inference.

    4.3 Compression Forcing for Game Simulation

    We next evaluate Compression Forcing on action-conditioned game simulation using Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO), a popular 3D first-person shooting game. This environment is particularly challenging due to its highly stochastic dynamics and partial observability, including rapid viewpoint changes, occlusions, and complex player-environment interactions. We adopt the online gameplay dataset of [Pearce and Zhu (2022)] (5.5M frames, 95 hours) and compare against DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)], a strong autoregressive diffusion-based world model. All other baselines share the same backbone architecture and training budget of 550k gradient steps. Both tokenizers ElasticTok and DAT were trained for 100k gradient steps, for the same token dimensions and count per window. During inference, we condition on 4 context frames and autoregressively roll out 12 predicted frames. We use HG-H for models with ElasticTok and DAT tokenizers. Further details are provided in Appendix C.6.

    As shown in Table 2, DAT outperforms the existing popular baseline DIAMOND and other tokenization methods using the same diffusion-backbone architecture and training budget. The results for models with ElasticTok and DAT showcase the effectiveness of HG-H, and its amplification when combined with DAT.

    4.4 Compression Forcing for Robot Manipulation

    Robot Manipulation is another great task to measure a world model’s capability, especially in real environments and physical constraints provided by the RT-1 dataset [(Collaboration, 2023)]. The RT-1 dataset contains 130k episodes and 700+ distinct tasks. We use the same setup for baselines as in CS:GO and train DAT and the other baselines for 80k gradient steps. Both tokenizers ElasticTok and DAT were trained for 40k gradient step, with same number of tokens and their dimension. For evaluation we roll out 16 generated frames from a context of 8 frames. We compare our method against two world-modeling paradigms: DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)] a diffusion-based world model and Dreamer 4 [(Hafner et al., 2025)], a latent dynamics RL agent. Further details and extended visualizations are provided in Appendix C.7 and Appendix D.5.

    As shown in Table 3, we observe a substantial performance gap between these established baselines and our diffusion-backbone variants. While DIAMOND and Dreamer 4 struggle with structural drift and temporal blurring in the RT-1 domain, Compression Forcing maintains high-fidelity reconstructions and motion continuity.

    4.5 Analysis

    Emergence of Hierarchical Features in Tokenization.

    To verify whether our Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT) learns hierarchical representations ordered by dynamic saliency, we visualize cross-attention maps between DAT tokens and image patches in the dynamic decoder. As shown in Figure 2, the attention maps exhibits a clear saliency-ordered hierarchy. Leading tokens assign high attention weights to regions of active motion (the athlete in motion), while higher-index slots progressively shift toward static background elements such as the court boundaries. This confirms that our joint schedule-weighted objective induces DAT to decouple dynamic interactions from visual nuisances, effectively encoding historical information into hierarchical representations.

    Spatial Distribution of Prediction Errors.

    To assess whether this hierarchical tokenization translates to improved prediction in dynamics-critical regions, we analyze per-pixel prediction error across autoregressive rollouts on RT-1 (Figure 6). While baseline tokenizers (SD-VAE and ElasticTok) accumulate substantial and progressive errors around the manipulated target object and the robot’s end-effector, regions most critical for accurate physical interaction, Compression Forcing maintains markedly low error in these dynamic regions throughout the prediction horizon, showcasing practical benefits of aligning history compression with predictive saliency rather than perceptual fidelity. Additional visualizations and further analysis can be found in Appendix D.6

    5 Conclusion

    We introduce Compression Forcing, a novel world modeling framework for built upon the principle of partial compression as partial masking. Through the co-design of Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a prefix-conditioned diffusion backbone, and Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), our approach compresses history into sequences ordered by dynamic saliency and selectively amplifies dynamics-critical information at inference time. Extensive experiments across real-world video forecasting, 3D game simulation, and robotic manipulation demonstrate that Compression Forcing achieves improved prediction fidelity and downstream decision-making performance compared to prior methods, showcasing the broad applicability of our method.

    While we believe this work marks significant progress in rethinking world model design principles in a task-centric manner, there is substantial room for improvement. Promising directions include extending prediction beyond single next-frame to multi-step [(Bar et al., 2024)] or variable-horizon [(Huang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026)] futures, and differentiating truncation budgets between recent and distant history to better capture their distinct roles in prediction. More broadly, we hope that the principle of partial compression as partial masking serves as a useful foundation for future exploration in world models and beyond.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Theoretical Analysis

    We provide a linear motivation for DAT’s residual formulation by comparing low-rank projections of dynamics residuals and raw future sequences.

    Setup.

    Let xₜ∈\mdmathbbRᵈ denote the current observation and Y\triangleqx_t+1:t+τ-xₜ∈\mdmathbbR^d×τ the ground-truth dynamics residual (stacked as columns). We model the raw future as F\triangleqx_t+1:t+τ=xₜ1^⊤+Y, i.e. a static component plus a dynamics component. We assume access to N i.i.d. samples {(xₜ⁽ⁿ⁾,F⁽ⁿ⁾,Y⁽ⁿ⁾)}ₙ₌₁^N, and define the empirical uncentered second-moment matrices:

    C_F\triangleq1/N∑ₙ₌₁^Nvec(F⁽ⁿ⁾) vec(F⁽ⁿ⁾)^⊤,(A.1)
    C_Y\triangleq1/N∑ₙ₌₁^Nvec(Y⁽ⁿ⁾) vec(Y⁽ⁿ⁾)^⊤,(A.2)

    where vec(·) denotes column-wise vectorization. We then denote the static uncentered second-moment matrix as C_S\triangleq1/N∑ₙvec(xₜ⁽ⁿ⁾1^⊤) vec(xₜ⁽ⁿ⁾1^⊤)^⊤.

    Assumption A.1(Static-Dynamics Decomposition).

    For future sequence decomposition of F=S+Y, where S=xₜ1^⊤ is the static component and Y=x_t+1:t+τ-xₜ is the dynamics residual, we assume that the cross second moment 1/N∑ₙvec(S⁽ⁿ⁾) vec(Y⁽ⁿ⁾)^⊤ vanishes, which implies C_F=C_S+C_Y.

    Two projection problems.

    In the projection objectives and errors below, F and Y denote their vectorized forms, and expectations are taken over the empirical sample distribution. We consider learning a rank-m orthogonal projector P∈\mdmathbbR^dτ×dτ (with P^⊤=P, P²=P, rank(P)=m) that best preserves the data under ridge regularization:

  • •

    Raw projection (analogous to ElasticTok / standard tokenization):

    P^*_F=\argmin_rank(P)=m \mdmathbbE[∥F-P F∥²]+λ∥P∥_F².

    		(A.3)
  • •

    Residual projection (analogous to DAT’s dynamic prediction objective):

    P^*_Y=\argmin_rank(P)=m \mdmathbbE[∥Y-P Y∥²]+λ∥P∥_F².

    		(A.4)

    • Proposition A.1(Dynamics prediction gap).

    Under Assumption A.1, assume C_S≠0, λ>0, 1≤mλₘ₊₁(C_Y), where eigenvalues are ordered in descending order. The dynamics prediction error satisfies:

    \mdmathbbE[∥Y-P^*_YY∥²] ≤ \mdmathbbE[∥Y-P^*_FY∥²],

    		(A.5)

    with equality if and only if the selected top-m eigenspaces of C_F and C_Y coincide (i.e. the static component introduces no spectral interference).

    To formally prove Proposition A.1, we first establish two supporting lemmas regarding the properties of orthogonal projectors and second-moment matrices.

    Lemma A.2(Projection Error as Trace).

    For any random vector z with finite second moment C=\mdmathbbE[zz^⊤], the expected reconstruction error using an orthogonal projection matrix P is given by:

    \mdmathbbE[∥z-Pz∥²]=tr((I-P)C).

    		(A.6)

    Proof.

    Using the property ∥v∥²=tr(vv^⊤) and the idempotence of the orthogonal projector (I-P)^⊤(I-P)=(I-P), we have:

    \mdmathbbE[∥z-Pz∥²]=\mdmathbbE[tr((z-Pz)(z-Pz)^⊤)]
    =\mdmathbbE[tr((I-P)zz^⊤(I-P))]
    =tr((I-P)\mdmathbbE[zz^⊤])=tr((I-P)C).(A.7)

    ∎

    Lemma A.3(Optimality of Eigenspace).

    For the regularized rank-m projection problem:

    \argmin_rank(P)=m\mdmathbbE[∥z-Pz∥²]+λ∥P∥_F²,

    		(A.8)

    the optimal solution is P^*=UₘUₘ^⊤, where Uₘ spans the top-m eigenvectors of the uncentered second-moment matrix C.

    Proof.

    For any rank-m orthogonal projector, the Frobenius norm squared is constant:

    ∥P∥_F²=tr(P^⊤P)=tr(P)=m.

    		(A.9)

    Thus, the regularization term λm does not affect the optimization landscape. Then by Lemma A.2, the problem reduces to:

    \argmin_rank(P)=mtr((I-P)C).
item.content:encoded:
一句话：世界模型借了视频生成的架构，但目标不同：要能按需压历史、按预算换精度。

要点：

  • 背景差异讲得清楚：世界模型借用视频生成的架构与训练范式，能力提升显著，但两者目标本质不同——视频生成追求观感，世界模型要在有限上下文里支持规划与决策
  • Compression Forcing 把历史做**分层 token 化**：不同时间尺度/重要度的历史用不同粒度表示，从而在推理时按预算选择读多少历史
  • 因此模型可以「灵活」：同一套权重在不同显存/时延条件下给出不同精度-成本折中，而不是固定上下文窗口

为什么值得看：长时程世界模型最实际的约束是上下文预算。把历史压成分层 token，等于把「记多久」从架构常数变成运行时参数——这对要同时上云端与端侧的系统很关键。

中文摘要：世界模型近年借用视频生成的架构与训练范式，生成与预测能力提升明显，但两类模型的目标其实不同：视频生成优化观感，世界模型要在有限上下文里支撑规划与决策。Compression Forcing 因此把「历史」当作可压缩的对象：用分层的方式对历史做 token 化，不同时间尺度或重要度的历史用不同粒度表示，推理时按预算选择读入多少历史。这样同一套权重可以在不同显存与时延条件下给出不同的精度—成本折中，把「能记多久」从架构常数变成运行时可变参数。对需要同时覆盖云端与端侧的长时程世界模型，这是很实用的一层。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

1 Introduction

World models [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; LeCun, 2022)] have emerged as a cornerstone of intelligent decision-making, enabling agents to plan and act by simulating future trajectories conditioned on past observations and actions [(Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2025)]. Recently, by adopting architectural designs and training paradigms from video generation models, world models have achieved unprecedented generative and predictive capabilities across diverse domains [(Huang et al., 2025a; Guo et al., 2025; Pai et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026)]. Despite remarkable progress, the objectives of the two paradigms are fundamentally distinct: video generation optimizes for perceptual fidelity and visual realism, whereas world modeling demands faithfully capturing environment dynamics to support accurate downstream prediction and planning. This distinction raises a natural question: From first principles, how should we design a sequential generative model specifically tailored to the requirements of world model applications?

The use of historical information (e.g. frames) is a central consideration. Standard autoregressive approaches treat history in a binary manner: frames within the context window are fully conditioned upon, while those outside are entirely discarded. Diffusion Forcing [(Chen et al., 2024; Song et al., 2025)] introduces a more flexible alternative by enabling conditioning on partially noised histories at inference time. By interpolating between isotropic Gaussian noise and clean observations, this essentially acts as a frequency-based low-pass filter [(Dieleman, 2024)] of history information, treating partial noising as partial masking. While this mechanism aligns well with perceptual objectives in video generation, where low-frequency structure dominates human sensitivity, it is less aligned with the predictive purposes of world modeling.

Instead, we introduce an alternative principle: partial compression as partial masking. Rather than relying on human-imposed prior for masking, we learn an ordered tokenization where hierarchy is induced by a task-specific objective. By conditioning on variable-length prefixes of this learned sequence, truncation naturally serves as a structured form of partial masking, aligning information decomposition in a data-centric fashion. As a concrete realization of this principle in the context of world modeling, we introduce Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a tokenization method compressing historical information into a hierarchical sequence ordered by dynamic saliency. Through training via a task-specific objective, DAT prioritizes dynamic motions in earlier tokens, whereas static visual information is encapsulated in later tokens.

Building upon this structured tokenization, we further introduce Compression Forcing (CF), a training and sampling framework that operationalizes partial compression as partial masking within diffusion-based world models. Specifically, CF trains a diffusion-based backbone to condition on variable-length prefixes of DAT tokens, enabling prediction under partial history compression (Figure1), used as a residual stream to make dynamics-relevant information accessible to network attention queries (Figure3, Section3.2). Crucially, this architectural design unlocks a novel inference-time capability: Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H, Section3.3). By composing score functions derived from the full history sequence and DAT’s leading subset, the model is equipped with the inference-time flexibility to selectively amplify dynamic-relevant history, effectively suppressing visual nuisances to ensure robust world modeling.

Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that Compression Forcing achieves high-fidelity future prediction across a diverse set of environments and action spaces, including dynamic video forecasting [(Carreira et al., 2018)], 3D game simulation [(Pearce and Zhu, 2022)], and real-world robotic manipulation [(Collaboration, 2023; Google, 2023)]. Moreover, beyond perceptual metrics, we show that our world model translates to stronger downstream policy evaluation [(Li et al., 2025)] performance, verifying Compression Forcing’s effectiveness in aiding downstream decision-making.

Our main contributions are as follows: (1) We propose partial compression as partial masking, a general principle that replaces noise-based history conditioning with learned, task-driven hierarchical compression, applicable beyond world modeling. (2) We instantiate this principle through Compression Forcing, a framework comprising Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT) for saliency-ordered history compression, a diffusion-based backbone for prefix-flexible conditioning, and Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H) for inference-time amplification of dynamics-critical information. (3) We validate the effectiveness of our approach across various domains, demonstrating improved prediction fidelity and effective downstream decision-making performance.

2 Preliminaries and Related Work

2.1 World Models

World Models [(LeCun, 2022; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018)] are predictive models learned by agents to capture the dynamics of the environment, commonly formulated as Partially-Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) [(Kaelbling et al., 1998)]. Concretely, a POMDP is specified by the tuple (S,O,Ω,A,T,r,γ), where the environment evolves over an underlying Markovian state sₜ∈S according to a transition function T:S×A→Δ(S). Since the states sₜ are inaccessible, agents rely on observations oₜ∼Ω(·|sₜ) to perceive the environment. Consequently, the primary objective of world models is to approximate the environment dynamics by estimating the distribution of future observations conditioned on history observations and actions: p_θ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,a_≤t). In this paper, we focus on pixel-space observations O≡\mdmathbbR^H×W×C, and denote each frame as xₜ, following conventions in diffusion-based generation.

2.2 Diffusion Models

Diffusion Models [(Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021)] generate high-fidelity samples by learning to reverse a gradual noise-injection process. Formally, the forward process gradually converts data x⁰∼q into noise x^K∼ℕ(0,I) through a Markov Chain, defined as

q(xᵏ|xᵏ⁻¹)=ℕ(√1-βᵏxᵏ⁻¹,βₖI),

(2.1)

where β_0:K is a pre-defined schedule of noise levels. Sampling is implemented via a reverse process, given by

p_θ(xᵏ⁻¹|xᵏ)=ℕ(μ_θ(xᵏ,k),ₖI).

(2.2)

Rather than explicitly modeling the transition densities, modern approaches often reparameterize this by learning to approximate the noise component added at each step εᵏ=(√1-ᾱₖ)⁻¹(xᵏ-√ᾱₖ x⁰), where αₖ=1-βₖ and ᾱₖ=∏ᵢ₌₁ᵏαᵢ. The training objective is then simplified to minimizing the mean square loss:

L(θ)=\mdmathbbE_k,ε,x⁰[||ε-ε_θ(xᵏ,k)||²].

(2.3)

Sampling is performed by iterative ancestral denoising:

xᵏ⁻¹←(1)/(√αₖ)(xᵏ-(1-αₖ)/(√1-ᾱₖ)ε_θ(xᵏ,k))+σₖw,wherew∼ℕ(0,I).

(2.4)

2.3 Sequential Video Generation and History Guidance

Sequential video generation predicts future frames x_G⁰ conditioned on history observations x_H⁰, enabling long-context video generation with flexible horizon [(Huang et al., 2025b; Cui et al., 2025)] and on-the-fly streaming [(Yin et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025)]. Beyond standard teacher forcing approaches [(Yan et al., 2021)], a prevailing paradigm utilizes Diffusion Forcing[(Chen et al., 2024)] to enable flexible history conditioning compatible with diffusion architectures. By sampling independent noise levels for each frame during training, it allows for diffusion-based auto-regressive rollouts conditioned on clean history. Building on this, DFoT [(Song et al., 2025)] proposes to treat the history sequence as an external control signal [(Ho and Salimans, 2022)], steering future generation by composing score functions conditioned on history interpolated with isotropic Gaussian noise of varying levels k_H:

∇\logpₖ(x_Gᵏ|x_H⁰)+ω[∇\logpₖ(x_Gᵏ|x_H^k_H)-∇\logpₖ(x_Gᵏ)].

(2.5)

By operationalizing guidance through noised history tokens x_H^k_H, this history-conditioning mechanism acts as a frequency-based low-pass filter to enforce conditioning on low-frequency components in history observations. While this frequency-based prior is well-suited for general video synthesis, it is less suited for world modeling, where context differentiation should be governed by predictive salience (i.e., dynamics) rather than spatial frequency.

2.4 Vision Tokenization

Visual tokenization serves as a foundational component of modern generative architectures, compressing high-dimensional observations into computationally tractable representations for backbone processing. Classical generative approaches, such as SD-VAE [(Rombach et al., 2022)] and VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2020)], focus on optimizing perceptual fidelity through continuous regularization or discrete codebooks. Concurrently, emerging research [(Zheng et al., 2025)] demonstrates that representation encoders commonly seen in VLMs [(Oquab et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025)], originally designed for semantic understanding, are also highly effective tokenizers for generative tasks. On the structural front, approaches like Semanticist [(Wen et al., 2025)] and ElasticTok [(Yan et al., 2024)] explore hierarchical tokenization via nested dropout, enabling adaptive reconstruction with variable token counts. However, while recent world models have shown impressive results [(Bar et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024)], they predominantly rely on tokenizers inherited from video generation models, allocating a fixed, uniform number of tokens per frame regardless of their predictive importance. The potential of vision tokenization methods specifically tailored for the predictive needs of world models remains largely unexplored.

3 Compression Forcing

In this section, we introduce Compression Forcing, a general framework for constructing flexible world models via hierarchical history tokenization. Departing from standard approaches [(Alonso et al., 2024; Bar et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a)] that employ history tokenization methods which allocates fixed, uniform budgets for each frame, Compression Forcing compresses history into sequences ordered by dynamic saliency, enabling world modeling with flexible amplification of dynamics-salient history information at inference time.

We first introduce Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses historical observations into hierarchical token sequences ordered by dynamic saliency (Section 3.1). Building on this structured representation, we detail the design of our Diffusion-based World Model Backbone, designed to condition on arbitrary-length prefixes of the DAT compressed token sequences (Section 3.2). Finally, we demonstrate that these designs unlock a novel inference-time capability: Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), a guidance mechanism that allows selective amplification of the role of dynamics-critical history information in generation guidance to facilitate flexible future prediction (Section 3.3).

3.1 Dynamics-Aware Tokenizer (DAT)

Standard vision tokenizers in video generation models [(van den Oord et al., 2017; Esser et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022)] are optimized for pixel-level reconstruction objectives, resulting in representations that allocate uniform budgets per frame. Especially combined with history guidance methods that interpolate between isotropic Gaussian noise and clean images, this creates a “frequency-based bias"[(Dieleman, 2024)] where guidance is performed by enforcing conditioning on low-frequency components, i.e. treating partial noising as partial masking. While this human-imposed prior aligns well with perceptual objectives in video generation, it is misaligned with the predictive demands of world modeling. We propose a more general alternative: partial compression as partial masking. Rather than relying on a fixed frequency-based decomposition, we learn a tokenization whose hierarchy is induced by dynamic saliency, so that truncating the token sequence naturally serves as a task-aligned form of partial masking that effectively retains dynamics-critical information.

Dynamics-Aware Objective.

To realize this principle, we design Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses history frames into a sequence ordered by dynamic saliency, disentangling dynamic motions from static visual nuisances. We achieve this through two complementary decoding objectives: static reconstruction and dynamic prediction, whose relative weighting across variable-length prefixes induces the desired hierarchy. Concretely, an encoder 𝔼 compresses the history frames x_t:t+τ into a latent sequence z_1:L=𝔼(x_t:t+τ),and a diffusion-based decoder D is trained to decode variable-length prefixes z_1:m (m≤L) under two distinct objectives:

  • (a)

    Static Reconstruction: Given only the prefix z_1:m and no external context, the decoder is trained to reconstruct the full clip \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008x_t:t+τ. Since the prefix alone must account for all visual content, this compels tokens to capture a lossless compression of information:

    \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008L_static=\mdmathbbE_k,ε[∥\color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008x_t:t+τ-D(z_1:m,\color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008xᵏ_t:t+τ,a_t:t+τ-1,k)∥²].

    		(3.1)
  • (b)

    Dynamic Prediction: Given the prefix z_1:m and the initial frame xₜ as additional context, the decoder is trained to predict target frames \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0x_t+1:t+τ given z_1:m. Essentially, xₜ allows the model to act as a residual learner, enabling the prefix to only focus on dynamic changes:

    \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0L_dyn=\mdmathbbE_k,ε[∥\color[rgb]0.6523,0,0x_t+1:t+τ-D(z_1:m,\color[rgb]0.6523,0,0xᵏ_t+1:t+τ,\color[rgb]0.5,0,0.5xₜ,a_t:t+τ-1,k)∥²].

    		(3.2)

    • We enforce the desired hierarchy through a schedule-weighted combination of these two objectives. During training, we randomly sample prefix lengths m∈[1,L] and minimize:

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ=\mdmathbbEₘ[ω(m) \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008L_static+(1-ω(m)) \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0L_dyn],

    		(3.3)

    where ω(m) is a monotonic increasing function. When m is small, the objective is dominated by dynamic prediction \color[rgb]0.1602,0.4375,0.8008L_dyn, compelling leading tokens to prioritize motion dynamics; as m grows, \color[rgb]0.6523,0,0L_static takes over, shifting focus toward full visual reconstruction. This yields a naturally ordered sequence: earlier tokens encode dynamic changes, while later tokens progressively capture static visual details.

    Tokenizer Architecture.

    The tokenizer 𝔼 is built based on the Video Vision Transformer (ViViT) [(Arnab et al., 2021)] architecture. To produce the ordered sequence z_1:L, we append L learnable Slot Tokens at the end of the patchified video sequence. Information flow is regulated through a Hybrid Attention Mechanism: video patch tokens attend bidirectionally to each other but are masked from attending to slot tokens, whereas the i-th slot token zᵢ attends globally to all video patches but causally to preceding slots z_i, any prefix z_1:m remains a self-consistent representation regardless of the truncation point.

    For the diffusion decoder D, we adopt a video diffusion transformer architecture [(Ma et al., 2024)]. Notably, rather than maintaining separate networks for each objective, we implement the Static and Dynamic Decoders as a single model with shared parameters. The distinction between tasks is achieved through noise conditioning [(Chen et al., 2024)]: for Static Reconstruction, we apply identical noise levels to all frames; for Dynamic Prediction, we set the noise level of the condition frame xₜ to zero and identical noise levels to other frames.

    3.2 Prefix-Conditioned World Model Backbone

    Backbone Architecture.

    Building upon the hierarchical history representation produced by DAT, we instantiate the world model backbone W_θ as a conditional diffusion transformer [(Peebles and Xie, 2023; Bar et al., 2024)]. The backbone predicts the next frame xₜ₊₁ conditioned on the agent’s recent actions aₜ and observations x_t-n+1:t. Within each transformer block, we employ a dual-conditioning mechanism: the fine-grained history representation H is injected via cross-attention. Meanwhile, the low-dimensional conditions (action aₜ and diffusion noise level k) are projected into a joint embedding ξ=MLP_act(aₜ)+MLPₙₒᵢₛₑ(k), modulating intermediate features h via AdaLN [(Xu et al., 2019)]:

    AdaLN(h,ξ)=γ(ξ)⊙LayerNorm(h)+β(ξ),

    		(3.4)

    where γ(·) and β(·) are learned scale and shift parameters regressed from ξ.

    History Prefix Conditioning.

    Since DAT accepts a fixed-length input of τ frames, a discrepancy exists between its limited receptive field and the backbone’s need for broader history context (where n>τ). To bridge this gap, we encode the history context x_t-n+1:t using a sliding window approach with a temporal stride s. We extract I=⌊n-τ/s⌋+1 overlapping frame sequences. Each window x⁽ⁱ⁾is independently tokenized by the frozen DAT encoder, and the resulting latents are concatenated to form an encoded global history context Hᵉⁿᶜ:

    Hᵉⁿᶜ=Concat(𝔼(x⁽¹⁾),𝔼(x⁽²⁾),…,𝔼(x^(I)))∈\mdmathbbR^(I·L)×D.

    		(3.5)

    To fully leverage the saliency ordering within H, the world model backbone must learn to condition on variable-length prefixes of each history window. During training, for each encoded window 𝔼(x⁽ⁱ⁾), we independently sample a truncation budgetlₜ∼U[0,L] and construct a binary mask M_lᵢ that preserves the leading lᵢ tokens and masks out the rest. The training objective is defined as:

    L_backbone=\mdmathbbE_k,ε,l[∥ε-ε_θ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ,k,Hᵉⁿᶜ⊙Mₗ,aₜ)∥²],

    		(3.6)

    where l=[l₁,...,l_I] is the budget vector and Mₗ=Concat(M_l₁,...,M_l_I). This training objective equips the backbone with the ability to condition on any prefix length of the the DAT-encoded history, laying the foundation for controllable guidance of history information at inference time detailed in Section 3.3.

    3.3 Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H)

    Given the world model backbone’s flexibility to condition on arbitrary-length prefixes of the DAT-encoded history, we introduce Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), an inference-time guidance mechanism that amplifies dynamics-salient history information through score composition [(Ho and Salimans, 2022)].

    General Guidance Formulation.

    Let H⁽ˡ⁾ denote the encoded history context masked by a budget vector l. The diffusion backbone functions as a learned score estimator s_θ(xₜ₊₁,H⁽ˡ⁾,aₜ,k)≈∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁|H⁽ˡ⁾,aₜ). Given a set of budget vectors {lⱼ}^Jⱼ₌₁, we can guide generation via composing ∇̃\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁) as a weighted sum of conditional scores:

    ∇̃\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ)=∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|∅,aₜ)
    +∑ⱼ₌₁^Jωⱼ·[∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|H^(lⱼ),aₜ)-∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|∅,aₜ)],

    where ωⱼ controls the guidance strength for each component. Essentially, this formulation allows flexible amplification on specific historical information components based on their predictive utility.

    Hierarchical History Guidance.

    As the primary instantiation of this guidance formulation, we propose Hierarchical History Guidance(HG-H), prioritizing high-saliency dynamics over visual details. For every j∈{1,...,J}, we assign a uniform saliency budgetlⱼᵈʸⁿ=[mⱼ,…,mⱼ], where mⱼ≤L represents the truncation threshold across all history windows. The guidance objective simplifies to:

    ∇̃\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ)=∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|∅,aₜ)
    +∑ⱼ₌₁^J-1ωⱼ·[∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|H^lⱼ₊₁ᵈʸⁿ,aₜ)-∇\logpₖ(xₜ₊₁ᵏ|H^lⱼᵈʸⁿ,aₜ)].

    By guiding generation with truncated prefixes of each history window, HG-H amplifies the influence of motion dynamics encoded in the leading tokens, while suppressing stochastic visual nuances captured by later tokens. Essentially, this operationalizes the partial compression as partial masking principle: the saliency ordering imposed by DAT ensures that prefix truncation serves as a task-aligned form of partial masking, with ωⱼs controlling the degree of amplification at inference time.

    4 Experiments

    In this section, we evaluate Compression Forcing under three distinct world modeling environments, and compare their performance against state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate competitive performance against existing methods in a variety of tasks (Section 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4) and conduct in-depth analysis on tokenization and generation error distribution to understand the effects of DAT and HG-H (Section 4.5). Experimental Details can be found in Appendix C.

    4.1 Experimental Setting

    Environments.

    We evaluate Compression Forcing across three domains: general video prediction, game simulation, and robot manipulation. For video prediction, we use Kinetics-600 [(Carreira et al., 2018)], a large-scale benchmark with diverse, motion-rich videos, utilizing it for history-conditioned video prediction. For game simulation, we adopt Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO), using a 5.5M-frame online gameplay dataset [(Pearce and Zhu, 2022)]. For robot manipulation, we use RT-1 [(Collaboration, 2023)], comprising real-world manipulation tasks such as picking and placing. The action spaces differ across domains: Kinetics-600 is action-free; CS:GO involves discretized keyboard and mouse inputs; and RT-1 uses a 7D continuous end-effector action space. Together, these environments span a broad spectrum of dynamics complexity, action dependence, and visual diversity, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of Compression Forcing across both virtual and real-world settings. Further details can be found in Appendix C.1.

    Evaluation Metrics.

    We evaluate video prediction performance using a variety of widely-adopted metrics, measuring pixel-level fidelity and perceptual similarity. For pixel-level fidelity, we utilize PSNR [(Hore and Ziou, 2010)], and for perceptual similarity, we report SSIM[(Wang et al., 2004)], FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)], FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. Details are shown in Appendix C.2. Finally, we evaluate fidelity to physical dynamics through two downstream metrics deferred to Appendix D: (1) object tracking fidelity, where we sample query points within SAM-generated object masks, track them with CoTracker3 across ground-truth and predicted videos, and measure point-trajectory deviations and penalties for lost tracks, and (2) policy evaluation correlation via Real2Sim evaluation protocol of [Li et al. (2025)], capturing how reliable Compression Forcing is in predicting and ranking policy performance.

    Baselines.

    We compare Compression Forcing against two distinct sets of baselines. The first shares our backbone architecture but conditions on alternative latent spaces for history compression: SD-VAE [(Rombach et al., 2022)], which compresses each frame into a fix-budget representation, and ElasticTok [(Yan et al., 2024)], which compresses video segments into a 1D sequence with leading tokens prioritizing reconstruction fidelity, akin to a learned PCA. The second comprises strong existing world models, including DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)] in CS:GO and DreamerV4 [(Hafner et al., 2025)] in RT-1. Baseline details are shown in Appendix C.3.

    4.2 Compression Forcing for Dynamic Video Generation

    We first evaluate Compression Forcing on action-free video prediction using Kinetics-600 [(Carreira et al., 2018)], a large-scale benchmark featuring diverse, motion-rich natural videos. This setting is particularly informative as it isolates our DAT from action conditioning: the hierarchical structure must emerge purely from visual dynamics, instead of relying on actions to aid dynamic prediction. Across all baselines, we train the diffusion-based backbone for 160k gradient steps. We train the DAT tokenizer for 120k gradient steps and the ElasticTok tokenizer for 175k gradient steps. During inference, we condition our model on 16 history frames, and autoregressively rollout 8 frames. Further training and inference details are provided in Appendix C.5.

    As shown in Table 1, Compression Forcing consistently outperforms all existing baselines in all metrics evaluated. Even without guidance, where the model is exposed to all DAT tokens, the performance of our model consistently outperforms SD-VAE and ElasticTok, showcasing the efficacy of leveraging dynamics-aware tokenization for precise prediction. Performance gains yielded by HG-H further demonstrate that partial compression serves as an effective mechanism for targeted probability steering during inference.

    4.3 Compression Forcing for Game Simulation

    We next evaluate Compression Forcing on action-conditioned game simulation using Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO), a popular 3D first-person shooting game. This environment is particularly challenging due to its highly stochastic dynamics and partial observability, including rapid viewpoint changes, occlusions, and complex player-environment interactions. We adopt the online gameplay dataset of [Pearce and Zhu (2022)] (5.5M frames, 95 hours) and compare against DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)], a strong autoregressive diffusion-based world model. All other baselines share the same backbone architecture and training budget of 550k gradient steps. Both tokenizers ElasticTok and DAT were trained for 100k gradient steps, for the same token dimensions and count per window. During inference, we condition on 4 context frames and autoregressively roll out 12 predicted frames. We use HG-H for models with ElasticTok and DAT tokenizers. Further details are provided in Appendix C.6.

    As shown in Table 2, DAT outperforms the existing popular baseline DIAMOND and other tokenization methods using the same diffusion-backbone architecture and training budget. The results for models with ElasticTok and DAT showcase the effectiveness of HG-H, and its amplification when combined with DAT.

    4.4 Compression Forcing for Robot Manipulation

    Robot Manipulation is another great task to measure a world model’s capability, especially in real environments and physical constraints provided by the RT-1 dataset [(Collaboration, 2023)]. The RT-1 dataset contains 130k episodes and 700+ distinct tasks. We use the same setup for baselines as in CS:GO and train DAT and the other baselines for 80k gradient steps. Both tokenizers ElasticTok and DAT were trained for 40k gradient step, with same number of tokens and their dimension. For evaluation we roll out 16 generated frames from a context of 8 frames. We compare our method against two world-modeling paradigms: DIAMOND [(Alonso et al., 2024)] a diffusion-based world model and Dreamer 4 [(Hafner et al., 2025)], a latent dynamics RL agent. Further details and extended visualizations are provided in Appendix C.7 and Appendix D.5.

    As shown in Table 3, we observe a substantial performance gap between these established baselines and our diffusion-backbone variants. While DIAMOND and Dreamer 4 struggle with structural drift and temporal blurring in the RT-1 domain, Compression Forcing maintains high-fidelity reconstructions and motion continuity.

    4.5 Analysis

    Emergence of Hierarchical Features in Tokenization.

    To verify whether our Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT) learns hierarchical representations ordered by dynamic saliency, we visualize cross-attention maps between DAT tokens and image patches in the dynamic decoder. As shown in Figure 2, the attention maps exhibits a clear saliency-ordered hierarchy. Leading tokens assign high attention weights to regions of active motion (the athlete in motion), while higher-index slots progressively shift toward static background elements such as the court boundaries. This confirms that our joint schedule-weighted objective induces DAT to decouple dynamic interactions from visual nuisances, effectively encoding historical information into hierarchical representations.

    Spatial Distribution of Prediction Errors.

    To assess whether this hierarchical tokenization translates to improved prediction in dynamics-critical regions, we analyze per-pixel prediction error across autoregressive rollouts on RT-1 (Figure 6). While baseline tokenizers (SD-VAE and ElasticTok) accumulate substantial and progressive errors around the manipulated target object and the robot’s end-effector, regions most critical for accurate physical interaction, Compression Forcing maintains markedly low error in these dynamic regions throughout the prediction horizon, showcasing practical benefits of aligning history compression with predictive saliency rather than perceptual fidelity. Additional visualizations and further analysis can be found in Appendix D.6

    5 Conclusion

    We introduce Compression Forcing, a novel world modeling framework for built upon the principle of partial compression as partial masking. Through the co-design of Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a prefix-conditioned diffusion backbone, and Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), our approach compresses history into sequences ordered by dynamic saliency and selectively amplifies dynamics-critical information at inference time. Extensive experiments across real-world video forecasting, 3D game simulation, and robotic manipulation demonstrate that Compression Forcing achieves improved prediction fidelity and downstream decision-making performance compared to prior methods, showcasing the broad applicability of our method.

    While we believe this work marks significant progress in rethinking world model design principles in a task-centric manner, there is substantial room for improvement. Promising directions include extending prediction beyond single next-frame to multi-step [(Bar et al., 2024)] or variable-horizon [(Huang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026)] futures, and differentiating truncation budgets between recent and distant history to better capture their distinct roles in prediction. More broadly, we hope that the principle of partial compression as partial masking serves as a useful foundation for future exploration in world models and beyond.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Theoretical Analysis

    We provide a linear motivation for DAT’s residual formulation by comparing low-rank projections of dynamics residuals and raw future sequences.

    Setup.

    Let xₜ∈\mdmathbbRᵈ denote the current observation and Y\triangleqx_t+1:t+τ-xₜ∈\mdmathbbR^d×τ the ground-truth dynamics residual (stacked as columns). We model the raw future as F\triangleqx_t+1:t+τ=xₜ1^⊤+Y, i.e. a static component plus a dynamics component. We assume access to N i.i.d. samples {(xₜ⁽ⁿ⁾,F⁽ⁿ⁾,Y⁽ⁿ⁾)}ₙ₌₁^N, and define the empirical uncentered second-moment matrices:

    C_F\triangleq1/N∑ₙ₌₁^Nvec(F⁽ⁿ⁾) vec(F⁽ⁿ⁾)^⊤,(A.1)
    C_Y\triangleq1/N∑ₙ₌₁^Nvec(Y⁽ⁿ⁾) vec(Y⁽ⁿ⁾)^⊤,(A.2)

    where vec(·) denotes column-wise vectorization. We then denote the static uncentered second-moment matrix as C_S\triangleq1/N∑ₙvec(xₜ⁽ⁿ⁾1^⊤) vec(xₜ⁽ⁿ⁾1^⊤)^⊤.

    Assumption A.1(Static-Dynamics Decomposition).

    For future sequence decomposition of F=S+Y, where S=xₜ1^⊤ is the static component and Y=x_t+1:t+τ-xₜ is the dynamics residual, we assume that the cross second moment 1/N∑ₙvec(S⁽ⁿ⁾) vec(Y⁽ⁿ⁾)^⊤ vanishes, which implies C_F=C_S+C_Y.

    Two projection problems.

    In the projection objectives and errors below, F and Y denote their vectorized forms, and expectations are taken over the empirical sample distribution. We consider learning a rank-m orthogonal projector P∈\mdmathbbR^dτ×dτ (with P^⊤=P, P²=P, rank(P)=m) that best preserves the data under ridge regularization:

  • •

    Raw projection (analogous to ElasticTok / standard tokenization):

    P^*_F=\argmin_rank(P)=m \mdmathbbE[∥F-P F∥²]+λ∥P∥_F².

    		(A.3)
  • •

    Residual projection (analogous to DAT’s dynamic prediction objective):

    P^*_Y=\argmin_rank(P)=m \mdmathbbE[∥Y-P Y∥²]+λ∥P∥_F².

    		(A.4)

    • Proposition A.1(Dynamics prediction gap).

    Under Assumption A.1, assume C_S≠0, λ>0, 1≤mλₘ₊₁(C_Y), where eigenvalues are ordered in descending order. The dynamics prediction error satisfies:

    \mdmathbbE[∥Y-P^*_YY∥²] ≤ \mdmathbbE[∥Y-P^*_FY∥²],

    		(A.5)

    with equality if and only if the selected top-m eigenspaces of C_F and C_Y coincide (i.e. the static component introduces no spectral interference).

    To formally prove Proposition A.1, we first establish two supporting lemmas regarding the properties of orthogonal projectors and second-moment matrices.

    Lemma A.2(Projection Error as Trace).

    For any random vector z with finite second moment C=\mdmathbbE[zz^⊤], the expected reconstruction error using an orthogonal projection matrix P is given by:

    \mdmathbbE[∥z-Pz∥²]=tr((I-P)C).

    		(A.6)

    Proof.

    Using the property ∥v∥²=tr(vv^⊤) and the idempotence of the orthogonal projector (I-P)^⊤(I-P)=(I-P), we have:

    \mdmathbbE[∥z-Pz∥²]=\mdmathbbE[tr((z-Pz)(z-Pz)^⊤)]
    =\mdmathbbE[tr((I-P)zz^⊤(I-P))]
    =tr((I-P)\mdmathbbE[zz^⊤])=tr((I-P)C).(A.7)

    ∎

    Lemma A.3(Optimality of Eigenspace).

    For the regularized rank-m projection problem:

    \argmin_rank(P)=m\mdmathbbE[∥z-Pz∥²]+λ∥P∥_F²,

    		(A.8)

    the optimal solution is P^*=UₘUₘ^⊤, where Uₘ spans the top-m eigenvectors of the uncentered second-moment matrix C.

    Proof.

    For any rank-m orthogonal projector, the Frobenius norm squared is constant:

    ∥P∥_F²=tr(P^⊤P)=tr(P)=m.

    		(A.9)

    Thus, the regularization term λm does not affect the optimization landscape. Then by Lemma A.2, the problem reduces to:

    \argmin_rank(P)=mtr((I-P)C).

item.title: 「渲染图好看」不等于「资产能用」：这篇用三视图 + 冻结 ViT 分诊，把 3D 资产可用性做成可自动筛的判据 ｜ Is This 3D Asset Usable? Beyond the Beauty Render for Asset Curation
item.description:
一句话：RGB 里看着合理的资产，可能藏着断开的几何、糟糕的 UV 与导入后解析失败的材质。

要点：

  • 问题非常工程：3D 资产库里「能收集」不等于「能复用」——它在场景拼装、编辑、渲染、游戏生产与训练数据构建里都可能翻车
  • 失效模式具体：一张好看的 RGB 渲染可以掩盖断开/悬浮的几何、混乱的 UV 组织、以及导入后无法正确解析的材质
  • 作者提出 Diagnostic Rendered Evidence（DRE）：把 beauty、wireframe、UV 缝 + wireframe 三种视图对齐，交给按检查项专用的冻结 ViT 分类器打分，再做后期融合

为什么值得看：AI 批量生成/爬取资产的最大成本是「人肉筛」。把可用性拆成可视证据 + 专用分类器，意味着资产入库前就能自动拦掉断几何、坏 UV 与坏材质——这正是资产管线最该自动化的一段。

中文摘要：大型 3D 资产库让「收集」变容易，却让「能否可靠复用」变难：同一个资产要在场景拼装、编辑、渲染、游戏生产与训练数据构建中都成立。问题在于一张看起来合理的 RGB 渲染图，完全可能掩盖断开的几何、混乱的 UV 组织，或导入后解析失败的材质。作者提出 Diagnostic Rendered Evidence（DRE）：把「美观渲染」「线框」「UV 缝叠加线框」三种视图对齐起来，分别交给按检查项冻结的 ViT 分类器打分，再做后期融合得到可用性判断。对依赖批量生成或抓取资产的管线，这等于在入库前加了一道自动分诊。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

Is This 3D Asset Usable? Beyond the Beauty Render for Asset Curation

Abstract

Large 3D repositories make it easy to collect assets, but difficult to determine whether they can be reused reliably across scene assembly, editing, rendering, game production, and training-data construction. An asset can look plausible in RGB while hiding disconnected geometry, problematic UV organization, or materials that fail to resolve correctly after import. We introduce Diagnostic Rendered Evidence (DRE): aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views scored by pass-specific frozen ViT classifiers and combined through late fusion. On 1,234 human labeled TexVerse assets, nested grouped evaluation achieves 86.36% balanced accuracy and 88.32% bad-asset recall. On a separate, balanced 764 external reference test, DRE achieved 88.9% balanced reference-label accuracy. Our method requires only an imported asset and renderer-derived evidence, without repository identity, creator, popularity, text, or source metadata at inference. Our results support cross-corpus portability and show that purpose built diagnostic views expose defects that just the beauty views can miss. Webpage: https://rbz-99.github.io/is-this-3d-asset-usable/

1 Introduction

Consider a common workflow where we download a model from a large 3D repository. It can look perfectly fine and still be difficult to use. A few RGB views look convincing: the shape is recognizable, the texture appears detailed, and nothing is obviously broken. Yet once the asset enters a 3D workflow, different problems can emerge. The mesh may contain disconnected or irregular geometry, the UV layout may complicate texturing, or materials may fail to resolve correctly after import. None of these problems necessarily prevents the asset from producing an attractive preview.

Repository assets are increasingly reused as structured 3D objects: retrieved and arranged into scenes [25, 1, 17], edited [11], rigged for animation [15], or used in modern image-to-3D pipelines that explicitly represent geometry, UVs, textures, and PBR attributes [3, 19, 23]. Across these uses, plausible RGB appearance does not guarantee reliable reuse.

Large repositories such as ShapeNet [4], Objaverse and Objaverse-XL [8, 7], and TexVerse [26] make this a repository-scale curation problem: How can we determine whether a 3D asset is fit for reuse before selecting it from a large repository?

This requires expert review, that considers appearance, geometry, UV structure, and material behavior. We therefore construct a 1,234-asset TexVerse set annotated by 3D researchers and introduce diagnostic rendered evidence: aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views that expose complementary properties of the same asset. Separate models score each evidence type before late fusion produces the final keep/reject decision. Our scope is operational fitness for reusable textured/PBR assets rather than universal aesthetic quality or asset provenance. On our human-labeled assets, our method reaches 86.36% balanced accuracy and 88.32% bad-asset recall. Controlled ablations show that the structural diagnostic passes provide information beyond a matched beauty-only representation. Our contributions are: 1: We introduce diagnostic rendered evidence for 3D asset curation using aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views. 2: We develop a robust rendering pipeline for heterogeneous repository assets, including guarded material fallbacks and explicit material-resolution provenance. 3: We provide a 1,234-asset expert-annotated benchmark for reusable textured/PBR assets, with a keep/reject rubric covering geometry, UV, material, render, and composition failures.

2 Related Work and Scope

3D assets as reusable components: Recent systems increasingly treat existing 3D assets as reusable components. Holodeck retrieves and arranges Objaverse assets for scene generation [25]; Open-Universe similarly retrieves meshes from uncurated databases and optimizes their placement [1]; and Lay-A-Scene studies object arrangement [17]. Existing assets are also edited [11] and automatically rigged for animation [15]. These settings motivate evaluating asset properties that are not fully captured by a beauty render.

3D curation and quality assessment: Objaverse++ and MeshFleet use filtering and human review to construct higher-quality 3D corpora [14, 2], while generative-3D benchmarks evaluate geometry, texture, and cross-view consistency [13, 20, 27, 10]. Perceptual mesh-quality studies likewise show that geometry and texture jointly affect human judgments [12, 16]. Full-reference metrics assume a known reference [16, 24]; repository curation instead requires judging a single asset without one.

Structured evidence for asset quality: Modern 3D systems explicitly represent geometry, UVs, and materials. Hunyuan3D separates mesh and texture generation [28], SF3D predicts UV-unwrapped geometry and material properties [3], and AssetGen reconstructs geometry and PBR appearance [19]. Related work further models UV and material structure explicitly [5, 22, 23], while UV-specific methods motivate interpreting parameterization in surface context [21, 18]. Our method uses rendered views of these structures as no-reference evidence for asset curation.

3 Methodology

Evidence Generation and Provenance: For each imported GLB, we render synchronized diagnostic passes using fixed camera poses, lighting, background, and framing. Four aligned views are generated per pass and scored independently before late fusion. The beauty pass captures overall appearance and visible rendering or material failures, but may hide structural defects through texture, shading, and lighting. The wireframe pass exposes mesh structure, including disconnected components, irregular triangulation, excessive density, and geometric clutter. These patterns are treated as evidence rather than fixed quality rules. The UV-seam-plus-wireframe pass overlays UV boundaries on the mesh, allowing seam organization to be interpreted in its 3D surface context rather than from a flattened atlas alone.

Repository-Agnostic Evidence: DRE is designed around information that can be obtained from an imported asset rather than from a particular repository. The renderer uses no asset ID, creator, source label, caption, popularity statistic, or repository-specific metadata. It first resolves standard Principled-BSDF base-color inputs, then follows supported graph-connected image textures and guarded fallbacks; when resolution is not possible, it records an explicit unresolved-material state rather than inventing a material interpretation. We also generated 2D UV-island layouts and measurements such as coverage, angular distortion, and texel density. These signals were reviewed by 3D experts and evaluated in additional classifier configurations, but provided little improvement over the surface-aligned diagnostic views. We therefore retain them for review and audit rather than classifier input, particularly since UV packing conventions vary across asset categories and authoring workflows. Figure 1 illustrates the synchronized evidence available to both the reviewer and the classifier. No individual diagnostic pass is treated as ground truth. Human review separates several kinds of concern: low overall curation value, geometry integrity or clutter, UV organization, material-resolution anomalies, missing evidence, and other import or composition problems.

Multi-view Scoring and Fusion: For pass m and view v, a frozen ImageNet ViT-B/16 encoder [9] produces z_m,v∈ℝ⁷⁶⁸. We summarize the four aligned views with their feature-wise mean and standard deviation. A standardized, class-balanced logistic-regression model is then trained separately for beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe evidence. Each model produces a probability pₘ(good) describing how strongly that particular type of evidence supports keeping the asset.

4 Learning and Evaluation

We use TexVerse [26] to create our set under CC BY, CC BY-SA, or CC0 licenses. Our supervised set contains 1,234 assets annotated by expert 3D researchers: 866 good and 368 bad. An additional 6,685 assets based on the deterministic render QA and their metadata are used as less weighted auxiliary training data. We use five-fold nested stratified group cross-validation, grouping by creator or source where available. Inner folds train the pass-specific classifiers, generate out-of-fold predictions for fusion, and select weak-label weights, regularization, pass combinations, and the decision threshold. Auxiliary samples sharing a group with the held-out fold are excluded. Metadata and strict full-PBR inventory provide weak-label sources, while terms such as Rodin, photogrammetry, or scan identify low-weight negative candidates rather than evaluation labels. Face count, texture resolution, creator, and source are retained only for audit and stratification. Table 1 reports outer-fold predictions.

Modality Ablation: Table 1 keeps the labels, grouped folds, ViT representation, classifier family, fusion method, and threshold-selection protocol fixed while changing only the render evidence. UV-seam-wire achieves the highest balanced accuracy, while the full three-pass model gives the highest bad recall and fewest false accepts. Thus, the benefit is not simply due to using more views: the structural passes provide information complementary to beauty renders. We exclude material-only views because their appearance is difficult to separate from renderer behavior. A gray render, for example, may indicate an intentional material, scalar input, vertex color, missing texture, or failed graph resolution. Material behavior is therefore audited separately rather than used as a learned visual modality.

Baselines: The matched beauty-only ViT in Table 1 is our primary representation baseline. It keeps the labels, groups, backbone, classifier, fusion, and threshold-selection protocol fixed, isolating the contribution of diagnostic evidence. We also evaluate the released Objaverse++ [14] on our dataset using its 40-view protocol. Our method uses no popularity, creator, source, or text features at inference and requires 12 diagnostic images per asset, compared with 40 RGB views for Objaverse++. Objaverse++ outputs are mapped as High/Superior = keep and Low/Medium = reject.

Our method retains 731 of 866 good assets and admits 43 of 368 bad assets. Objaverse++ retains 245 good assets and admits 62 bad assets. A paired exact McNemar test gives p=1.31×10⁻¹⁰², with 568 assets correct only for our method and 63 correct only for Objaverse++. Further we additionally evaluate cross-corpus portability on a fixed, balanced external reference set of 382 good and 382 bad assets from strict-PBR ABO [6] and Objaverse assets. DRE achieves 88.9% balanced reference-label accuracy, with 80.4% good-reference recall and 97.4% bad-reference recall. Objaverse got about 47.0% balanced reference-label accuracy: although it retains 88.7% of the strict-PBR reference assets, it rejects only 5.2% of the bad assets, admitting 94.8% as good.

Figure 2 shows how diagnostic passes make different failure modes inspectable. Some failures are visible in conventional appearance renders, while others become clear only when the same camera poses expose geometry or UV seams. The diagnostic representation does not turn mesh density or seam count into hard rules. It gives reviewers and the classifier evidence that can be interpreted in the context of the asset and its intended downstream use.

5 Conclusion

A beauty render can indicate whether an asset looks plausible, but not whether it is operationally fit for reliable reuse. Diagnostic evidence for appearance, topology, UV structure, and material resolution makes the relevant conditions inspectable from the asset itself. By separating these evidence types before fusion, DRE provides a repository-agnostic basis for quality-controlled asset selection for various workflows.

（参考文献见原文。）
