item.description:
一句话：静态绑骨质量好但不能控骨骼数、逐帧套用会抖；4D 方法又要逐序列优化。

要点：

  • 现状痛点对称：静态 3D 绑骨方法质量不错，但对骨骼数量控制有限，逐帧套到动态网格上还会时序不稳；4D 方法则通常依赖昂贵的逐序列优化
  • FlowRig 是模板无关、数据高效的统一框架：用 flow matching 同时支持静态 3D 与动态 4D 网格的骨架生成
  • 目标是给出一个前馈解，既不逐序列优化，也不在动态序列上抖动

为什么值得看：角色管线里绑骨是最贵的手工环节之一，而「有动作的扫描」越来越多（4D 捕捉、体积视频）。能用同一个前馈模型覆盖 3D 与 4D，意味着扫描进来的动态资产可以直接拿到可驱动骨架。

中文摘要：自动绑骨对静态 3D 网格与动态 4D 网格都是基础任务，但现有方法没有给出统一的前馈解：静态 3D 绑骨质量不错，却对骨骼数量缺乏控制，把它逐帧套到动态网格上还会出现时序不稳定；4D 方法则往往依赖昂贵的逐序列优化。FlowRig 提出模板无关、数据高效的统一框架，用 flow matching 同时生成 3D 与 4D 网格的骨架，从而避免逐序列优化，并改善动态序列上的稳定性。对同时处理扫描静态资产与 4D 捕捉内容的角色管线，这减少了一套专属流程。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

FlowRig: Unified Skeleton Generation for
3D and 4D Meshes via Flow Matching

Abstract

Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose FlowRig, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, FlowRig generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that FlowRig achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.

1 Introduction

Automatic rigging is a core problem in computer graphics, which turns raw geometry into animatable assets. This need spans both static 3D and dynamic 4D meshes: 3D assets require high-quality, controllable skeletons for downstream animation workflows, while 4D assets additionally require temporal consistency across time. At the same time, temporally coherent 4D meshes are becoming increasingly available from modern reconstruction and generation pipelines. Recent systems can recover or synthesize dynamic 4D geometry directly from videos or generative models, making 4D meshes a practical representation rather than a niche output [(Sabathier et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025b; Xie et al., 2026)]. However, geometry alone is not enough for downstream animation, editing, simulation, and control. To make these assets truly useful, we need a unified feedforward rigging model that works for both 3D and 4D meshes, produces informative skeletons, supports controllable bone complexity, and remains stable across diverse poses and motions.

Unfortunately, this capability is still missing. On one side, existing rigging methods are predominantly designed for static 3D inputs, ranging from classical optimization systems [(Baran and Popović, 2007)] to modern feedforward and autoregressive models [(Xu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026a)]. These methods have substantially improved 3D rigging quality and efficiency, but they are fundamentally static, and many of them provide limited control over skeleton density or bone count for downstream applications. When applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes, they also typically fail to maintain temporal consistency [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. On the other hand, existing 4D methods mainly focus on per-sequence optimization, reconstruction, or motion transfer [(Li et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026a; Dabhi et al., 2026; Muralikrishnan et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026)]. While these methods are valuable, they do not provide a unified feedforward rigging solution that bridges controllable 3D rigging, dynamic 4D reconstruction, and predictive temporal reasoning within one framework.

Building such a unified model is challenging for two reasons. First, many strong static rigging methods are autoregressive, which makes explicit bone-count control less natural and global temporal reasoning inefficient for dynamic sequences. Second, paired 4D mesh-skeleton data remains far scarcer than static 3D rigging data, so a practical model must learn temporal consistency from limited 4D supervision while preserving strong 3D rigging quality.

In this work, we propose FlowRig, a data-efficient feedforward framework for unified skeleton generation on 3D and 4D meshes. Built on flow matching, FlowRig predicts temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in one pass, while naturally handling 3D rigging with explicit skeleton-count control. The model also includes a graph head for temporally consistent topology prediction and an uncertainty head for confidence estimation. The masking-based training further enables 4D prediction including interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited 4D supervision, we initialize from large-scale 3D rigging data and then adapt to mid-scale 4D rigging data. Experiments show that FlowRig achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose FlowRig, a unified flow-matching model for controllable 3D/4D skeleton generation.

  • •

    We introduce a 3D-to-4D curriculum for data-efficient training under limited 4D supervision.

  • •

    We achieve strong 3D rigging, high-quality 4D reconstruction, and flexible 4D prediction.

    • 2 Related Work

    Static Automatic Rigging and Skinning. Automatic rigging has been studied extensively in the static 3D setting. Early methods relied on template fitting and per-shape optimization, as in Pinocchio [(Baran and Popović, 2007)], while later data-driven approaches improved both speed and generalization. RigNet [(Xu et al., 2020)] introduced graph neural networks for direct skeleton and skinning prediction from meshes. Subsequent methods such as UniRig [(Zhang et al., 2025a)], RigAnything [(Liu et al., 2025a)], ARMO [(Sun et al., 2025a)], Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)], and Skin Tokens [(Zhang et al., 2026b)] further improved structural validity through autoregressive or language-model-style generation [(Song et al., 2025b)]. These methods are strong baselines for static 3D rigging, but not for general-purpose 4D rigging. In particular, autoregressive generation is less suitable for 4D sequences, where one must reason jointly over skeletal slots and time; applying static models per-frame often leads to temporal flickering and inconsistent topologies [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. Their discrete formulation can also make skeleton density control harder for downstream 4D use.

    Dynamic and 4D Rigging. As 4D meshes become more accessible, there is growing interest in rigging dynamic assets directly from videos or mesh sequences. Existing 4D rigging-related methods mainly fall into two categories. The first consists of per-sequence optimization methods, such as AKD [(Li et al., 2025)], RigGS [(Yao et al., 2025b)], AniMimic [(Xie et al., 2026)], GaussiAnimate [(Wang et al., 2026a)], and RAT4D [(Dabhi et al., 2026)], which align articulated structure to multi-frame observations or dynamic 3D representations. These methods can achieve high fidelity, but their reliance on per-scene optimization makes them computationally expensive and less suitable for scalable deployment. The second involves consistency-oriented extensions of static riggers, such as SPRig [(Wang et al., 2026b)], which improve cross-frame consistency through additional self-supervision. While promising, these methods do not yet provide a unified feedforward framework for raw 4D mesh sequences that supports both reconstruction and prediction. Related animation methods, including Gaussian bone representation, zero-shot pose transfer and morphology-aware motion transfer [(Guo et al., 2025; Muralikrishnan et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a)], are complementary rather than direct solutions to general-purpose 4D rigging.

    4D Mesh Availability and Upstream Geometry Models. Our work is motivated in part by the increasing availability of temporally coherent 4D meshes from upstream reconstruction and generation systems. The field has seen rapid expansion, ranging from text- and image-to-4D generation [(Yin et al., 2023; Ling et al., 2024; Bahmani et al., 2024a; Miao et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024a; Bahmani et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2023a; Gao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2025; Nag et al., 2025)] to video-based dynamic reconstruction [(Jiang et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2024)]. In particular, recent methods such as ActionMesh [(Sabathier et al., 2026)] and AniMimic [(Xie et al., 2026)] show that high-quality dynamic geometry can now be derived from monocular videos and learned priors. While these systems expand the supply of dynamic geometry, they do not solve the downstream rigging problem. Instead, they highlight the need for a feedforward 4D rigging model that converts temporally aligned geometry into informative and animation-ready skeletons. In this sense, our method is complementary: upstream models provide the dynamic geometry, while FlowRig provides the rigging for downstream animation and control.

    Generative Models for 3D and 4D Assets. A separate line of work studies the co-generation of geometry and rigging information. AniGen [(Huang et al., 2026)] generates animatable 3D assets together with rigging information, while AKD [(Li et al., 2025)] uses score distillation to generate articulated 4D assets from images or text. Related directions include skeleton-guided 3D generation [(Xu et al., 2025)], creative articulated asset generation [(Lu et al., 2026)], sketch-based rigging [(Zhao et al., 2026)], and rig-based generative synthesis of dynamic 3D Gaussians [(Wu et al., 2026)]. However, these works are not for general-purpose feedforward rigging of raw 4D mesh sequences. Instead, our focus is to take 3D or 4D geometry as input and produce temporally consistent skeletons with controllable complexity and prediction capability, making our setting complementary to asset generation.

    3 Proposed Method

    3.1 Problem Formulation

    Let M_1:N=(m₁,…,m_N) denote a observation sequence of mesh mᵢ, where each frame is represented as a sampled point cloud with normals Pᵢ∈ℝ^Nₚ×6 and Nₚ is the size of the point cloud. Our goal is to predict a corresponding skeleton sequence S_1:N=(S₁,…,S_N), where each Sᵢ is a set of bones with 3D endpoints and a tree topology. We consider static and dynamic tasks below.

    Static skeleton reconstruction. When N=1, we generate a skeleton set S₁ conditioned on a single mesh observation P₁. Formally, we model the conditional distribution p(S₁|P₁).

    Dynamic skeleton reconstruction and prediction. Given observed frames O⊆{1,…,N} and observations ℙ_O={Pᵢ}_i∈O, we generate the full skeleton sequence using p(S_1:N|ℙ_O). Reconstruction corresponds to O={1,…,N}, while prediction corresponds to O⊂{1,…,N}.

    3.2 Flow Matching on An Optimal-Transport Path

    Instead of learning a reverse denoising process as in diffusion models, flow matching learns a continuous-time vector field that transports noise to data. Let x₀ denote a clean sample and x₁∼ℕ(0,σ²I) be Gaussian noise. We use the optimal-transport straight-line path xₜ=(1-t)x₀+tx₁ for t∈(0,1), whose target velocity is constant: v^⋆(xₜ,t)=x₁-x₀. Given mesh-derived conditioning tokens c, the network M predicts the velocity field v̂=M(xₜ,t,c;Θ) and is trained to match v^⋆ with mean-squared error, together with our matching and auxiliary losses. At inference time, we start from xₜ₌₁∼ℕ(0,σ²I) and integrate the learned ODE from t=1 to t=0 with an Euler solver: x_t-Δt=xₜ-Δt·v̂(xₜ,t,c), yielding the clean sample x₀.

    3.3 4D Skeleton Flow Matching Model

    Figure 2 shows an overview of FlowRig. Given a static mesh or a mesh sequence, we encode each frame with the frozen Michelangelo encoder [(Zhao et al., 2023b)] to obtain mesh conditioning tokens c∈ℝ^N×Lₘ×H. In parallel, we initialize a fixed set of noisy skeleton slots xₜ∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7 and optionally inject a target skeleton-count condition to control the number of generated bones. We set Lₛ=128 to cover all training instances, similar to prior slot-based methods such as Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)], and allow N to vary by sampling different window lengths during training. The DiT embeds the skeleton slots into H-dimensional tokens, concatenates them with the mesh tokens, and processes the resulting sequence of length N·(Lₛ+Lₘ) with temporal rotational positional encoding (RoPE) using the frame index as the shared temporal reference. It then performs slot-based set prediction over the full sequence and predicts a velocity tensor v̂∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7, which is decoded into up to Lₛ bones per frame as 7D slot states x₀∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7, where each slot is x_0,i,j=[e_i,j,p_i,j,0,p_i,j,1] with an existence indicator e∈{0,1} and two 3D endpoints p_i,j,0,p_i,j,1∈ℝ³. After the transformer predicts the aligned skeleton slots, a graph head infers the kinematic tree and an uncertainty head estimates confidence, producing the final controllable 3D or 4D rigging output.

    Besides the skeleton head, we use two additional lightweight heads: a graph head and an uncertainty head. A naive way to build a skeleton tree is to connect bones by distance, but this can lead to unstable topology over time as the joints move. Instead, the graph head predicts parent indices from the hidden features {hᵢ} and the predicted skeletons {x̂ᵢ}, yielding a more temporally consistent tree structure. The uncertainty head takes the hidden features as input and predicts per-frame per-bone uncertainty σ̂∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7. Intuitively, it estimates how reliable each generated bone is, so we can use uncertainty as a score when drawing multiple samples and select the most confident result.

    Skeleton-count conditioning and classifier-free guidance (CFG). In addition to mesh tokens, we condition the model on a scalar skeleton or bone count y, which serves as a guidance label. During training we apply classifier-free guidance by randomly dropping the condition with probability p_drop, that is, replacing y with an unconditional token y=-1 in the embedding layer. The conditional and unconditional predictors share parameters and differ only in the presence of y:

    v̂_cond=M(xₜ,t,c,y;Θ), v̂_uncond=M(xₜ,t,c,-1;Θ).

    		(1)

    During inference, we form the guided velocity with CFG scale s as v̂_cfg=v̂_uncond+s·(v̂_cond-v̂_uncond), and integrate the ODE with v̂_cfg.

    3.4 Training Objective

    Our training objective combines flow matching with the auxiliary supervision terms.

    One-to-one supervision via sequence Hungarian matching. To handle variable ground-truth bone counts while preserving a fixed tensor interface, we follow the DETR-style one-to-one supervision [(Carion et al., 2020)]. Each Sᵢ is represented using Lₛ permutation-invariant skeleton slots, and the model is trained with hungarian matching for each predicted and ground-truth skeleton pair. For each frame we extract raw endpoints gᵢ∈ℝ^N_gt×6 and pad them to a fixed tensor size. Since slot indices are permutation-invariant, we compute a single assignment per sequence, shared across frames, using the Hungarian algorithm. We first recover a predicted clean state by

    x̂₀=xₜ-t v̂∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7,(2)

    and build a cost matrix between slot endpoints p̂_j,0 and p̂_j,1 and the ground-truth endpoints gⱼ. To align the static and dynamic training objectives, we set the anchor frame i=1 for hungarian matching in all training stages. The matching cost is a weighted sum of endpoint Euclidean distance. The resulting assignment maps each ground-truth bone to one slot, producing matched targets x̃.

    Flow matching loss. The primary objective is a weighted flow-matching mean-squared error on the matched optimal-transport velocity:

    L_FM=1/NLₛ∑_i,jw_i,j \lVertv̂_i,j-ṽ^⋆_i,j\rVert₂², ṽ^⋆=x₁-x̃₀.(3)

    where per-slot weights w∈ℝ^N×Lₛ upweight matched slots and control supervision on empty slots with less focus. Intuitively, we set the unmatched slot endpoints with zero weight since they have no contribution to the final results, thus forcing the model to focus on the matched pairs.

    Uncertainty loss. To quantify the confidence of skeletons, we add a Gaussian negative log-likelihood (NLL) term to estimate the uncertainty of bone existence and the joint positions. Following IDDPM [(Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021)], we stop gradients through the mean prediction in the NLL branch:

    L_NLL=1/NLₛ∑_i,jw_b,j(\lVertsg(v̂_b,i,j)-ṽ^⋆_b,i,j\rVert₂²/(σ̂_v,b,i,j²+ε)+\log(σ̂_v,b,i,j²+ε)),

    		(4)

    where ε is a small value and sg(·) denotes the stop-gradient operator. This way, L_NLL can guide σ̂² without affecting the training of transformer backbone and skeleton head.

    Graph head loss. To build the kinematic tree for the generated skeleton, we supervise a parent index classifier over slots. Specifically, to handle temporal aggregation and derive a temporal-consistent tree, we pool time by averaging to obtain a single parent distribution per slot for geometry x̄₀=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nx̂_0,i and high-level context h̄=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nhᵢ, concatenating them to form the input of the graph head z=concat(sg(h̄),sg(x̄₀))∈ℝ^Lₛ×(H+7). The graph head G will output p=G(z)∈ℝ^Lₛ×(Lₛ+2) where the additional two channels are used to represent the root and non-existing classes. Targets are constructed from the ground-truth joint graph and the Hungarian assignment, including root, non-root, and non-existing classes. The loss is

    L_graph=1/Lₛ∑ⱼCE(p_b,j,:,yᵖᵃʳᵉⁿᵗ_b,j)·(1-t)^γₚ,

    		(5)

    where γₚ is a hyperparameter to control the denosing-step-aware weight (1-t)^γₚ in flow matching. Intuitively, small t means the noisy state is still close to a coherent skeleton, so parent index targets (via hungarian matching on x̂₀) are more reliable while large t means slots are dominated by noise, so downweighting parent CE reduces conflicting topology gradients. The exponent γₚ≥0 controls how sharply supervision is concentrated toward t≈0.

    Total objective. The final objective is a weighted sum:

    L=L_FM+λ_NLLL_NLL+λ_graphL_graph+λₐᵤₓLₐᵤₓ,

    		(6)

    where λ are the coefficients for each term and Lₐᵤₓ is used to regularize the geometry and temporal smoothness (defined in the Appendix B). Overall, the losses in our framework serve three purposes: (1) L_FM learns accurate skeleton generation through flow matching, (2) L_NLL and L_graph improve confidence estimation and kinematic topology prediction, and (3) Lₐᵤₓ regularizes geometric validity and temporal consistency. Together, these terms improve stability and produce controllable, temporally aligned skeletons for both 3D and 4D inputs.

    3.5 Curriculum Training from 3D Reconstruction to 4D Prediction

    We train the model with a curriculum progressively increasing temporal complexity while keeping the architecture fixed. As shown in Figure 3, we start with static single-frame skeleton generation initializing the model with a strong geometry prior. We then switch to dynamic reconstruction, training on different time windows with full guidance of mesh. Finally, we emphasize dynamic prediction by randomly masking mesh tokens to force the model to simulate missing observations.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate FlowRig across diverse rigging scenarios, focusing on its ability to maintain 4D consistency and performance as a static rigger. Unless otherwise specified, we use unconditional guidance at inference time, since the ground-truth bone count is unavailable at test time.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, we utilize three primary data sources spanning static and dynamic domains. (1) For static rigging, we follow the protocol established in Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)] and employ Articulation-XL [(Song et al., 2025b)], a massive collection of 33,000 high-quality rigged 3D models covering humanoids, animals, and mechanical objects. (2) We also evaluate on the classic ModelsResource dataset [(Xu et al., 2020)], which contains a curated set of character models with professionally designed skeletons, serving as a standard benchmark for topological accuracy. (3) For dynamic 4D rigging, we utilize a curated dynamic dataset derived from TexVerse [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. We manually filtered the TexVerse animated subset to retain around 2,500 object-centric instances where the skeleton and mesh remain strictly aligned across temporal sequences, providing a high-fidelity ground truth for evaluating consistency and predictive forecasting. More details about the curated dataset can be found in Appendix A.

    Evaluation metrics. We evaluate skeleton quality with three Chamfer Distance (CD) variants: Joint-to-Joint (J2J), Joint-to-Bone (J2B), and Bone-to-Bone (B2B), which measure joint accuracy, joint-to-bone alignment, and structural fidelity, respectively. For 4D tasks, we average these over time. We also evaluate temporal consistency using bone distance deviation (BDD), which measures temporal jitter in bone lengths; Graph Structural Distance (GSD), which measures structural consistency through Hamming distance (HD) [(Wang et al., 2026b)]; and bone number deviation (BND), which measures changes in bone count relative to the anchor frame. More details are provided in Appendix C.1.

    Baselines. We compare FlowRig against both classical and modern rigging baselines. Classical methods include Pinocchio [(Baran and Popović, 2007)], a template-fitting optimization-based rigging system, and RigNet [(Xu et al., 2020)], a graph-neural-network-based feedforward rigger. Among recent generative or transformer-based methods, we consider MagicArticulate [(Song et al., 2025b)], Anymate [(Deng et al., 2025)], UniRig [(Zhang et al., 2025a)], RigAnything [(Liu et al., 2025a)], and Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)]. These methods cover a broad spectrum from optimization-based pipelines to modern feedforward sequence models. While several of them are strong for static 3D meshes, our results show that FlowRig remains competitive in the static setting while additionally providing the native 4D consistency and predictive capability required for dynamic sequences.

    4.2 3D Skeleton Reconstruction

    FlowRig supports both static and dynamic meshes, and with a single mesh as input it becomes a strong 3D rigging model. As shown in Table 1, our method ranks among the best across all three datasets, clearly outperforming classical baselines such as Pinocchio and RigNet. Among recent methods, Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)] and RigAnything [(Liu et al., 2025a)] are the strongest competitors, but FlowRig achieves the best overall results on Articulation-XL 2.0 and Diverse-Pose and remains competitive on ModelsResource in the zero-shot setting, even if RigAnything is trained directly on that training dataset. Overall, these results show that our unified 3D/4D formulation preserves strong static rigging performance and improves further with uncertainty-based selection in Ours*. Figure 4 shows that our method recovers more detailed and better mesh-aligned skeletons compared with baselines; more results are shown in Appendix E and the demo video.

    4.3 4D Skeleton Reconstruction and Prediction

    Our model naturally handles 4D reconstruction and prediction. For dynamic meshes, we study two settings. In 4D reconstruction, the full mesh sequence is observed with the goal of recovering a temporally consistent skeleton for every frame. In 4D prediction, only part of the sequence is observed and the model must infer the missing skeletons for interpolation, forecasting, or backcasting. Table 2 shows that FlowRig consistently outperforms the fine-tuned Puppeteer baseline Puppeteer-D* on both reconstruction accuracy and 4D consistency. As the temporal window N increases, our model achieves lower J2J-W, J2B-W, and B2B-W errors, where W represents averaging over the time window, indicating more accurate per-frame skeleton reconstruction with stronger temporal context. More importantly, FlowRig maintains perfect structural consistency across the full sequence, with zero BND, GSD, and HD for all reported settings, meaning that the predicted bone count and kinematic topology remain stable over time. In contrast, Puppeteer-D* exhibits clear temporal degradation as N grows, with increasing BND, BDD, GSD, and HD, indicating both geometric drift and topological flickering. The uncertainty-based selection in Ours* further improves reconstruction quality while preserving the same structural behavior, showing that FlowRig produces not only accurate per-frame skeletons but also temporally coherent 4D rigs. Figure 5(a) provides qualitative examples showing that our model preserves 4D consistency over time while also recovering finer skeletal details, such as the structure of the human hand. In addition, FlowRig supports 4D prediction, enabling interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting within a unified framework. Figure 5(b) presents qualitative evaluations of these settings and demonstrates FlowRig’s flexibility for downstream tasks. More qualitative results are shown in Appendix E and the demo video.

    4.4 Further Analysis and Ablation Studies

    Efficient Training Curriculum. We apply curriculum training: pre-train on large-scale static assets and fine-tune on dynamic sequences. Table 3 shows that static pre-training improves accuracy and reduces temporal instability compared with training on dynamic data alone. This suggests that large-scale static supervision provides a strong geometric prior for learning skeletal dynamics.

    Ablation of the Graph Head. The graph head is introduced to maintain a temporally consistent kinematic hierarchy across the full 4D sequence. We evaluate its effect by replacing it with a simple 1-Nearest Neighbor tree-building heuristic. As shown in Table 4, removing the graph head significantly increases Hamming distance, indicating frequent topological changes and unstable parent assignments over time. The corresponding rise in GSD further shows that the graph head is essential for preserving structural coherence and avoiding topological flickering in dynamic rigging.

    Controllable Skeletal Complexity. A unique advantage of our flow-matching framework is the ability to explicitly control skeletal density via Classifier-Free Guidance. While our model can autonomously determine a plausible bone count through unconditional generation, it also supports bone-count conditioning as a user-defined input. This allows FlowRig to synthesize skeletons with arbitrary bone counts ranging from 1 to 128, providing direct and flexible control over the output granularity that is absent in existing autoregressive methods. As illustrated in Figure 6, FlowRig can adapt the skeletal detail to satisfy specific animation requirements, varying from sparse armatures for background characters to high-density rigs for complex manual dexterity, whereas other baselines remain restricted to a single, uncontrolled output density.

    Additional Notes. We report inference speed in Appendix C.2, where FlowRig is faster than all baselines. We also develop a feedforward skinning model for downstream use in Appendix F, which is competitive with prior baselines.

    5 Conclusion and Future Works

    We propose FlowRig, a unified framework for 3D and 4D skeleton rigging from static meshes and dynamic mesh sequences. Built on flow matching, FlowRig generates temporally aligned skeletons while maintaining strong static reconstruction quality. By combining mesh-conditioned skeleton generation with a graph head for consistent topology and an uncertainty head for confidence-based sample selection, the model achieves competitive 3D performance and clear gains in 4D consistency and controllability. For future work, we plan to build stronger benchmarks for dynamic prediction under partial observations, extend the framework to jointly predict skinning weights and deformation, and introduce richer user controls such as semantic constraints or text-guided rig specification. We hope FlowRig serves as a step toward a more general and controllable rigger for 3D and 4D content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Table of Contents in Appendix

    Appendix A Curated Dataset

    TexVerse provides a large-scale collection of animated mesh-skeleton pairs [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. However, the raw dataset is not limited to clean object-centric motions, and many sequences exhibit quasi-static motion, inconsistent temporal alignment, or incorrect skeleton annotations. To construct a reliable evaluation set, we first use Qwen3.5 [(Qwen Team, 2026)] for preliminary filtering and then perform additional manual verification, resulting in 2,500 clean object-centric animated instances with correct mesh-skeleton alignment. The bone count distribution is shown in Figure S1. For training and evaluation, we divide into a train set with 2000 instances and a test set with 500 instances.

    Appendix B Training and model details

    Mesh-to-token conditioning We first sample Nₚ surface points and normals from each input mesh to form point-cloud frames Pᵢ∈ℝ^Nₚ×6. We encode each frame independently using a off-the-shelf Michelangelo point-cloud VAE to obtain a compact set of mesh tokens [(Zhao et al., 2023b)]. Concretely, we flatten the sequence to P_flat∈ℝ^N×Nₚ×6 and pass {Pᵢ} independently through the point cloud encoder. The resulting conditioning tokens are reshaped to C∈ℝ^N×Lₘ×H. For partially observed sequences, we mask the tokens of unobserved frames and replace with a learnable token for all masked frames.

    Model architecture. We use a DiT-L backbone with depth 24, hidden size H=1152, and 16 attention heads. Following the notation in the main method section, for each frame i, the input token sequence concatenates (a) Lₛ skeleton-slot tokens obtained by linearly projecting the 7D state x_t,i,:,:∈ℝ^Lₛ×7 to ℝ^Lₛ×H and (b) Lₘ mesh conditioning tokens Cᵢ∈ℝ^Lₘ×H produced by the Michelangelo point-cloud VAE encoder. Here Lₛ is the maximum number of skeleton slots, Lₘ is the number of mesh tokens per frame, and N is the sequence length. This yields a per-frame token set of size (Lₛ+Lₘ) and a packed transformer stream of length N·(Lₛ+Lₘ). We employ an alternating attention schedule, denoted frame-global alternating, that interleaves frame-wise attention on frame-indexed sequences with global attention on the packed sequence, and we apply temporal RoPE using the frame index across the concatenated token stream.

    Training auxiliary loss. The auxiliary loss includes geometry loss and temporal smooth loss. First, we apply the geometry loss to regularize the joints outside the mesh by including a signed distance (SD) penality term:

    L_geo=1/NLₛ∑_i,jReLU(SD(x̂_0,i,j,Mᵢ))·(1-t)^γᵢₙ,

    		(S1)

    where γᵢₙ is another hyperparameter for denoising-step-aware weight.

    Second, to encourage coherent dynamics and reduce temporal jitter, we additionally apply lightweight temporal regularizers on slot sequences, including bone-length consistency across adjacent frames and velocity smoothness across frame triplets:

    Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ=λ_bl 1/N-1∑ᵢ₌₂^Nℓ_bl(sᵢ,sᵢ₋₁)+λᵥₑₗ 1/N-2∑ᵢ₌₃^Nℓᵥₑₗ(sᵢ,sᵢ₋₁,sᵢ₋₂),

    		(S2)

    where sᵢ∈ℝ^Lₛ×7 denotes the slot tensor at frame i, and λ_bl and λᵥₑₗ are the bone length and velocity smoothness coefficients. As a result, the total auxiliary loss is:

    Lₐᵤₓ=λ_geoL_geo+λₛₘₒₒₜₕLₛₘₒₒₜₕ

    		(S3)

    Curriculum training. In the first stage, we set N=1 and optimize the full objective with one-to-one matching. In the second stage, we train on variable-length windows and apply full-frame conditioning. In the third stage, we apply masked-conditioning mechanism: for each training sample we draw an observed index set O and replace mesh tokens for unobserved frames with a mask token while injecting an observed-frame pooled summary into those positions. In practice, we increase the frequency of structured masks such as biasing the masking distribution toward structured patterns corresponding to forecasting and backcasting, including forecast masks with O={1,…,⌊N/2⌋}, backcast masks with O={⌊N/2⌋+1,…,N}, both-ends masks with O={1,N}, and full observation with O={1,…,N}. These strategies align the training distribution with inference-time use cases without changing the underlying objective.

    Optimization and guidance. We optimize the model with AdamW under mixed precision using bf16, together with cosine learning-rate decay and warmup. We set the starting learning rate to 1e-4, 5e-5, 3e-5 for the three training stages of static reconstruction, dynamic reconstruction, and dynamic prediction. Skeleton-count conditioning is trained with classifier-free guidance by dropping the count label y with probability p_drop=0.5, which forces the model to predict the reasonable skeleton count when no bone count guidance is provided. At inference time we apply CFG with scale s=5 to control the trade-off between fidelity and diversity.

    Appendix C Evaluation Details

    C.1 Evaluation Metrics

    Temporal topological consistency. We evaluate temporal topology with graph structure distance (GSD). Following the notation in the main method, each sequence contains N frames and each frame is represented by at most Lₛ skeleton slots. For methods without persistent slots, we first recover per-frame predicted skeletons {x̂_0,i}ᵢ₌₁^N and use the sequence-level Hungarian assignment defined in Section 3 to establish bone correspondence across time. Let J⊆{1,…,Lₛ} denote the set of matched and existing bones in the anchor frame i=1, and let J=|J|.

    For each frame i, let πᵢ(j) denote the parent index of matched bone j∈J. We compare the predicted topology at frame i against the anchor-frame topology π₁(j) using the Hamming distance

    Hᵢ=∑_j∈J\mathbbm1[πᵢ(j)≠π₁(j)],

    		(S4)

    and normalize it to obtain the per-frame graph structure distance

    GSDᵢ=Hᵢ/J.

    		(S5)

    We then report the sequence-level averages

    H̄=1/N-1∑ᵢ₌₂^NHᵢ, GSD̄=1/N-1∑ᵢ₌₂^NGSDᵢ.

    		(S6)

    For fixed-slot methods, the same definition applies directly because slot correspondence is given by the slot index.

    Bone displacement deviation (BDD). We evaluate temporal geometric stability with bone displacement deviation (BDD). Using the same correspondence set J, let dⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ denote the length of matched bone j∈J at frame i. We measure how much each corresponding bone deviates from its anchor-frame length and average over all matched bones and non-anchor frames:

    BDD=1/J(N-1)∑_j∈J∑ᵢ₌₂^N|dⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾-dⱼ⁽¹⁾|.

    		(S7)

    This correspondence-based definition ensures that BDD is computed on aligned bones rather than unmatched slots.

    C.2 Inference Details.

    To accurately evaluate the model performance, we sample 5 times for each instance and report the average evaluation metrics to reduce the variance of the metrics.

    Inference Time. We compare average inference times among baselines. FlowRig requires 1.1s for single-mesh inference. As shown in Table S1, it is 3.5× faster than Pinocchio, 4.1× faster than RigNet, 2.6× faster than UniRig, 2.2× faster than MagicArticulate, and 1.4× faster than Puppeteer. Table S2 further shows how inference time scales with the temporal window size. These results indicate that FlowRig remains efficient for single-frame 3D rigging while scaling reasonably to longer 4D windows.

    Appendix D More Quantitative Rigging Results

    D.1 Generalization and Per-Sequence Optimization Comparison

    Data. To evaluate the generalization capability of FlowRig in dynamic reconstruction, we built a second dynamic evaluation set from Objaverse [(Deitke et al., 2023)], a different source from the TexVerse data the model trains on, using the same VLM pre-filter, manual verification, and quality predicates detailed in Appendix A. This new dataset contains 1,656 verified animated instances across ten categories. Details of the per-category breakdown can be seen in Table S3.

    Per-Sequence Optimization Baseline. To perform a more comprehensive evaluation of FlowRig in dynamic reconstruction, we include a per-sequence optimization 4D baseline, RigGS [(Yao et al., 2025b)]. This model takes video as input and produces a skeleton together with 3D Gaussians, so we render each mesh sequence to video and supply the ground-truth masks its pipeline requires. Additionally, its output lives in its own coordinate frame, so we align the generated skeleton to the ground truth in scale, position, and orientation before computing metrics. Both steps are concessions in RigGS’s favour.

    Experiment Setup. RigGS optimizes every sequence from scratch and takes 17 minutes per 8-frame instance on an H200, so running it on the full 1,656-instance Objaverse set of W3 would cost 469 H200 GPU hours, against about 2 GPU hours for FlowRig. We therefore sample up to 20 instances per category, giving 193 instances across the ten categories and roughly 57 H200 GPU hours. All methods are evaluated on the same subsample at T=8.

    Results. We conclude the following based on the results in Tables S6, S6, and S6:

  • •

    FlowRig leads in 28 of the 30 category-metric cells. In aggregate, Ours* is 19.3% below RigGS and 19.2% below Puppeteer-D* on MACRO J2J, 20.2% and 25.5% below on J2B, and 22.5% and 26.6% below on B2B; MICRO gives the same picture. The two exceptions are fish on J2J and J2B, where RigGS leads by 0.4% and 0.5%, plausibly because fish motion is smooth and low in degrees of freedom, which suits per-sequence fitting.

  • •

    Per-sequence optimization is not uniformly stronger than a fine-tuned static rigger. RigGS and Puppeteer-D* are level on MACRO J2J (0.0636 vs. 0.0635), and RigGS leads only on J2B and B2B (6.7% and 5.2%). Optimizing each sequence individually does not by itself buy joint accuracy.

  • •

    The cost gap is over two orders of magnitude. RigGS needs 17 minutes per 8-frame instance where FlowRig needs 4.4s in a single feedforward pass (Table S2), roughly 230 times faster, which is what makes evaluation at the scale of the full set practical at all.

    • Appendix E More Qualitative Rigging Results

    More static and dynamic instances are shown in Figure S2 and Figure S3, respectively.

    Appendix F Skinning Model

    To animate mesh by the generated skeleton, we additionally train an attention-based skinning network, denoted SkinningTransformer, to predict soft skinning weights from a mesh observation and its associated skeletal rig. Given a mesh and a rig with J≤J_\max joints, our goal is to predict, for each queried surface point q∈{1,…,N_q}, a categorical distribution over valid joints. Each sample contains N_q sampled query points with normals, a padded bone tensor storing parent and child joint coordinates for each bone slot, a validity mask over joint slots, and a ground-truth skinning distribution over valid joints. Formally, for a query point q we model

    p(w_q|M,B,p_q,G), w_q∈ℝ^J_\max, ∑ⱼ₌₁^J_\maxw_q,j=1,

    		(S8)

    where p_q∈ℝ⁶ is the queried point-and-normal feature, M denotes the frozen mesh encoders, and G denotes the skeletal graph structure.

    Frozen geometry encoders. We condition the skinning model on two frozen geometry pathways. First, a Michelangelo shape encoder [(Zhao et al., 2023b)] produces a compact set of global shape tokens Fₛₕₐₚₑ∈ℝ^257×768. Second, the PartField encoder [(Liu et al., 2025b)] produces dense query features on sampled surface locations, F_pf^surf∈ℝ^N_q×448, where N_q is the number of sampled surface queries and PF(·) denotes the frozen part-aware field encoder. When skeleton-side part features are enabled, we also evaluate this field at the parent and child joint locations xᵖᵃʳⱼ,xᶜʰᵈⱼ∈ℝ³ of bone j and average them per bone,

    F_pf,jˢᵏᵉˡ=\tfrac12(PF(xᵖᵃʳⱼ)+PF(xᶜʰᵈⱼ))∈ℝ⁴⁴⁸.

    		(S9)

    These encoders remain frozen throughout training.

    Shape-skeleton fusion encoder. All conditioning features are projected into a shared transformer width d. Let B∈ℝ^J_\max×6 denote the padded bone tensor, where each row stores the concatenated parent and child joint coordinates of one bone. The learned projection matrices satisfy Wₛ∈ℝ^768×d, Wⱼ∈ℝ^6×d, Wˢᵖ∈ℝ^448×d, and Wₚ∈ℝ^448×d. We form projected shape and bone tokens as

    F^′ₛₕₐₚₑ=FₛₕₐₚₑWₛ, H⁽⁰⁾_bone=BWⱼ+𝔼ᵖᵒˢ_:J_\max+[F_pfˢᵏᵉˡWˢᵖ],

    		(S10)

    where 𝔼ᵖᵒˢ_:J_\max∈ℝ^J_\max×d is a learnable positional embedding for bone slots and the last term is optional. The encoder input is then

    Z⁽⁰⁾=Concat(F^′ₛₕₐₚₑ,H⁽⁰⁾_bone)∈ℝ^L_enc×d, L_enc=257+J_\max.

    		(S11)

    A stack of transformer encoder blocks updates Z, while invalid joint slots are masked so that padded joints do not participate in attention.

    Topology-aware joint attention. To encode skeletal structure explicitly, we inject a topology-aware bias into self-attention over the bone tokens [(Song et al., 2025a)]. Let D∈ℝ^J_\max×J_\max denote the pairwise graph-distance matrix on the skeleton. Distances are clamped into a small set of buckets and projected into per-head biases. The attention score for head h, with query/key head dimension dₕ, becomes

    score⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=(Q⁽ʰ⁾ᵢK⁽ʰ⁾ⱼ^⊤)/(√dₕ)+λₜₐⱼₐ b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ(D),

    		(S12)

    for bone-token indices i and j. This topology-aware joint attention encourages joints that are nearby in the kinematic tree to exchange information more strongly.

    Point-wise cross-attention decoder. Surface query tokens are initialized from projected part-aware point features,

    H⁽⁰⁾ₚₜ=F^surf_pfWₚ∈ℝ^N_q×d.

    		(S13)

    Optionally, Fourier positional encodings of the queried coordinates and normals are added to these tokens. The decoder then refines point tokens purely through cross-attention to the encoder memory. There is no decoder self-attention; interaction among queries is mediated through the shared shape-skeleton memory.

    Scaled cosine prediction head. The final logits are computed by cosine similarity between normalized point embeddings and normalized joint embeddings, scaled by a learnable factor α, where z_qj is the logit for assigning query point q to joint j,

    z_qj=(|α|+ε)·(Fᵒᵘᵗₚₜ(q))/(∥Fᵒᵘᵗₚₜ(q)∥₂)·(Fʲᵒⁱⁿᵗ_bone(j))/(∥Fʲᵒⁱⁿᵗ_bone(j)∥₂).

    		(S14)

    Invalid joint logits are masked before normalization, and skinning probabilities are obtained by

    w_q=softmax(z_q).

    		(S15)

    This design makes the prediction explicitly probabilistic and naturally handles variable valid-joint sets through masking.

    Training objective. We optimize the skinning network with a masked soft cross-entropy objective together with an L₁ loss in probability space. Let Y denote the target weight distributions and let Z denote the predicted logits. The overall loss is

    L=L_CE(Y,Z;m)+λ_ℓ₁ L_L₁(σ(Z),Y;m),

    		(S16)

一句话：静态绑骨质量好但不能控骨骼数、逐帧套用会抖；4D 方法又要逐序列优化。

要点：

  • 现状痛点对称：静态 3D 绑骨方法质量不错，但对骨骼数量控制有限，逐帧套到动态网格上还会时序不稳；4D 方法则通常依赖昂贵的逐序列优化
  • FlowRig 是模板无关、数据高效的统一框架：用 flow matching 同时支持静态 3D 与动态 4D 网格的骨架生成
  • 目标是给出一个前馈解，既不逐序列优化，也不在动态序列上抖动

为什么值得看：角色管线里绑骨是最贵的手工环节之一，而「有动作的扫描」越来越多（4D 捕捉、体积视频）。能用同一个前馈模型覆盖 3D 与 4D，意味着扫描进来的动态资产可以直接拿到可驱动骨架。

中文摘要：自动绑骨对静态 3D 网格与动态 4D 网格都是基础任务，但现有方法没有给出统一的前馈解：静态 3D 绑骨质量不错，却对骨骼数量缺乏控制，把它逐帧套到动态网格上还会出现时序不稳定；4D 方法则往往依赖昂贵的逐序列优化。FlowRig 提出模板无关、数据高效的统一框架，用 flow matching 同时生成 3D 与 4D 网格的骨架，从而避免逐序列优化，并改善动态序列上的稳定性。对同时处理扫描静态资产与 4D 捕捉内容的角色管线，这减少了一套专属流程。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

FlowRig: Unified Skeleton Generation for
3D and 4D Meshes via Flow Matching

Abstract

Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose FlowRig, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, FlowRig generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that FlowRig achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.

1 Introduction

Automatic rigging is a core problem in computer graphics, which turns raw geometry into animatable assets. This need spans both static 3D and dynamic 4D meshes: 3D assets require high-quality, controllable skeletons for downstream animation workflows, while 4D assets additionally require temporal consistency across time. At the same time, temporally coherent 4D meshes are becoming increasingly available from modern reconstruction and generation pipelines. Recent systems can recover or synthesize dynamic 4D geometry directly from videos or generative models, making 4D meshes a practical representation rather than a niche output [(Sabathier et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025b; Xie et al., 2026)]. However, geometry alone is not enough for downstream animation, editing, simulation, and control. To make these assets truly useful, we need a unified feedforward rigging model that works for both 3D and 4D meshes, produces informative skeletons, supports controllable bone complexity, and remains stable across diverse poses and motions.

Unfortunately, this capability is still missing. On one side, existing rigging methods are predominantly designed for static 3D inputs, ranging from classical optimization systems [(Baran and Popović, 2007)] to modern feedforward and autoregressive models [(Xu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026a)]. These methods have substantially improved 3D rigging quality and efficiency, but they are fundamentally static, and many of them provide limited control over skeleton density or bone count for downstream applications. When applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes, they also typically fail to maintain temporal consistency [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. On the other hand, existing 4D methods mainly focus on per-sequence optimization, reconstruction, or motion transfer [(Li et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026a; Dabhi et al., 2026; Muralikrishnan et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026)]. While these methods are valuable, they do not provide a unified feedforward rigging solution that bridges controllable 3D rigging, dynamic 4D reconstruction, and predictive temporal reasoning within one framework.

Building such a unified model is challenging for two reasons. First, many strong static rigging methods are autoregressive, which makes explicit bone-count control less natural and global temporal reasoning inefficient for dynamic sequences. Second, paired 4D mesh-skeleton data remains far scarcer than static 3D rigging data, so a practical model must learn temporal consistency from limited 4D supervision while preserving strong 3D rigging quality.

In this work, we propose FlowRig, a data-efficient feedforward framework for unified skeleton generation on 3D and 4D meshes. Built on flow matching, FlowRig predicts temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in one pass, while naturally handling 3D rigging with explicit skeleton-count control. The model also includes a graph head for temporally consistent topology prediction and an uncertainty head for confidence estimation. The masking-based training further enables 4D prediction including interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited 4D supervision, we initialize from large-scale 3D rigging data and then adapt to mid-scale 4D rigging data. Experiments show that FlowRig achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose FlowRig, a unified flow-matching model for controllable 3D/4D skeleton generation.

  • •

    We introduce a 3D-to-4D curriculum for data-efficient training under limited 4D supervision.

  • •

    We achieve strong 3D rigging, high-quality 4D reconstruction, and flexible 4D prediction.

    • 2 Related Work

    Static Automatic Rigging and Skinning. Automatic rigging has been studied extensively in the static 3D setting. Early methods relied on template fitting and per-shape optimization, as in Pinocchio [(Baran and Popović, 2007)], while later data-driven approaches improved both speed and generalization. RigNet [(Xu et al., 2020)] introduced graph neural networks for direct skeleton and skinning prediction from meshes. Subsequent methods such as UniRig [(Zhang et al., 2025a)], RigAnything [(Liu et al., 2025a)], ARMO [(Sun et al., 2025a)], Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)], and Skin Tokens [(Zhang et al., 2026b)] further improved structural validity through autoregressive or language-model-style generation [(Song et al., 2025b)]. These methods are strong baselines for static 3D rigging, but not for general-purpose 4D rigging. In particular, autoregressive generation is less suitable for 4D sequences, where one must reason jointly over skeletal slots and time; applying static models per-frame often leads to temporal flickering and inconsistent topologies [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. Their discrete formulation can also make skeleton density control harder for downstream 4D use.

    Dynamic and 4D Rigging. As 4D meshes become more accessible, there is growing interest in rigging dynamic assets directly from videos or mesh sequences. Existing 4D rigging-related methods mainly fall into two categories. The first consists of per-sequence optimization methods, such as AKD [(Li et al., 2025)], RigGS [(Yao et al., 2025b)], AniMimic [(Xie et al., 2026)], GaussiAnimate [(Wang et al., 2026a)], and RAT4D [(Dabhi et al., 2026)], which align articulated structure to multi-frame observations or dynamic 3D representations. These methods can achieve high fidelity, but their reliance on per-scene optimization makes them computationally expensive and less suitable for scalable deployment. The second involves consistency-oriented extensions of static riggers, such as SPRig [(Wang et al., 2026b)], which improve cross-frame consistency through additional self-supervision. While promising, these methods do not yet provide a unified feedforward framework for raw 4D mesh sequences that supports both reconstruction and prediction. Related animation methods, including Gaussian bone representation, zero-shot pose transfer and morphology-aware motion transfer [(Guo et al., 2025; Muralikrishnan et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a)], are complementary rather than direct solutions to general-purpose 4D rigging.

    4D Mesh Availability and Upstream Geometry Models. Our work is motivated in part by the increasing availability of temporally coherent 4D meshes from upstream reconstruction and generation systems. The field has seen rapid expansion, ranging from text- and image-to-4D generation [(Yin et al., 2023; Ling et al., 2024; Bahmani et al., 2024a; Miao et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024a; Bahmani et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2023a; Gao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2025; Nag et al., 2025)] to video-based dynamic reconstruction [(Jiang et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2024)]. In particular, recent methods such as ActionMesh [(Sabathier et al., 2026)] and AniMimic [(Xie et al., 2026)] show that high-quality dynamic geometry can now be derived from monocular videos and learned priors. While these systems expand the supply of dynamic geometry, they do not solve the downstream rigging problem. Instead, they highlight the need for a feedforward 4D rigging model that converts temporally aligned geometry into informative and animation-ready skeletons. In this sense, our method is complementary: upstream models provide the dynamic geometry, while FlowRig provides the rigging for downstream animation and control.

    Generative Models for 3D and 4D Assets. A separate line of work studies the co-generation of geometry and rigging information. AniGen [(Huang et al., 2026)] generates animatable 3D assets together with rigging information, while AKD [(Li et al., 2025)] uses score distillation to generate articulated 4D assets from images or text. Related directions include skeleton-guided 3D generation [(Xu et al., 2025)], creative articulated asset generation [(Lu et al., 2026)], sketch-based rigging [(Zhao et al., 2026)], and rig-based generative synthesis of dynamic 3D Gaussians [(Wu et al., 2026)]. However, these works are not for general-purpose feedforward rigging of raw 4D mesh sequences. Instead, our focus is to take 3D or 4D geometry as input and produce temporally consistent skeletons with controllable complexity and prediction capability, making our setting complementary to asset generation.

    3 Proposed Method

    3.1 Problem Formulation

    Let M_1:N=(m₁,…,m_N) denote a observation sequence of mesh mᵢ, where each frame is represented as a sampled point cloud with normals Pᵢ∈ℝ^Nₚ×6 and Nₚ is the size of the point cloud. Our goal is to predict a corresponding skeleton sequence S_1:N=(S₁,…,S_N), where each Sᵢ is a set of bones with 3D endpoints and a tree topology. We consider static and dynamic tasks below.

    Static skeleton reconstruction. When N=1, we generate a skeleton set S₁ conditioned on a single mesh observation P₁. Formally, we model the conditional distribution p(S₁|P₁).

    Dynamic skeleton reconstruction and prediction. Given observed frames O⊆{1,…,N} and observations ℙ_O={Pᵢ}_i∈O, we generate the full skeleton sequence using p(S_1:N|ℙ_O). Reconstruction corresponds to O={1,…,N}, while prediction corresponds to O⊂{1,…,N}.

    3.2 Flow Matching on An Optimal-Transport Path

    Instead of learning a reverse denoising process as in diffusion models, flow matching learns a continuous-time vector field that transports noise to data. Let x₀ denote a clean sample and x₁∼ℕ(0,σ²I) be Gaussian noise. We use the optimal-transport straight-line path xₜ=(1-t)x₀+tx₁ for t∈(0,1), whose target velocity is constant: v^⋆(xₜ,t)=x₁-x₀. Given mesh-derived conditioning tokens c, the network M predicts the velocity field v̂=M(xₜ,t,c;Θ) and is trained to match v^⋆ with mean-squared error, together with our matching and auxiliary losses. At inference time, we start from xₜ₌₁∼ℕ(0,σ²I) and integrate the learned ODE from t=1 to t=0 with an Euler solver: x_t-Δt=xₜ-Δt·v̂(xₜ,t,c), yielding the clean sample x₀.

    3.3 4D Skeleton Flow Matching Model

    Figure 2 shows an overview of FlowRig. Given a static mesh or a mesh sequence, we encode each frame with the frozen Michelangelo encoder [(Zhao et al., 2023b)] to obtain mesh conditioning tokens c∈ℝ^N×Lₘ×H. In parallel, we initialize a fixed set of noisy skeleton slots xₜ∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7 and optionally inject a target skeleton-count condition to control the number of generated bones. We set Lₛ=128 to cover all training instances, similar to prior slot-based methods such as Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)], and allow N to vary by sampling different window lengths during training. The DiT embeds the skeleton slots into H-dimensional tokens, concatenates them with the mesh tokens, and processes the resulting sequence of length N·(Lₛ+Lₘ) with temporal rotational positional encoding (RoPE) using the frame index as the shared temporal reference. It then performs slot-based set prediction over the full sequence and predicts a velocity tensor v̂∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7, which is decoded into up to Lₛ bones per frame as 7D slot states x₀∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7, where each slot is x_0,i,j=[e_i,j,p_i,j,0,p_i,j,1] with an existence indicator e∈{0,1} and two 3D endpoints p_i,j,0,p_i,j,1∈ℝ³. After the transformer predicts the aligned skeleton slots, a graph head infers the kinematic tree and an uncertainty head estimates confidence, producing the final controllable 3D or 4D rigging output.

    Besides the skeleton head, we use two additional lightweight heads: a graph head and an uncertainty head. A naive way to build a skeleton tree is to connect bones by distance, but this can lead to unstable topology over time as the joints move. Instead, the graph head predicts parent indices from the hidden features {hᵢ} and the predicted skeletons {x̂ᵢ}, yielding a more temporally consistent tree structure. The uncertainty head takes the hidden features as input and predicts per-frame per-bone uncertainty σ̂∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7. Intuitively, it estimates how reliable each generated bone is, so we can use uncertainty as a score when drawing multiple samples and select the most confident result.

    Skeleton-count conditioning and classifier-free guidance (CFG). In addition to mesh tokens, we condition the model on a scalar skeleton or bone count y, which serves as a guidance label. During training we apply classifier-free guidance by randomly dropping the condition with probability p_drop, that is, replacing y with an unconditional token y=-1 in the embedding layer. The conditional and unconditional predictors share parameters and differ only in the presence of y:

    v̂_cond=M(xₜ,t,c,y;Θ), v̂_uncond=M(xₜ,t,c,-1;Θ).

    		(1)

    During inference, we form the guided velocity with CFG scale s as v̂_cfg=v̂_uncond+s·(v̂_cond-v̂_uncond), and integrate the ODE with v̂_cfg.

    3.4 Training Objective

    Our training objective combines flow matching with the auxiliary supervision terms.

    One-to-one supervision via sequence Hungarian matching. To handle variable ground-truth bone counts while preserving a fixed tensor interface, we follow the DETR-style one-to-one supervision [(Carion et al., 2020)]. Each Sᵢ is represented using Lₛ permutation-invariant skeleton slots, and the model is trained with hungarian matching for each predicted and ground-truth skeleton pair. For each frame we extract raw endpoints gᵢ∈ℝ^N_gt×6 and pad them to a fixed tensor size. Since slot indices are permutation-invariant, we compute a single assignment per sequence, shared across frames, using the Hungarian algorithm. We first recover a predicted clean state by

    x̂₀=xₜ-t v̂∈ℝ^N×Lₛ×7,(2)

    and build a cost matrix between slot endpoints p̂_j,0 and p̂_j,1 and the ground-truth endpoints gⱼ. To align the static and dynamic training objectives, we set the anchor frame i=1 for hungarian matching in all training stages. The matching cost is a weighted sum of endpoint Euclidean distance. The resulting assignment maps each ground-truth bone to one slot, producing matched targets x̃.

    Flow matching loss. The primary objective is a weighted flow-matching mean-squared error on the matched optimal-transport velocity:

    L_FM=1/NLₛ∑_i,jw_i,j \lVertv̂_i,j-ṽ^⋆_i,j\rVert₂², ṽ^⋆=x₁-x̃₀.(3)

    where per-slot weights w∈ℝ^N×Lₛ upweight matched slots and control supervision on empty slots with less focus. Intuitively, we set the unmatched slot endpoints with zero weight since they have no contribution to the final results, thus forcing the model to focus on the matched pairs.

    Uncertainty loss. To quantify the confidence of skeletons, we add a Gaussian negative log-likelihood (NLL) term to estimate the uncertainty of bone existence and the joint positions. Following IDDPM [(Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021)], we stop gradients through the mean prediction in the NLL branch:

    L_NLL=1/NLₛ∑_i,jw_b,j(\lVertsg(v̂_b,i,j)-ṽ^⋆_b,i,j\rVert₂²/(σ̂_v,b,i,j²+ε)+\log(σ̂_v,b,i,j²+ε)),

    		(4)

    where ε is a small value and sg(·) denotes the stop-gradient operator. This way, L_NLL can guide σ̂² without affecting the training of transformer backbone and skeleton head.

    Graph head loss. To build the kinematic tree for the generated skeleton, we supervise a parent index classifier over slots. Specifically, to handle temporal aggregation and derive a temporal-consistent tree, we pool time by averaging to obtain a single parent distribution per slot for geometry x̄₀=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nx̂_0,i and high-level context h̄=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nhᵢ, concatenating them to form the input of the graph head z=concat(sg(h̄),sg(x̄₀))∈ℝ^Lₛ×(H+7). The graph head G will output p=G(z)∈ℝ^Lₛ×(Lₛ+2) where the additional two channels are used to represent the root and non-existing classes. Targets are constructed from the ground-truth joint graph and the Hungarian assignment, including root, non-root, and non-existing classes. The loss is

    L_graph=1/Lₛ∑ⱼCE(p_b,j,:,yᵖᵃʳᵉⁿᵗ_b,j)·(1-t)^γₚ,

    		(5)

    where γₚ is a hyperparameter to control the denosing-step-aware weight (1-t)^γₚ in flow matching. Intuitively, small t means the noisy state is still close to a coherent skeleton, so parent index targets (via hungarian matching on x̂₀) are more reliable while large t means slots are dominated by noise, so downweighting parent CE reduces conflicting topology gradients. The exponent γₚ≥0 controls how sharply supervision is concentrated toward t≈0.

    Total objective. The final objective is a weighted sum:

    L=L_FM+λ_NLLL_NLL+λ_graphL_graph+λₐᵤₓLₐᵤₓ,

    		(6)

    where λ are the coefficients for each term and Lₐᵤₓ is used to regularize the geometry and temporal smoothness (defined in the Appendix B). Overall, the losses in our framework serve three purposes: (1) L_FM learns accurate skeleton generation through flow matching, (2) L_NLL and L_graph improve confidence estimation and kinematic topology prediction, and (3) Lₐᵤₓ regularizes geometric validity and temporal consistency. Together, these terms improve stability and produce controllable, temporally aligned skeletons for both 3D and 4D inputs.

    3.5 Curriculum Training from 3D Reconstruction to 4D Prediction

    We train the model with a curriculum progressively increasing temporal complexity while keeping the architecture fixed. As shown in Figure 3, we start with static single-frame skeleton generation initializing the model with a strong geometry prior. We then switch to dynamic reconstruction, training on different time windows with full guidance of mesh. Finally, we emphasize dynamic prediction by randomly masking mesh tokens to force the model to simulate missing observations.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate FlowRig across diverse rigging scenarios, focusing on its ability to maintain 4D consistency and performance as a static rigger. Unless otherwise specified, we use unconditional guidance at inference time, since the ground-truth bone count is unavailable at test time.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, we utilize three primary data sources spanning static and dynamic domains. (1) For static rigging, we follow the protocol established in Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)] and employ Articulation-XL [(Song et al., 2025b)], a massive collection of 33,000 high-quality rigged 3D models covering humanoids, animals, and mechanical objects. (2) We also evaluate on the classic ModelsResource dataset [(Xu et al., 2020)], which contains a curated set of character models with professionally designed skeletons, serving as a standard benchmark for topological accuracy. (3) For dynamic 4D rigging, we utilize a curated dynamic dataset derived from TexVerse [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. We manually filtered the TexVerse animated subset to retain around 2,500 object-centric instances where the skeleton and mesh remain strictly aligned across temporal sequences, providing a high-fidelity ground truth for evaluating consistency and predictive forecasting. More details about the curated dataset can be found in Appendix A.

    Evaluation metrics. We evaluate skeleton quality with three Chamfer Distance (CD) variants: Joint-to-Joint (J2J), Joint-to-Bone (J2B), and Bone-to-Bone (B2B), which measure joint accuracy, joint-to-bone alignment, and structural fidelity, respectively. For 4D tasks, we average these over time. We also evaluate temporal consistency using bone distance deviation (BDD), which measures temporal jitter in bone lengths; Graph Structural Distance (GSD), which measures structural consistency through Hamming distance (HD) [(Wang et al., 2026b)]; and bone number deviation (BND), which measures changes in bone count relative to the anchor frame. More details are provided in Appendix C.1.

    Baselines. We compare FlowRig against both classical and modern rigging baselines. Classical methods include Pinocchio [(Baran and Popović, 2007)], a template-fitting optimization-based rigging system, and RigNet [(Xu et al., 2020)], a graph-neural-network-based feedforward rigger. Among recent generative or transformer-based methods, we consider MagicArticulate [(Song et al., 2025b)], Anymate [(Deng et al., 2025)], UniRig [(Zhang et al., 2025a)], RigAnything [(Liu et al., 2025a)], and Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)]. These methods cover a broad spectrum from optimization-based pipelines to modern feedforward sequence models. While several of them are strong for static 3D meshes, our results show that FlowRig remains competitive in the static setting while additionally providing the native 4D consistency and predictive capability required for dynamic sequences.

    4.2 3D Skeleton Reconstruction

    FlowRig supports both static and dynamic meshes, and with a single mesh as input it becomes a strong 3D rigging model. As shown in Table 1, our method ranks among the best across all three datasets, clearly outperforming classical baselines such as Pinocchio and RigNet. Among recent methods, Puppeteer [(Song et al., 2025a)] and RigAnything [(Liu et al., 2025a)] are the strongest competitors, but FlowRig achieves the best overall results on Articulation-XL 2.0 and Diverse-Pose and remains competitive on ModelsResource in the zero-shot setting, even if RigAnything is trained directly on that training dataset. Overall, these results show that our unified 3D/4D formulation preserves strong static rigging performance and improves further with uncertainty-based selection in Ours*. Figure 4 shows that our method recovers more detailed and better mesh-aligned skeletons compared with baselines; more results are shown in Appendix E and the demo video.

    4.3 4D Skeleton Reconstruction and Prediction

    Our model naturally handles 4D reconstruction and prediction. For dynamic meshes, we study two settings. In 4D reconstruction, the full mesh sequence is observed with the goal of recovering a temporally consistent skeleton for every frame. In 4D prediction, only part of the sequence is observed and the model must infer the missing skeletons for interpolation, forecasting, or backcasting. Table 2 shows that FlowRig consistently outperforms the fine-tuned Puppeteer baseline Puppeteer-D* on both reconstruction accuracy and 4D consistency. As the temporal window N increases, our model achieves lower J2J-W, J2B-W, and B2B-W errors, where W represents averaging over the time window, indicating more accurate per-frame skeleton reconstruction with stronger temporal context. More importantly, FlowRig maintains perfect structural consistency across the full sequence, with zero BND, GSD, and HD for all reported settings, meaning that the predicted bone count and kinematic topology remain stable over time. In contrast, Puppeteer-D* exhibits clear temporal degradation as N grows, with increasing BND, BDD, GSD, and HD, indicating both geometric drift and topological flickering. The uncertainty-based selection in Ours* further improves reconstruction quality while preserving the same structural behavior, showing that FlowRig produces not only accurate per-frame skeletons but also temporally coherent 4D rigs. Figure 5(a) provides qualitative examples showing that our model preserves 4D consistency over time while also recovering finer skeletal details, such as the structure of the human hand. In addition, FlowRig supports 4D prediction, enabling interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting within a unified framework. Figure 5(b) presents qualitative evaluations of these settings and demonstrates FlowRig’s flexibility for downstream tasks. More qualitative results are shown in Appendix E and the demo video.

    4.4 Further Analysis and Ablation Studies

    Efficient Training Curriculum. We apply curriculum training: pre-train on large-scale static assets and fine-tune on dynamic sequences. Table 3 shows that static pre-training improves accuracy and reduces temporal instability compared with training on dynamic data alone. This suggests that large-scale static supervision provides a strong geometric prior for learning skeletal dynamics.

    Ablation of the Graph Head. The graph head is introduced to maintain a temporally consistent kinematic hierarchy across the full 4D sequence. We evaluate its effect by replacing it with a simple 1-Nearest Neighbor tree-building heuristic. As shown in Table 4, removing the graph head significantly increases Hamming distance, indicating frequent topological changes and unstable parent assignments over time. The corresponding rise in GSD further shows that the graph head is essential for preserving structural coherence and avoiding topological flickering in dynamic rigging.

    Controllable Skeletal Complexity. A unique advantage of our flow-matching framework is the ability to explicitly control skeletal density via Classifier-Free Guidance. While our model can autonomously determine a plausible bone count through unconditional generation, it also supports bone-count conditioning as a user-defined input. This allows FlowRig to synthesize skeletons with arbitrary bone counts ranging from 1 to 128, providing direct and flexible control over the output granularity that is absent in existing autoregressive methods. As illustrated in Figure 6, FlowRig can adapt the skeletal detail to satisfy specific animation requirements, varying from sparse armatures for background characters to high-density rigs for complex manual dexterity, whereas other baselines remain restricted to a single, uncontrolled output density.

    Additional Notes. We report inference speed in Appendix C.2, where FlowRig is faster than all baselines. We also develop a feedforward skinning model for downstream use in Appendix F, which is competitive with prior baselines.

    5 Conclusion and Future Works

    We propose FlowRig, a unified framework for 3D and 4D skeleton rigging from static meshes and dynamic mesh sequences. Built on flow matching, FlowRig generates temporally aligned skeletons while maintaining strong static reconstruction quality. By combining mesh-conditioned skeleton generation with a graph head for consistent topology and an uncertainty head for confidence-based sample selection, the model achieves competitive 3D performance and clear gains in 4D consistency and controllability. For future work, we plan to build stronger benchmarks for dynamic prediction under partial observations, extend the framework to jointly predict skinning weights and deformation, and introduce richer user controls such as semantic constraints or text-guided rig specification. We hope FlowRig serves as a step toward a more general and controllable rigger for 3D and 4D content.
