    Appendix A Curated Dataset

    TexVerse provides a large-scale collection of animated mesh-skeleton pairs [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. However, the raw dataset is not limited to clean object-centric motions, and many sequences exhibit quasi-static motion, inconsistent temporal alignment, or incorrect skeleton annotations. To construct a reliable evaluation set, we first use Qwen3.5 [(Qwen Team, 2026)] for preliminary filtering and then perform additional manual verification, resulting in 2,500 clean object-centric animated instances with correct mesh-skeleton alignment. The bone count distribution is shown in Figure S1. For training and evaluation, we divide into a train set with 2000 instances and a test set with 500 instances.

    Appendix B Training and model details

    Mesh-to-token conditioning We first sample Nₚ surface points and normals from each input mesh to form point-cloud frames Pᵢ∈ℝ^Nₚ×6. We encode each frame independently using a off-the-shelf Michelangelo point-cloud VAE to obtain a compact set of mesh tokens [(Zhao et al., 2023b)]. Concretely, we flatten the sequence to P_flat∈ℝ^N×Nₚ×6 and pass {Pᵢ} independently through the point cloud encoder. The resulting conditioning tokens are reshaped to C∈ℝ^N×Lₘ×H. For partially observed sequences, we mask the tokens of unobserved frames and replace with a learnable token for all masked frames.

    Model architecture. We use a DiT-L backbone with depth 24, hidden size H=1152, and 16 attention heads. Following the notation in the main method section, for each frame i, the input token sequence concatenates (a) Lₛ skeleton-slot tokens obtained by linearly projecting the 7D state x_t,i,:,:∈ℝ^Lₛ×7 to ℝ^Lₛ×H and (b) Lₘ mesh conditioning tokens Cᵢ∈ℝ^Lₘ×H produced by the Michelangelo point-cloud VAE encoder. Here Lₛ is the maximum number of skeleton slots, Lₘ is the number of mesh tokens per frame, and N is the sequence length. This yields a per-frame token set of size (Lₛ+Lₘ) and a packed transformer stream of length N·(Lₛ+Lₘ). We employ an alternating attention schedule, denoted frame-global alternating, that interleaves frame-wise attention on frame-indexed sequences with global attention on the packed sequence, and we apply temporal RoPE using the frame index across the concatenated token stream.

    Training auxiliary loss. The auxiliary loss includes geometry loss and temporal smooth loss. First, we apply the geometry loss to regularize the joints outside the mesh by including a signed distance (SD) penality term:

    L_geo=1/NLₛ∑_i,jReLU(SD(x̂_0,i,j,Mᵢ))·(1-t)^γᵢₙ,

    		(S1)

    where γᵢₙ is another hyperparameter for denoising-step-aware weight.

    Second, to encourage coherent dynamics and reduce temporal jitter, we additionally apply lightweight temporal regularizers on slot sequences, including bone-length consistency across adjacent frames and velocity smoothness across frame triplets:

    Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ=λ_bl 1/N-1∑ᵢ₌₂^Nℓ_bl(sᵢ,sᵢ₋₁)+λᵥₑₗ 1/N-2∑ᵢ₌₃^Nℓᵥₑₗ(sᵢ,sᵢ₋₁,sᵢ₋₂),

    		(S2)

    where sᵢ∈ℝ^Lₛ×7 denotes the slot tensor at frame i, and λ_bl and λᵥₑₗ are the bone length and velocity smoothness coefficients. As a result, the total auxiliary loss is:

    Lₐᵤₓ=λ_geoL_geo+λₛₘₒₒₜₕLₛₘₒₒₜₕ

    		(S3)

    Curriculum training. In the first stage, we set N=1 and optimize the full objective with one-to-one matching. In the second stage, we train on variable-length windows and apply full-frame conditioning. In the third stage, we apply masked-conditioning mechanism: for each training sample we draw an observed index set O and replace mesh tokens for unobserved frames with a mask token while injecting an observed-frame pooled summary into those positions. In practice, we increase the frequency of structured masks such as biasing the masking distribution toward structured patterns corresponding to forecasting and backcasting, including forecast masks with O={1,…,⌊N/2⌋}, backcast masks with O={⌊N/2⌋+1,…,N}, both-ends masks with O={1,N}, and full observation with O={1,…,N}. These strategies align the training distribution with inference-time use cases without changing the underlying objective.

    Optimization and guidance. We optimize the model with AdamW under mixed precision using bf16, together with cosine learning-rate decay and warmup. We set the starting learning rate to 1e-4, 5e-5, 3e-5 for the three training stages of static reconstruction, dynamic reconstruction, and dynamic prediction. Skeleton-count conditioning is trained with classifier-free guidance by dropping the count label y with probability p_drop=0.5, which forces the model to predict the reasonable skeleton count when no bone count guidance is provided. At inference time we apply CFG with scale s=5 to control the trade-off between fidelity and diversity.

    Appendix C Evaluation Details

    C.1 Evaluation Metrics

    Temporal topological consistency. We evaluate temporal topology with graph structure distance (GSD). Following the notation in the main method, each sequence contains N frames and each frame is represented by at most Lₛ skeleton slots. For methods without persistent slots, we first recover per-frame predicted skeletons {x̂_0,i}ᵢ₌₁^N and use the sequence-level Hungarian assignment defined in Section 3 to establish bone correspondence across time. Let J⊆{1,…,Lₛ} denote the set of matched and existing bones in the anchor frame i=1, and let J=|J|.

    For each frame i, let πᵢ(j) denote the parent index of matched bone j∈J. We compare the predicted topology at frame i against the anchor-frame topology π₁(j) using the Hamming distance

    Hᵢ=∑_j∈J\mathbbm1[πᵢ(j)≠π₁(j)],

    		(S4)

    and normalize it to obtain the per-frame graph structure distance

    GSDᵢ=Hᵢ/J.

    		(S5)

    We then report the sequence-level averages

    H̄=1/N-1∑ᵢ₌₂^NHᵢ, GSD̄=1/N-1∑ᵢ₌₂^NGSDᵢ.

    		(S6)

    For fixed-slot methods, the same definition applies directly because slot correspondence is given by the slot index.

    Bone displacement deviation (BDD). We evaluate temporal geometric stability with bone displacement deviation (BDD). Using the same correspondence set J, let dⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ denote the length of matched bone j∈J at frame i. We measure how much each corresponding bone deviates from its anchor-frame length and average over all matched bones and non-anchor frames:

    BDD=1/J(N-1)∑_j∈J∑ᵢ₌₂^N|dⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾-dⱼ⁽¹⁾|.

    		(S7)

    This correspondence-based definition ensures that BDD is computed on aligned bones rather than unmatched slots.

    C.2 Inference Details.

    To accurately evaluate the model performance, we sample 5 times for each instance and report the average evaluation metrics to reduce the variance of the metrics.

    Inference Time. We compare average inference times among baselines. FlowRig requires 1.1s for single-mesh inference. As shown in Table S1, it is 3.5× faster than Pinocchio, 4.1× faster than RigNet, 2.6× faster than UniRig, 2.2× faster than MagicArticulate, and 1.4× faster than Puppeteer. Table S2 further shows how inference time scales with the temporal window size. These results indicate that FlowRig remains efficient for single-frame 3D rigging while scaling reasonably to longer 4D windows.

    Appendix D More Quantitative Rigging Results

    D.1 Generalization and Per-Sequence Optimization Comparison

    Data. To evaluate the generalization capability of FlowRig in dynamic reconstruction, we built a second dynamic evaluation set from Objaverse [(Deitke et al., 2023)], a different source from the TexVerse data the model trains on, using the same VLM pre-filter, manual verification, and quality predicates detailed in Appendix A. This new dataset contains 1,656 verified animated instances across ten categories. Details of the per-category breakdown can be seen in Table S3.

    Per-Sequence Optimization Baseline. To perform a more comprehensive evaluation of FlowRig in dynamic reconstruction, we include a per-sequence optimization 4D baseline, RigGS [(Yao et al., 2025b)]. This model takes video as input and produces a skeleton together with 3D Gaussians, so we render each mesh sequence to video and supply the ground-truth masks its pipeline requires. Additionally, its output lives in its own coordinate frame, so we align the generated skeleton to the ground truth in scale, position, and orientation before computing metrics. Both steps are concessions in RigGS’s favour.

    Experiment Setup. RigGS optimizes every sequence from scratch and takes 17 minutes per 8-frame instance on an H200, so running it on the full 1,656-instance Objaverse set of W3 would cost 469 H200 GPU hours, against about 2 GPU hours for FlowRig. We therefore sample up to 20 instances per category, giving 193 instances across the ten categories and roughly 57 H200 GPU hours. All methods are evaluated on the same subsample at T=8.

    Results. We conclude the following based on the results in Tables S6, S6, and S6:

  • •

    FlowRig leads in 28 of the 30 category-metric cells. In aggregate, Ours* is 19.3% below RigGS and 19.2% below Puppeteer-D* on MACRO J2J, 20.2% and 25.5% below on J2B, and 22.5% and 26.6% below on B2B; MICRO gives the same picture. The two exceptions are fish on J2J and J2B, where RigGS leads by 0.4% and 0.5%, plausibly because fish motion is smooth and low in degrees of freedom, which suits per-sequence fitting.

  • •

    Per-sequence optimization is not uniformly stronger than a fine-tuned static rigger. RigGS and Puppeteer-D* are level on MACRO J2J (0.0636 vs. 0.0635), and RigGS leads only on J2B and B2B (6.7% and 5.2%). Optimizing each sequence individually does not by itself buy joint accuracy.

  • •

    The cost gap is over two orders of magnitude. RigGS needs 17 minutes per 8-frame instance where FlowRig needs 4.4s in a single feedforward pass (Table S2), roughly 230 times faster, which is what makes evaluation at the scale of the full set practical at all.

    Appendix F Skinning Model

    To animate mesh by the generated skeleton, we additionally train an attention-based skinning network, denoted SkinningTransformer, to predict soft skinning weights from a mesh observation and its associated skeletal rig. Given a mesh and a rig with J≤J_\max joints, our goal is to predict, for each queried surface point q∈{1,…,N_q}, a categorical distribution over valid joints. Each sample contains N_q sampled query points with normals, a padded bone tensor storing parent and child joint coordinates for each bone slot, a validity mask over joint slots, and a ground-truth skinning distribution over valid joints. Formally, for a query point q we model

    p(w_q|M,B,p_q,G), w_q∈ℝ^J_\max, ∑ⱼ₌₁^J_\maxw_q,j=1,

    		(S8)

    where p_q∈ℝ⁶ is the queried point-and-normal feature, M denotes the frozen mesh encoders, and G denotes the skeletal graph structure.

    Frozen geometry encoders. We condition the skinning model on two frozen geometry pathways. First, a Michelangelo shape encoder [(Zhao et al., 2023b)] produces a compact set of global shape tokens Fₛₕₐₚₑ∈ℝ^257×768. Second, the PartField encoder [(Liu et al., 2025b)] produces dense query features on sampled surface locations, F_pf^surf∈ℝ^N_q×448, where N_q is the number of sampled surface queries and PF(·) denotes the frozen part-aware field encoder. When skeleton-side part features are enabled, we also evaluate this field at the parent and child joint locations xᵖᵃʳⱼ,xᶜʰᵈⱼ∈ℝ³ of bone j and average them per bone,

    F_pf,jˢᵏᵉˡ=\tfrac12(PF(xᵖᵃʳⱼ)+PF(xᶜʰᵈⱼ))∈ℝ⁴⁴⁸.

    		(S9)

    These encoders remain frozen throughout training.

    Shape-skeleton fusion encoder. All conditioning features are projected into a shared transformer width d. Let B∈ℝ^J_\max×6 denote the padded bone tensor, where each row stores the concatenated parent and child joint coordinates of one bone. The learned projection matrices satisfy Wₛ∈ℝ^768×d, Wⱼ∈ℝ^6×d, Wˢᵖ∈ℝ^448×d, and Wₚ∈ℝ^448×d. We form projected shape and bone tokens as

    F^′ₛₕₐₚₑ=FₛₕₐₚₑWₛ, H⁽⁰⁾_bone=BWⱼ+𝔼ᵖᵒˢ_:J_\max+[F_pfˢᵏᵉˡWˢᵖ],

    		(S10)

    where 𝔼ᵖᵒˢ_:J_\max∈ℝ^J_\max×d is a learnable positional embedding for bone slots and the last term is optional. The encoder input is then

    Z⁽⁰⁾=Concat(F^′ₛₕₐₚₑ,H⁽⁰⁾_bone)∈ℝ^L_enc×d, L_enc=257+J_\max.

    		(S11)

    A stack of transformer encoder blocks updates Z, while invalid joint slots are masked so that padded joints do not participate in attention.

    Topology-aware joint attention. To encode skeletal structure explicitly, we inject a topology-aware bias into self-attention over the bone tokens [(Song et al., 2025a)]. Let D∈ℝ^J_\max×J_\max denote the pairwise graph-distance matrix on the skeleton. Distances are clamped into a small set of buckets and projected into per-head biases. The attention score for head h, with query/key head dimension dₕ, becomes

    score⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ=(Q⁽ʰ⁾ᵢK⁽ʰ⁾ⱼ^⊤)/(√dₕ)+λₜₐⱼₐ b⁽ʰ⁾ᵢⱼ(D),

    		(S12)

    for bone-token indices i and j. This topology-aware joint attention encourages joints that are nearby in the kinematic tree to exchange information more strongly.

    Point-wise cross-attention decoder. Surface query tokens are initialized from projected part-aware point features,

    H⁽⁰⁾ₚₜ=F^surf_pfWₚ∈ℝ^N_q×d.

    		(S13)

    Optionally, Fourier positional encodings of the queried coordinates and normals are added to these tokens. The decoder then refines point tokens purely through cross-attention to the encoder memory. There is no decoder self-attention; interaction among queries is mediated through the shared shape-skeleton memory.

    Scaled cosine prediction head. The final logits are computed by cosine similarity between normalized point embeddings and normalized joint embeddings, scaled by a learnable factor α, where z_qj is the logit for assigning query point q to joint j,

    z_qj=(|α|+ε)·(Fᵒᵘᵗₚₜ(q))/(∥Fᵒᵘᵗₚₜ(q)∥₂)·(Fʲᵒⁱⁿᵗ_bone(j))/(∥Fʲᵒⁱⁿᵗ_bone(j)∥₂).

    		(S14)

    Invalid joint logits are masked before normalization, and skinning probabilities are obtained by

    w_q=softmax(z_q).

    		(S15)

    This design makes the prediction explicitly probabilistic and naturally handles variable valid-joint sets through masking.

    Training objective. We optimize the skinning network with a masked soft cross-entropy objective together with an L₁ loss in probability space. Let Y denote the target weight distributions and let Z denote the predicted logits. The overall loss is

    L=L_CE(Y,Z;m)+λ_ℓ₁ L_L₁(σ(Z),Y;m),

    		(S16)

item.title: 只有一张参考图也能个性化：One Image Is Enough 在推理时自己造监督，把姿态驱动的人物视频做稳 ｜ One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time
item.description:
一句话：个性化缺的是监督信号：一张图只固定一个姿态，多姿态人物视频又不一定有。

要点：

  • 任务与失效：姿态驱动的人物视频扩散能从单张参考图和目标姿态序列生成动作，但姿态偏离参考图后身份保持变差，脸和衣服走形
  • 个性化的标准解法需要监督，而这里恰好没有：单张图只固定了一个姿态，实践中又不能假设存在多姿态的人物视频
  • 做法是把缺失的监督造出来：用一个域内微调、姿态条件的生成器在关键姿态上产出伪真值帧，再配合推理期的仅参考采样

为什么值得看：虚拟人、NPC 与数字主播都要「一张图就能动」，而现在多要求一段多视角或多姿态素材。把个性化搬到测试时、用自生成监督补上，等于把素材门槛从「一段视频」降到「一张图」。

中文摘要：姿态驱动的人物视频扩散模型能从单张参考图和目标姿态序列生成动作，但姿态一旦偏离参考图，身份保持就会变差，脸与服装出现走形。标准解法是个性化，可它需要监督信号——而这里恰恰没有：一张图只固定了单一姿态，实践中又不能假设存在多姿态的人物视频。作者的思路是把缺失的监督造出来：先用一个域内微调、以姿态为条件的生成器在若干关键姿态上合成伪真值帧，再配合推理阶段「仅依赖参考图」的采样策略完成个性化。对虚拟人、NPC 与数字主播这类需要「一张图就能动」的场景，这把素材门槛从一段视频降到一张图。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-02

本期推送：2026-11-05

One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time

Abstract

Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.

1 Introduction

Given a single reference image of a person and a driving pose sequence, pose-driven human video diffusion models aim to animate the reference subject under the target motion. Recent advances in large-scale video diffusion have substantially improved motion realism, temporal coherence, and overall visual fidelity. However, it is still a challenging problem to faithfully preserve the subject’s identity. For example, facial appearance may be generated inconsistently across frames, while fine-grained garment details, text, and logos can be distorted, altered, or hallucinated.

Rather than relying solely on a larger video diffusion backbone, we focus on personalizing the model to the input subject at test time. A single reference image, however, provides limited adaptation signals: it captures the subject in only one pose and cannot supervise identity preservation across the diverse poses in the driving sequence. We therefore construct pose-diverse pseudo-supervision at inference time.

Specifically, a pose-conditioned, reference-following image diffusion model synthesizes subject-specific images for poses sampled from the driving sequence. More importantly, an inference-time particle-steering procedure, guided by body-similarity and facial-identity rewards, selects high-quality identity-consistent samples without subject videos, target-frame annotations, or human feedback.

Given the pseudo ground truth frames, directly adapting a video diffusion model to static subject images can weaken its motion prior, reducing dynamics and temporal consistency. This identity-and-motion trade-off  [4, 61, 23, 22] is particularly challenging for unified attention video DiTs  [45, 62, 9], whose 3D self-attention jointly models appearance and motion without separable appearance-only parameters [45, 62, 9]. We address this issue by repeating each synthetic image into a static clip and optimizing a lightweight subject-specific LoRA on these appearance-focused clips. This strategy improves identity preservation while retaining the backbone’s motion capability and video quality.

We validate the approach on the TikTok and UBC Fashion benchmarks. The largest gain is on video quality: adaptation substantially lowers FVD where naive personalization is expected to degrade it, so identity and video quality improve together rather than trading off. The same adaptation transfers to in-the-wild videos unseen during training, since the supervision is generated for each test subject rather than learned from a dataset-specific prior. The adaptation restores the face and fine garment detail that the base model distorts as the body turns away from the reference pose. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We propose a test-time personalization framework for pose-driven human video diffusion from a single image, requiring no ground truth, no real captured frames, and no human feedback.

  • •

    A reward-guided generation approach is proposed for synthesizing pseudo-ground-truth images, using body-similarity and facial-identity rewards that measure consistency with the reference image.

  • •

    Our method achieves the best results on most metrics across benchmarks, surpassing the non-personalized base on every metric and matching or surpassing a model personalized with real captured subject frames.

    • 2 Related Work

    Pose-driven human animation. Pose-driven human image animation has converged on the setting we study: a single reference image is animated according to a target body-pose or motion sequence. Early diffusion models established the now-standard recipe of reference appearance injection, pose-guided denoising, and temporal modules for video synthesis [14, 53]. Follow-up work makes this recipe practical in open-source form [39, 31] and improves pose confidence and long-video fusion [59]. Others inject SMPL-derived depth, normal, semantic, and skeleton cues [63], study efficient control modules [33], and unify reference appearance and target-pose conditioning in a single video diffusion branch [44]. Recent DiT-based work further shows that larger video backbones, compact pose encoders, motion tokens, text/background control, and hard-motion training can substantially improve pose following and temporal quality [62, 45, 60, 9, 25, 51].

    These works are primarily trained as feed-forward general animators, and do not adapt the model to the test subject by constructing pose-specific supervision from the given reference image. Our work therefore focuses on reducing per-subject identity, clothing, and hard-pose errors after the target motion is known, rather than introducing another generic pose-control branch.

    Personalization and test-time adaptation. Diffusion personalization methods show that few-shot subject binding can be achieved by fine-tuning model weights, learning new tokens, or updating compact adapter parameters [34, 10, 19, 13, 11]. Video customization work highlights a related but sharper problem: static subject reconstruction can damage the motion prior, reducing dynamics, temporal consistency, or prompt adherence. Prior video customization methods study one-shot video tuning from real videos [49]. Others add subject and motion adapters, image-prompt conditioning, frozen videos, dynamic denoising weights, reward supervision, preference pairs, and DiT LoRA tuning [48, 17, 61, 30, 4, 50, 23, 22, 29]. These methods diagnose the same identity-versus-motion tension that appears in pose-driven animation. Still-Moving [4] originates the frozen-clip supervision we adopt, training adapters on still images replicated over time. There the construction is a liability: it leaves the model producing nearly static videos unless a Motion Adapter on the temporal-attention layers, trained on 1,600 real videos, absorbs the effect. Neither remedy transfers, since a unified 3D-attention DiT has no temporal-only layer and we use no real video. The difference is what the conditioning asks for. A text prompt demands motion the frozen clip does not show, whereas our pose is held constant across the clip. StableAnimator [41] attacks the same problem by training an identity adapter into a video diffusion model and steering denoising with a face reward at inference. The reward there acts on the delivered video, whereas ours acts on the supervision frames and the animator is never rewarded. Wan-Dancer [15] builds long dance videos on the same Wan backbone from music rather than a driving pose, and names identity consistency over long sequences as open future work, which is the failure mode our per-reference adaptation targets.

    In contrast, our input is one still reference image rather than a subject video, the control signal is an explicit target pose sequence, and we adapt at test time on pseudo-examples tied to the poses the model must render.

    Self-generated and synthetic supervision. Generated supervision is also well established in diffusion personalization and view synthesis. Prior work uses generated class images for prior preservation [34], distills synthetic expert customizations into amortized personalization models [6], and builds synthetic preference pairs for image personalization [1]. Other methods use synthetic motion, generated views, uncertainty weighting, hallucination maps, or partial-reference quality measures to avoid poisoning downstream optimization [18, 24, 40, 26, 7]. Test-time self-improvement and generated-support-view pipelines have also appeared for video generation and sparse-view NVS [27, 37, 52, 5].

    The distinction in our setting is the target and use of the generated supervision. The single test reference produces candidate human frames at poses sampled from the driving sequence. Those candidates are filtered for identity and image quality, and the selected pseudo-pairs supervise per-subject adaptation of the pose-driven video model. Thus, the self-generated data are neither generic class regularizers nor free-view support images, but pose-targeted evidence for the exact subject-motion pair being requested.

    Inference-time guidance and reward-guided sampling. A complementary line steers diffusion at inference time without retraining, either by resampling a population of particles toward a reward [36] or by searching the noise space with verifiers [28]. DINO- and identity-based rewards are standard signals for subject fidelity [32, 8, 47], and best-of-N selection is the simplest such scheme. Closest to our use, IPRO [35] optimizes an ArcFace identity reward, but as train-time reinforcement learning of the video model, and IPRO scores against ground-truth video frames.

    We instead apply a training-free, reference-only sampler at the pseudo-supervision stage. A DINO body-similarity reward steers candidate frames in-loop, and an ArcFace reward selects the final one, anchored entirely to the single reference image, with no ground truth and no model fine-tuning. Our contribution is this adaptation to the single-reference video-personalization setting.

    3 Method

    Our goal is to personalize a frozen pose-driven video model to a subject from a single reference image, with no subject video, ground-truth frames, or labels available. We therefore synthesize the supervision. From the reference image x_ref and the driving pose sequence ℙ, a pose-conditioned generator produces a pseudo-ground-truth frame of the subject at each of a few key poses sampled from ℙ. Each frame is steered and selected by its identity match to the reference (Sec.3.2). A per-subject LoRA then adapts the base animator on static clips of these frames (Sec.3.3). Fig.2 shows the pipeline, and Algorithm2 states it in full. We begin with the preliminaries and problem setup (Sec.3.1).

    3.1 Preliminaries

    At test time we are given a single reference image x_ref and a driving pose sequence ℙ={pₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, and seek a video V̂={v̂ₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ in which the subject of x_ref performs ℙ while retaining its appearance.

    The base animator F_θ is a latent video diffusion model. An encoder maps each frame to a latent z. A forward process adds Gaussian noise over diffusion steps τ,

    q(z_τ|z_τ-1)=ℕ (z_τ; √1-β_τ z_τ-1, β_τI),

    		(1)

    and F_θ is trained to reverse it under conditioning c=(x_ref,ℙ),

    L(θ)=𝔼_z, c, ε, τ\lVert ε-ε_θ(z_τ,τ,c) \rVert₂², ε∼ℕ(0,I).

    		(2)

    At inference F_θ maps (x_ref,ℙ) to a video but does not reliably preserve the reference identity as the pose departs from the reference.

    Personalization adapts the base through a small per-subject low-rank update Δθ, yielding the adapted model F_θ+Δθ. Since neither subject video nor ground-truth frames are available, we draw the supervision from a pose-conditioned generator G, whose selected pseudo frames D_pseudo stand in for the absent subject data (Sec.3.2).

    3.2 Reference-only reward-guided generation

    Pose-conditioned generator G. We build G from FLUX.1 Kontext [21], a FLUX.1 [20] variant with strong reference and prior preservation, augmented with a pose ControlNet [57]. We domain-tune G for this task. Given the reference image x_ref and a target pose, G renders the subject in that pose while preserving identity. During training, we freeze the base weights of G and optimize a low-rank LoRA injected into its DiT attention blocks. Each training step draws a two-frame pair from an in-domain video: one frame serves as the reference, and G must reconstruct the second frame from its 2D pose. The optimizer, schedule, and trained layers are in Appendix A.

    Pose-targeted synthesis. From the driving sequence ℙ we select K key poses ℙ_K⊂ℙ by farthest-point sampling in keypoint space, anchored at the reference pose. This concentrates the supervision on the hard poses the video model F_θ must render and spans the range of motion. For each key pose pₖ∈ℙ_K the generator must produce one frame that is faithful to the subject and of sufficient quality to supervise appearance.

    Reward-guided sampling. Rather than draw N independent candidates and keep the best (best-of-N), we sample the N candidates as an interacting particle system and steer them while they denoise. We adapt inference-time particle steering [36, 28] to our task with two novel changes specific to the single-reference setting. First, every reward is derived from the reference image alone. No ground-truth target frame exists, so the guidance signal is self-supervised. Second, we split the reward by role.

    An in-loop steering reward Rₛ(x)=w_b DINO(x,x_ref)+w_σ sharp(x) combines body and appearance similarity to the reference, read from a DINOv2 encoder [32], with an image-sharpness term. At scheduled denoising steps, the particles are resampled in proportion to \exp(λRₛ), so sampling compute concentrates on the trajectories that already resemble the subject (Algorithm1). We resample only in the back half of denoising. Early, high-noise particles lack the structure for the reward to be informative, so the first half runs as a plain deterministic ODE, and steering it would only collapse diversity. After each resampling, a churn step re-noises the particles at strength η, so that duplicated high-reward particles diverge rather than remaining identical under the deterministic dynamics.

    A final selection reward R_f(x)=ArcFace(x,x_ref)[8] then picks the surviving candidate with the highest face identity. We steer in-loop with the dense, inexpensive DINO signal and reserve the sharper but detector-sensitive ArcFace score for the single final choice, where it is most reliable. At an equal sampling budget, the reward-guided sampler improves identity and video quality over best-of-N (the no-steering rows of Tab.7).

    The selected pair (xₖ^*,pₖ) enters the pseudo-supervision set D_pseudo={(xₖ^*,pₖ)}ₖ₌₁^K. Each selected frame captures a single pose. Replicated into a static clip for adaptation (Sec.3.3), it carries no inter-frame motion, unlike real video frames captured from a subject in motion. Reward-guided sampling and DINO- or identity-based rewards are each established [36, 47, 35]. Unlike reward fine-tuning against ground-truth video [35, 54], ours is training-free, uses only the reference image as its target, and acts at the pseudo-supervision stage. The novelty in our setting is that these frames are pose-targeted to the test subject’s driving sequence, then reward-steered against the reference before they supervise.

    3.3 Test-time adaptation

    Static-clip adaptation. We adapt only a low-rank update Δθ (LoRA [13]) of rank r on F_θ, and keep θ frozen. We train Δθ by minimizing an adaptation loss L_adapt on D_pseudo. Each adaptation step uses one selected frame xₖ^*. We replicate xₖ^* into a clip and hold the pose pₖ constant across every frame of that clip, then train F_θ+Δθ to reconstruct it. The static clip carries no motion. Writing clip(x)=[x,…,x] for the T-frame replication and z_τᵏ for the noised latent of 𝔼(clip(xₖ^*)),

    L_adapt(Δθ)=∑ₖ₌₁^K𝔼_τ,ε\lVertε-ε_θ+Δθ(z_τᵏ,τ,(x_ref,pₖ))\rVert₂²,

    		(3)

    so the pose pₖ stays fixed across the clip and the temporal pathway sees no motion during adaptation.

    A multi-frame clip of distinct pseudo poses would re-introduce motion into the temporal pathways of the unified self-attention DiT. That motion reproduces the canonical motion-prior damage seen in video personalization [4, 61, 23, 22]. The static clip removes that signal, so adaptation updates appearance only. Prior fixes that decouple spatial parameters from temporal parameters [29] do not transfer to unified-attention DiTs, where one attention operation mixes both. We therefore control motion through the data rather than the parameterization. Removing the static clip drops identity below the base model and worsens temporal consistency, as we report in Tab.4. At inference, the adapted model F_θ+Δθ renders x_ref along the full driving sequence ℙ to produce V̂.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Datasets. For in-domain training and evaluation we use the TikTok [16] and UBC Fashion [56] benchmarks with their standard train and test splits. To probe cross-domain transfer, we additionally evaluate zero-shot on Unseen100-Val, a set of 100 in-the-wild videos spanning diverse subjects, motion, lighting, and backgrounds (Tab.2). Full dataset details are in Appendix D.

    Evaluation. We follow the evaluation protocol of RealisDance-DiT [62] for all comparisons, covering reconstruction, perceptual, identity, and video-quality metrics. Metric definitions are in Appendix B, and the full protocol in Appendix D.2.

    4.2 Implementation details

    Base animator. The base animator F_θ is UniAnimate-DiT [45], a pose-driven human video DiT built on Wan2.1-I2V (14B) [43]. It uses a single unified 3D self-attention stack that models space and time jointly. Reference conditioning enters through dual cross-attention with dedicated image-token projections, and the target pose is injected as a residual at the latent entry. We keep θ frozen and adapt only the low-rank update Δθ of rank r.

    Generator. We build the pose-conditioned generator G on FLUX.1 Kontext [21] with a pose ControlNet [57] and freeze its base. We train a low-rank LoRA on its DiT attention blocks ourselves, on the in-domain training split of each benchmark, with the two-frame reconstruction objective of Sec.3.2. We optimize with AdamW at a constant learning rate for 4,000 steps on a single H100 GPU. The LoRA rank, schedule, and trained layers are in Appendix A.

    Adaptation. By default we synthesize K=5 pseudo frames, each selected from N=8 reward-guided particles, and train the rank-r LoRA on static clips of these frames. The K target poses, and the K real frames of the Real-5 baseline, are the same indices, chosen by farthest-point sampling over the driving poses and seeded at the reference frame, so they span the pose range rather than the timeline. We study how cost and quality scale with the number of fine-tuning steps in Appendix C.1. Full hyperparameters are in Appendix A.

    Test-time cost.Table8 reports the wall-clock and peak GPU memory of each stage on a single H100. The method has two distinct costs, with different hardware requirements. Generation and adaptation run once per reference image and take 9.3 minutes together, peaking at 62.1 GiB. That peak is dominated by the frozen base model, which accounts for 70% of it, against 15% for the low-rank update and its optimizer state (Tab.18). Inference is the recurring cost. It is unchanged by adaptation, since merging the update adds no parameters at inference, and it peaks at 21.6 GiB, within a 24 GB card. The two costs separate in deployment: the one-time stage runs server-side and produces a 1.1 GiB adapter, after which inference proceeds at base cost. Appendix F gives the measurement protocol and the full breakdown.

    4.3 Comparison with the state of the art

    In-domain.Table1 compares against eight pose-driven animators on TikTok and Fashion dataset. Our test-time adaptation improves the UniAnimate-DiT base on every metric and gives the best result on most metrics. The largest gain is on video quality: FVD on TikTok falls below every prior method. Three aspects of this result are worth mentioning: the gain lands on the metric that personalization usually degrades, it requires no subject video, and reconstruction and identity improve in step rather than trading against video quality. Figure4 shows the effect on hard poses, where the base and competing animators reconstruct identity inconsistently while our adapted model preserves the face and garment. Additional qualitative results are in Appendix E.

    Out-of-domain. Trained on TikTok and evaluated on the out-of-domain Unseen100-Val set (Tab.2), the adaptation transfers. It leads all methods and improves over the base on every metric, cutting FVD by roughly a quarter, with the prior animators further behind. The advantage holds under domain shift because the supervision is generated for the test subject rather than learned from the training distribution, so it does not inherit a dataset-specific prior.

    Cross-reenactment. When one subject is driven by another subject’s motion, no aligned ground truth exists, so we measure identity against the reference (Tab.3). Adaptation improves appearance fidelity (FaceID, BodySIM) while pose obedience (PoseAcc) is essentially unchanged, since the pose-conditioning pathway stays frozen. The adaptation thus binds appearance without disturbing the motion pathway, the asymmetry the static-clip recipe is designed to produce.

    4.4 Ablations and analysis

    Contribution of each component.Table4 removes one component at a time. Removing the reward-guided frame selection raises FVD as lower-quality pseudo frames enter adaptation. Dropping the static clip is the most damaging: identity falls and temporal consistency degrades past the base itself (dtSSD 369.0→416.3). This confirms that multi-pose clips push motion back into the temporal pathway.

    The full system also improves on adaptation on five real subject frames (Real-5) in FVD while using none, and matches it on identity, inverting the usual trade-off. The standalone generator G attains the highest per-frame identity but has no temporal model and cannot produce coherent video.

    Supervision source. Holding the adaptation fixed and varying only the supervision source isolates what drives the gain (Tab.5). Self-distillation adapts the base on its own outputs. It does not improve reconstruction and worsens temporal consistency, pushing dtSSD above the base, and scarcely improves identity, since those outputs carry the motion artifacts of a video model. Real frames help more, and our clean, static pseudo-GT from G helps most, cutting FVD to 133.5. Figure5(b) summarizes this across all seven metrics.

    Number of pseudo frames. FVD is lowest at K=5, our default, and both FVD and identity degrade at K=9 as extra frames expose generator artifacts (Fig.5(a), Tab.6). A larger K=21 reaches the highest full-video FaceID (0.626) but trades away the balanced result, while a small K under-covers the motion the model must render. The fine-tuning-time and generator ablations are in Appendix C.

    Steering and selection rewards. The reward-guided sampler reads two reference-only rewards in distinct roles, and Tab.7 shows both assignments matter. Its no-steering (i.i.d.) rows are the best-of-N baseline, which in-loop steering improves on at an equal budget. The dense but coarse DINO reward steers the particle population best. The sharp but detector-sensitive ArcFace reward is unreliable as an in-loop signal on the occluded, fast-moving faces typical of dance, but is decisive as the final selection. Steering with DINO and selecting with ArcFace is therefore our default.

    Temporal stability. The gains do not come at the cost of motion. Figure3 shows that adaptation confines inter-frame residual to true motion boundaries rather than spreading it across the face and torso. Identity improves without the flicker that personalization usually introduces.

    5 Conclusion

    We personalize a pose-driven human video model to a subject from a single reference image, with no subject video and no ground truth. A pose-conditioned generator synthesizes pseudo-ground-truth frames at the poses the driving sequence requires, steered and selected by reference-only rewards, and a per-subject LoRA adapts the base animator on static clips of them. The static clip, which we adopt from prior work, supplies subject appearance while carrying no motion, so the adaptation binds identity without disturbing the temporal prior. Personalization then improves identity and reconstruction and even improves video quality (FVD), the metric it usually degrades, and the gains transfer to out-of-domain subjects because the supervision is generated for the test subject rather than learned from a training distribution. The adapted model surpasses its non-personalized base on every metric and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real subject frames despite using none, inverting the trade-off personalization usually incurs.

    Limitations and future work. The method inherits the quality of its generator G, since a degraded pseudo frame weakens the adaptation, so rejecting blurred or occluded frames is a simple safeguard (App. G). The reference-only rewards are fixed and hand-weighted, and learning them would raise the ceiling G imposes. The adapted model’s own outputs could re-supervise G in a closed loop. Because the adaptation never touches the backbone, it should carry over to stronger animators as they appear.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for
    Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time
    Supplementary Material

    Table of Contents

    Appendix A Further Implementation Details

    A.1 Base Model and Generator Architectures

    The base animator F_θ is UniAnimate-DiT [45], a pose-driven human video diffusion transformer built on the Wan2.1-I2V (14B) backbone [43]. It operates in the compressed latent space of a frozen video VAE and conditions on three streams: a reference-appearance stream, in which the source image is encoded by the frozen VAE encoder and concatenated with the noisy video latents to preserve high-frequency detail; a target-pose stream, which injects the driving skeleton as a residual at the latent entry; and dual cross-attention with dedicated image-token projections for reference alignment. The backbone uses a single unified 3D self-attention stack that models space and time jointly. We keep all pre-trained parameters frozen and adapt only a per-subject low-rank update Δθ.

    The generator G is built on FLUX.1 Kontext [21], a FLUX.1 [20] variant chosen for its strong reference and prior preservation, paired with a pose ControlNet [57] (Fig.6). We freeze the base and train a low-rank LoRA [13] on its DiT attention blocks with the two-frame reconstruction objective of the main paper, so that G renders the reference subject under a target pose while preserving identity.

    A.2 Key-pose and frame selection

    Which poses are supervised. We do not generate a frame for every pose in ℙ; we supervise only a small set of K key poses. The key poses are chosen by greedy farthest-point sampling in 2D keypoint space, initialized at the reference pose and adding, at each step, the pose whose minimum keypoint distance to the already-selected set is largest. This spreads the key poses across the range of motion and concentrates supervision on the poses farthest from the reference, which the base animator renders worst. The keypoint distance is the mean per-joint Euclidean distance between the normalized 2D whole-body keypoints (extracted by DWPose [55]) of the two frames. By default K=5: the reference pose plus the four farthest poses. For example, on TikTok sequence 07 the selected key frames are {0, 38, 53, 57, 71} of the 305-frame clip.

    Which frame is kept. For each key pose, the reward-guided sampler (Algorithm1) produces a single frame: N particles denoise under in-loop DINO steering toward x_ref, and the surviving candidate with the highest ArcFace identity is kept. There is no post-hoc filtering of a larger pool; selection is the in-loop steering followed by the final ArcFace pick. We use N=8 particles and resample at |ℝ|=3 points evenly spaced over the back half of the 30-step denoising schedule (start fraction 0.5; resample steps {18,22,25}), injecting churn η=0.5 so cloned winners diverge under the otherwise-deterministic dynamics. The in-loop steering reward weights a DINOv2 body-similarity term (w_b=1.0) and a Laplacian sharpness term (w_σ=0.5); the surviving per-pose candidate is then chosen by maximum ArcFace identity to x_ref.

    A.3 Efficient Adaptation via LoRA

    We inject LoRA [13] into the query, key, value, and output projections of the attention blocks and the two feed-forward layers (ffn.0,ffn.2) of every transformer block, with rank r and scaling α=r following standard convention. Freezing the backbone and adapting only these low-rank factors keeps the trainable parameter count a small fraction of the backbone and the adaptation fast. Concretely, the animator F uses r=128 (α=128) on {q,k,v,o,ffn.0,ffn.2} of each DiT block (≈ 0.61B trainable parameters, ∼ 4% of the frozen 14B backbone), and the generator G uses r=64 on its DiT attention, feed-forward, and modulation projections (≈ 0.31B trainable parameters).

    A.4 Training Details

    Generator training. We optimize G with AdamW at a constant learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴ for 4,000 steps on a single H100 GPU, on the in-domain training split of each benchmark. We train at LoRA rank r=64 with one (reference, target) frame pair per step and gradient checkpointing; supervision is real frame pairs, so no photometric augmentation is applied. The cross-frame pairing itself supplies the pose variation.

    Per-subject adaptation. At test time we synthesize K pseudo frames, replicate each into a static clip, and adapt Δθ on these clips. Adaptation is a one-time per-subject cost; once Δθ is obtained, inference along an arbitrary driving sequence requires no further optimization. Adaptation uses AdamW at learning rate 1×10⁻⁴ for 5 steps by default (Tab.10 sweeps 5–400).

    Appendix B Evaluation Metrics

    We provide the formulations of every metric used in our experiments. Let Iₜ and Îₜ denote the ground-truth and generated frames at time t, with spatial size H×W, C channels, and T total frames.

    PSNR. From the per-frame mean squared error MSE=\tfrac1HWC∑_x,y,c(Iₜ(x,y,c)-Îₜ(x,y,c))²,

    PSNR=20\log₁₀ ((255)/(√MSE)),

    		(4)

    averaged over frames. Higher is better.

    SSIM. Structural similarity [46] compares local luminance, contrast, and structure between Iₜ and Îₜ. We report the mean over all frames and channels. Higher is better.

    LPIPS. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity [58] measures the distance between deep features of Iₜ and Îₜ from a pre-trained backbone, averaged over frames. Lower is better.

    FID. Fréchet Inception Distance [12] compares Gaussian statistics (μᵣ,Σᵣ) and (μ_f,Σ_f) of real and generated frame features from a pre-trained Inception network,

    FID=\lVertμᵣ-μ_f\rVert₂²+Tr (Σᵣ+Σ_f-2(ΣᵣΣ_f)^1/2).

    		(5)

    FVD. Fréchet Video Distance [42] applies the same form to spatiotemporal features extracted by an Inflated 3D ConvNet [3] from fixed-length video segments, capturing temporal realism. Lower is better.

    FID-VID. A video-level variant [2] that aggregates clip embeddings into a single descriptor per sequence before computing the Fréchet distance, capturing long-range temporal consistency. Lower is better.

    FaceID. Facial identity preservation is the cosine similarity between ArcFace [8] embeddings of the generated and reference faces, averaged over frames. Higher is better.

    BodySIM. Body-appearance similarity is the cosine similarity between DINOv2 [32] embeddings of the generated and reference subject crops. Higher is better.

    dtSSD. Temporal consistency is measured on inter-frame differences: we compare the temporal gradient of the generated video, Îₜ₊₁-Îₜ, against that of the reference video, Iₜ₊₁-Iₜ, and report the mean squared deviation over time. Lower indicates motion closer to the ground truth without added flicker.

    PoseAcc. Pose-following accuracy compares the skeleton extracted from the generated frame against the driving skeleton, reporting keypoint agreement. Poses are extracted with DWPose [55] from both the generated and the ground-truth frame, and agreement is the percentage of correct keypoints (PCK@0.2): a predicted joint is counted correct when its distance to the corresponding ground-truth joint is within 0.2 of the person bounding-box size. Higher indicates closer adherence to the target motion.

    We follow the overall evaluation protocol of RealisDance-DiT [62] (see Sec.D.2).

    B.1 Identity under independent recognizers

    FaceID is ArcFace cosine and BodySIM is DINOv2 cosine, and those same two networks drive the pipeline: candidates are selected by ArcFace similarity to the reference and sampling is steered by DINOv2 body similarity. To verify that an identity gain measured with them reflects identity rather than the selection reward, Table9 re-scores the same rendered videos with recognizers that are not used at any stage of the pipeline. Two controls ensure a fair comparison: faces are detected and aligned once and every recognizer embeds the identical crop, so detector disagreement cannot appear as a difference between recognizers, and the scored set is fixed across arms, so no arm benefits from being evaluated on the frames on which its own faces are detectable.

    The gain persists and is larger under FaceNet512 (+0.059) and SFace (+0.067) than under ArcFace (+0.035). Exploiting ArcFace-specific artifacts would produce the opposite ordering. We also run the test in reverse, rebuilding the per-subject dataset by ranking the same candidate pool with FaceNet512 instead of ArcFace (Ours-FN in Tab.9). The two recognizers disagree on 7 of 12 selections, so the two training sets differ substantially. Scored with ArcFace, which it never optimized, Ours-FN gains +0.034 over the base. Although Ours-FN optimizes FaceNet512, it does not lead on FaceNet512: selection does not inflate the score of the network doing the selecting. Appearance evidence that does not depend on either reward is provided by LPIPS, which is computed on VGG features and improves substantially (0.177 vs 0.283, Tab.12). PSNR, SSIM and FVD are likewise reward-independent and all improve (Tab.1).

    B.2 Human preference study

    Every metric above is automatic, and two of them (FaceID, BodySIM) share their networks with the reward used to select pseudo-frames (Sec.B.1). We therefore also conducted a human study, which depends on neither.

    Thirty-four respondents rated clips from each method on a 1–5 scale along four axes: human appearance alignment, pose alignment, background alignment, and overall quality. Clips were drawn from the TikTok test split, method identities were hidden, and the presentation order of the four methods was shuffled per clip so that no position was systematically associated with one method. Each respondent saw the reference image alongside the clip, since appearance alignment is only meaningful relative to it. This yields 180 ratings per method per axis.

    Figure7 shows the resulting distributions. Ours places 93% of appearance-alignment ratings at 4–5 against 38% for the unadapted base, and leads on all four axes. The base model in turn leads both prior animators, which is consistent with the automatic metrics in Tab.1, and corroborates the perceptual metrics with judgments that depend on neither reward.

    Appendix C Further Ablation

    C.1 Additional Quantitative Results

    Quality versus fine-tuning time.Table10 studies how reconstruction, identity, and video quality scale with the number of per-subject fine-tuning steps and the corresponding wall-clock time on a single H100. Quality saturates by five steps, our default, and is flat over the rest of the sweep: five steps already match or exceed every larger budget on reconstruction and video quality, since the static clip presents the same target at every step and the low-rank update converges to it within a few updates. Longer budgets improve only identity, and not monotonically, so we adapt for five steps, at 5.8 s per subject. This sweep varies the step budget only. Peak GPU memory, the hardware requirement, and the cost of the other pipeline stages are reported separately in AppendixF.

    Per-subject LoRA rank.Table11 sweeps the rank r of the per-subject update on a tuning subset. Quality improves with adapter capacity up to r=128, our default. At r=256 the adapter over-fits the handful of pseudo-frames and quality regresses, marking 128 as a clear optimum.

    C.2 Generator and Reward-Guided Sampling

    Our pipeline contains a second trained model, the pose-conditioned generator G, and a reference-only reward-guided sampler. We ablate their components here.

    How much domain tuning does G need?G’s LoRA is trained on the in-domain split of each benchmark, so the pipeline assumes access to a human-video corpus before test time, even though no video of the test subject is ever used. Table12 quantifies the effect of that assumption by sweeping the amount of tuning G receives, from none to our default. Two conclusions follow. First, the dependence is present but bounded: with an entirely untuned generator the adapted model still improves over the base on every metric (21.88 vs 20.33 PSNR, 0.184 vs 0.283 LPIPS). Second, the benefit of tuning depends on the metric. Pixel and perceptual quality saturate early: 500 steps, one eighth of the default, already recovers 95% of the PSNR gain over base, and LPIPS, SSIM and BodySIM are flat from there on. Identity does not: FaceID continues to increase to 4,000 (0.699→0.714→0.720→0.764), so 500 steps recovers only 66% of that gain. Domain tuning of G therefore primarily improves identity fidelity, as expected of a LoRA that teaches G the appearance statistics of the domain. Reconstruction quality requires only light tuning on a human-video corpus rather than close matching to the benchmark. Consistent with this, the G used for Unseen100-Val is tuned on TikTok yet leads on in-the-wild subjects (Tab.2). The gains concentrate on the sequence where the base model performs worst, where PSNR rises from 12.12 (base) to 17.39 (untuned G) to 20.50 (default). On sequences where the base already performs well, the tuning levels are indistinguishable.

    Particle count N.Table13 sweeps the number of particles N in the reward-guided sampler, reporting the fidelity of the selected pseudo-frame to the real frame. Frame quality is already largely saturated by our default N=8, while per-frame sampling time grows roughly linearly, so larger populations cost compute without further gain. The value of in-loop steering over best-of-N selection at a matched budget is established separately in Tab.7.

    Resampling schedule.Table14 varies the denoising window over which particles are resampled and the churn strength η. Pseudo-frame fidelity is largely insensitive to the schedule. We default to resampling only the back half with churn for its downstream stability, since steering early, high-noise particles collapses diversity before subject structure emerges and the churn step keeps duplicated high-reward particles from remaining identical under the deterministic dynamics.

    Key-pose selection.Table15 compares strategies for choosing the K supervised poses from the driving sequence. At fixed K, farthest-point sampling in keypoint space (ours), random, and uniform-in-time selection are within noise of one another, indicating the gain comes from supervising diverse poses at all rather than from the specific selection rule. We use farthest-point sampling as a principled default.

    Appendix D Dataset Curation & Evaluation Protocol

    D.1 Datasets

    For in-domain training and evaluation we use the TikTok [16] and UBC Fashion [56] benchmarks with their standard train and test splits. To probe cross-domain transfer, we additionally evaluate zero-shot on Unseen100-Val, a set of 100 in-the-wild videos spanning diverse subjects, motion, lighting, and backgrounds.

    Motivation. Both standard benchmarks are limited for evaluating modern video diffusion models. The TikTok test set contains only 10 videos, too few for fine-grained comparison, while UBC Fashion, though larger, consists of simple catwalk sequences with uniform lighting and minimal background variation, so scores saturate across methods (Tab.1). Neither covers the diversity of real-world deployment, including varied skin tones, challenging lighting, and non-photorealistic subjects. We therefore curate Unseen100-Val, a 100-video zero-shot evaluation set designed to (a) better represent the visual diversity of real-world data and (b) stress-test models in challenging settings they were not trained on, such as difficult lighting, complex backgrounds, and animated characters.

    Collection and eligibility. Videos are sourced from a mix of TikTok and stock footage. Each clip features a single person or character performing a dancing motion, with no heavy occlusion of any body part (slight tolerance is allowed for an arm briefly disappearing during fast motion), and the pose skeleton must remain fully visible throughout, ensuring reliable pose extraction for both adaptation and evaluation.

    Composition and diversity.Table16 summarizes the dataset composition across several axes; each attribute group independently covers all 100 videos. We deliberately balance real and animated subjects and ensure broad coverage of appearance, motion complexity, and environmental conditions. Among the 80 real-human videos, skin tones span East Asian, South Asian, Caucasian, and darker-skinned appearances to promote evaluation fairness; the 20 animated videos split evenly between 2D (anime, cartoon) and 3D (rendered, stylized) characters, testing generalization beyond photorealistic subjects.

    Preprocessing and statistics. All clips are center-cropped and resized to a common resolution, with driving poses extracted by a 2D keypoint detector consistent with our training pipeline. The detector is DWPose [55], the same whole-body extractor used to render the training pose maps; keypoints are extracted at the clip’s native resolution and rendered as skeleton maps at the model input resolution of 832×480. The average clip duration is 14.4 seconds (±3.2 s), ranging from 8 to 24 s. At 100 videos, Unseen100-Val matches the test-set size of UBC Fashion while being 10× larger than TikTok’s test split; because it targets zero-shot cross-domain evaluation rather than statistical power over a narrow domain, 100 diverse videos provide sufficient coverage to surface meaningful failure modes and performance differences across methods.

    D.2 Evaluation Protocol

    We follow the evaluation settings of RealisDance-DiT [62]. All generated videos are center-cropped and resized to a common resolution for metric computation, ensuring a fair comparison across methods that train at different native resolutions. For competing methods we use officially released checkpoints and evaluation code where available, and directly report published numbers where applicable. Our base animator and adapted model are sampled with the Wan2.1 flow-matching solver for 50 steps at classifier-free guidance scale 1.0, and metrics are computed at a common 832×480 resolution (image metrics on the trimmed window, video metrics over full clips). Pseudo-frames are generated with the fixed prompt “The person is dancing.” We do not re-train any competing method: their scores come from official checkpoints and evaluation code, or from the published papers where applicable. All baselines in Tab.1, including the UniAnimate-DiT base, are quoted from MTVCraft [9]; the base rows of Tabs.4 and 5 re-evaluate it under our protocol, so its numbers there differ.

    Appendix E Additional Qualitative Results

    We provide extended visual comparisons across subjects, motion types, and visual domains, including cross-domain subjects unseen during training. Figures8 and 9 give in-domain comparisons spanning diverse motions, backgrounds, appearance, and illumination, and Fig.10 shows cross-domain results on animated characters. Across all examples, the adapted model preserves the subject’s appearance while maintaining temporal coherence under challenging lighting and complex motion.

    Appendix F Test-Time Cost

    This section reports the cost of serving one reference image on a single H100: the wall-clock and peak GPU memory of every stage, how that memory is allocated, how it amortizes over repeated use, and the implications for deployment.

    F.1 Measurement protocol

    All numbers are measured on one NVIDIA H100 80 GB (driver 580.173) on a single TikTok test subject, with adaptation and inference at 832×480 and pseudo-frame generation at the generator’s native 576×1024, using the default recipe of Sec.4.2 (K=5 pseudo frames from N=8 reward-guided particles, rank-128 adapter, 5 adaptation steps). Peak memory is the maximum device memory sampled every 250 ms for the lifetime of the stage, cross-checked against the per-process figure. We report the device-level number because it includes the CUDA context and allocator reserve and is therefore what a deployment must provision. For the inference rows we also report the torch allocator peak: it runs ∼ 1 GiB lower, and quoting only the allocator figure would understate the requirement. Inference times exclude the one-off model load, which a deployment pays once rather than per video.

    F.2 Composition of the memory peak

    Table18 decomposes the adaptation peak. The frozen base model accounts for 70% of it, the video DiT contributing 49% and the text encoder, image encoder and VAE a further 21% between them. The per-subject update accounts for 15%, and is dominated not by the adapter weights (613M parameters, ≈ 4% of the backbone) but by the optimizer state they require, since the low-rank tensors are upcast to fp32 and AdamW keeps two moments per parameter. The remaining 15% is activations, workspace and allocator reserve.

    The adaptation requirement is therefore a property of fine-tuning this animator rather than of the supervision we propose. The Real-5 and reference-only arms of Tab.5 run the identical trainer at the identical rank and differ only in which frames they consume, so they occupy the same footprint, as would any adapter-based personalization of a backbone this size.

    Minimum GPU. The minimum GPU is therefore set by the frozen base model, not by our update: adaptation needs an 80 GB card, while inference needs only 24 GB, the same requirement as running the base animator unadapted.

    Inference requires far less memory despite using the same backbone, because it streams the DiT: only a 6B-parameter working set is resident and the remaining blocks are fetched layer-by-layer during the forward pass.

    F.3 Deployment and amortization

    The two costs are distinct. Adaptation is a one-time, server-side job of 9.3 minutes whose entire output is a 1.1 GiB adapter file. The 2.3 GiB training checkpoint additionally carries optimizer state, which is not part of the deployment payload. Once obtained, the adapter is reused for every video generated from that reference. Inference is the recurring cost and is unchanged from the base model, at identical peak memory and the same generation time to within run-to-run variance, so a user never requires training-grade hardware: the adapter is downloaded and inference runs at base cost.

    Table19 quantifies the benefit of repeated use. Because adaptation is paid per reference image and not per video, the average cost per video falls as 1/n: a reference animated 25 times costs 1.05× what the unadapted base would cost for the same 25 videos, and approaches parity beyond that. The regime where the overhead dominates is the single-video case, where the one-time stage is 1.25× the inference it enables. Adaptation is thus better characterized as a provisioning cost, paid once when a reference is enrolled, than as a per-request cost.

    Appendix G Limitations

    The method inherits the quality of its generator: when the generator produces weak pseudo-ground-truth for a subject (for example under heavy occlusion, motion blur, or strong out-of-domain appearance), the downstream per-subject adaptation is correspondingly weaker, since adaptation can only bind the appearance that the pseudo-ground-truth actually exposes. This motivates both the reference-only selection that curates high-quality pseudo frames and the closed-loop direction discussed in the conclusion, where the adapted model’s own outputs re-supervise the generator. A complementary safeguard is an automatic frame-quality filter that rejects blurred or occluded pseudo frames before adaptation. Figure11 illustrates how the adapted output tracks the quality of the pseudo-supervision.

    Appendix H Ethical Considerations & Broader Impact

    Our method lowers the cost of personalizing a human video model to a new subject: it needs a single reference image, no subject video, and no manual labels. This benefits creative content production, accessibility, and avatar applications, but the same capability warrants a discussion of misuse.

    Risk of misuse. The ease of synthesizing realistic video of a person from one image raises the risk of non-consensual or deceptive media, such as impersonation or misinformation. We condemn any use that depicts an individual without their explicit consent, and we intend any release to be governed by terms that prohibit such use.

    Data bias. Like all generative models, ours can inherit biases in its training data. If the underlying datasets underrepresent particular skin tones, body types, ages, or styles of dress, personalization quality may be uneven across groups. We encourage evaluation across diverse subjects, and our Unseen100-Val set is curated to include a broad range of appearances and conditions toward this end.

    Mitigation strategies. To navigate these risks responsibly, we support provenance and detection measures, including digital watermarking of generated video and research on deepfake-detection methods that distinguish authentic from synthesized motion. Because our pipeline selects supervision by reference identity, it is also compatible with consent-based safeguards that verify the subject of the reference image before adaptation.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：个性化缺的是监督信号：一张图只固定一个姿态，多姿态人物视频又不一定有。

要点：

  • 任务与失效：姿态驱动的人物视频扩散能从单张参考图和目标姿态序列生成动作，但姿态偏离参考图后身份保持变差，脸和衣服走形
  • 个性化的标准解法需要监督，而这里恰好没有：单张图只固定了一个姿态，实践中又不能假设存在多姿态的人物视频
  • 做法是把缺失的监督造出来：用一个域内微调、姿态条件的生成器在关键姿态上产出伪真值帧，再配合推理期的仅参考采样

为什么值得看：虚拟人、NPC 与数字主播都要「一张图就能动」，而现在多要求一段多视角或多姿态素材。把个性化搬到测试时、用自生成监督补上，等于把素材门槛从「一段视频」降到「一张图」。

中文摘要：姿态驱动的人物视频扩散模型能从单张参考图和目标姿态序列生成动作，但姿态一旦偏离参考图，身份保持就会变差，脸与服装出现走形。标准解法是个性化，可它需要监督信号——而这里恰恰没有：一张图只固定了单一姿态，实践中又不能假设存在多姿态的人物视频。作者的思路是把缺失的监督造出来：先用一个域内微调、以姿态为条件的生成器在若干关键姿态上合成伪真值帧，再配合推理阶段「仅依赖参考图」的采样策略完成个性化。对虚拟人、NPC 与数字主播这类需要「一张图就能动」的场景，这把素材门槛从一段视频降到一张图。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-02

本期推送：2026-11-05

One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time

Abstract

Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.

1 Introduction

Given a single reference image of a person and a driving pose sequence, pose-driven human video diffusion models aim to animate the reference subject under the target motion. Recent advances in large-scale video diffusion have substantially improved motion realism, temporal coherence, and overall visual fidelity. However, it is still a challenging problem to faithfully preserve the subject’s identity. For example, facial appearance may be generated inconsistently across frames, while fine-grained garment details, text, and logos can be distorted, altered, or hallucinated.

Rather than relying solely on a larger video diffusion backbone, we focus on personalizing the model to the input subject at test time. A single reference image, however, provides limited adaptation signals: it captures the subject in only one pose and cannot supervise identity preservation across the diverse poses in the driving sequence. We therefore construct pose-diverse pseudo-supervision at inference time.

Specifically, a pose-conditioned, reference-following image diffusion model synthesizes subject-specific images for poses sampled from the driving sequence. More importantly, an inference-time particle-steering procedure, guided by body-similarity and facial-identity rewards, selects high-quality identity-consistent samples without subject videos, target-frame annotations, or human feedback.

Given the pseudo ground truth frames, directly adapting a video diffusion model to static subject images can weaken its motion prior, reducing dynamics and temporal consistency. This identity-and-motion trade-off  [4, 61, 23, 22] is particularly challenging for unified attention video DiTs  [45, 62, 9], whose 3D self-attention jointly models appearance and motion without separable appearance-only parameters [45, 62, 9]. We address this issue by repeating each synthetic image into a static clip and optimizing a lightweight subject-specific LoRA on these appearance-focused clips. This strategy improves identity preservation while retaining the backbone’s motion capability and video quality.

We validate the approach on the TikTok and UBC Fashion benchmarks. The largest gain is on video quality: adaptation substantially lowers FVD where naive personalization is expected to degrade it, so identity and video quality improve together rather than trading off. The same adaptation transfers to in-the-wild videos unseen during training, since the supervision is generated for each test subject rather than learned from a dataset-specific prior. The adaptation restores the face and fine garment detail that the base model distorts as the body turns away from the reference pose. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We propose a test-time personalization framework for pose-driven human video diffusion from a single image, requiring no ground truth, no real captured frames, and no human feedback.

  • •

    A reward-guided generation approach is proposed for synthesizing pseudo-ground-truth images, using body-similarity and facial-identity rewards that measure consistency with the reference image.

  • •

    Our method achieves the best results on most metrics across benchmarks, surpassing the non-personalized base on every metric and matching or surpassing a model personalized with real captured subject frames.

    • 2 Related Work

    Pose-driven human animation. Pose-driven human image animation has converged on the setting we study: a single reference image is animated according to a target body-pose or motion sequence. Early diffusion models established the now-standard recipe of reference appearance injection, pose-guided denoising, and temporal modules for video synthesis [14, 53]. Follow-up work makes this recipe practical in open-source form [39, 31] and improves pose confidence and long-video fusion [59]. Others inject SMPL-derived depth, normal, semantic, and skeleton cues [63], study efficient control modules [33], and unify reference appearance and target-pose conditioning in a single video diffusion branch [44]. Recent DiT-based work further shows that larger video backbones, compact pose encoders, motion tokens, text/background control, and hard-motion training can substantially improve pose following and temporal quality [62, 45, 60, 9, 25, 51].

    These works are primarily trained as feed-forward general animators, and do not adapt the model to the test subject by constructing pose-specific supervision from the given reference image. Our work therefore focuses on reducing per-subject identity, clothing, and hard-pose errors after the target motion is known, rather than introducing another generic pose-control branch.

    Personalization and test-time adaptation. Diffusion personalization methods show that few-shot subject binding can be achieved by fine-tuning model weights, learning new tokens, or updating compact adapter parameters [34, 10, 19, 13, 11]. Video customization work highlights a related but sharper problem: static subject reconstruction can damage the motion prior, reducing dynamics, temporal consistency, or prompt adherence. Prior video customization methods study one-shot video tuning from real videos [49]. Others add subject and motion adapters, image-prompt conditioning, frozen videos, dynamic denoising weights, reward supervision, preference pairs, and DiT LoRA tuning [48, 17, 61, 30, 4, 50, 23, 22, 29]. These methods diagnose the same identity-versus-motion tension that appears in pose-driven animation. Still-Moving [4] originates the frozen-clip supervision we adopt, training adapters on still images replicated over time. There the construction is a liability: it leaves the model producing nearly static videos unless a Motion Adapter on the temporal-attention layers, trained on 1,600 real videos, absorbs the effect. Neither remedy transfers, since a unified 3D-attention DiT has no temporal-only layer and we use no real video. The difference is what the conditioning asks for. A text prompt demands motion the frozen clip does not show, whereas our pose is held constant across the clip. StableAnimator [41] attacks the same problem by training an identity adapter into a video diffusion model and steering denoising with a face reward at inference. The reward there acts on the delivered video, whereas ours acts on the supervision frames and the animator is never rewarded. Wan-Dancer [15] builds long dance videos on the same Wan backbone from music rather than a driving pose, and names identity consistency over long sequences as open future work, which is the failure mode our per-reference adaptation targets.

    In contrast, our input is one still reference image rather than a subject video, the control signal is an explicit target pose sequence, and we adapt at test time on pseudo-examples tied to the poses the model must render.

    Self-generated and synthetic supervision. Generated supervision is also well established in diffusion personalization and view synthesis. Prior work uses generated class images for prior preservation [34], distills synthetic expert customizations into amortized personalization models [6], and builds synthetic preference pairs for image personalization [1]. Other methods use synthetic motion, generated views, uncertainty weighting, hallucination maps, or partial-reference quality measures to avoid poisoning downstream optimization [18, 24, 40, 26, 7]. Test-time self-improvement and generated-support-view pipelines have also appeared for video generation and sparse-view NVS [27, 37, 52, 5].

    The distinction in our setting is the target and use of the generated supervision. The single test reference produces candidate human frames at poses sampled from the driving sequence. Those candidates are filtered for identity and image quality, and the selected pseudo-pairs supervise per-subject adaptation of the pose-driven video model. Thus, the self-generated data are neither generic class regularizers nor free-view support images, but pose-targeted evidence for the exact subject-motion pair being requested.

    Inference-time guidance and reward-guided sampling. A complementary line steers diffusion at inference time without retraining, either by resampling a population of particles toward a reward [36] or by searching the noise space with verifiers [28]. DINO- and identity-based rewards are standard signals for subject fidelity [32, 8, 47], and best-of-N selection is the simplest such scheme. Closest to our use, IPRO [35] optimizes an ArcFace identity reward, but as train-time reinforcement learning of the video model, and IPRO scores against ground-truth video frames.

    We instead apply a training-free, reference-only sampler at the pseudo-supervision stage. A DINO body-similarity reward steers candidate frames in-loop, and an ArcFace reward selects the final one, anchored entirely to the single reference image, with no ground truth and no model fine-tuning. Our contribution is this adaptation to the single-reference video-personalization setting.

    3 Method

    Our goal is to personalize a frozen pose-driven video model to a subject from a single reference image, with no subject video, ground-truth frames, or labels available. We therefore synthesize the supervision. From the reference image x_ref and the driving pose sequence ℙ, a pose-conditioned generator produces a pseudo-ground-truth frame of the subject at each of a few key poses sampled from ℙ. Each frame is steered and selected by its identity match to the reference (Sec.3.2). A per-subject LoRA then adapts the base animator on static clips of these frames (Sec.3.3). Fig.2 shows the pipeline, and Algorithm2 states it in full. We begin with the preliminaries and problem setup (Sec.3.1).

    3.1 Preliminaries

    At test time we are given a single reference image x_ref and a driving pose sequence ℙ={pₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, and seek a video V̂={v̂ₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ in which the subject of x_ref performs ℙ while retaining its appearance.

    The base animator F_θ is a latent video diffusion model. An encoder maps each frame to a latent z. A forward process adds Gaussian noise over diffusion steps τ,

    q(z_τ|z_τ-1)=ℕ (z_τ; √1-β_τ z_τ-1, β_τI),

    		(1)

    and F_θ is trained to reverse it under conditioning c=(x_ref,ℙ),

    L(θ)=𝔼_z, c, ε, τ\lVert ε-ε_θ(z_τ,τ,c) \rVert₂², ε∼ℕ(0,I).

    		(2)

    At inference F_θ maps (x_ref,ℙ) to a video but does not reliably preserve the reference identity as the pose departs from the reference.

    Personalization adapts the base through a small per-subject low-rank update Δθ, yielding the adapted model F_θ+Δθ. Since neither subject video nor ground-truth frames are available, we draw the supervision from a pose-conditioned generator G, whose selected pseudo frames D_pseudo stand in for the absent subject data (Sec.3.2).

    3.2 Reference-only reward-guided generation

    Pose-conditioned generator G. We build G from FLUX.1 Kontext [21], a FLUX.1 [20] variant with strong reference and prior preservation, augmented with a pose ControlNet [57]. We domain-tune G for this task. Given the reference image x_ref and a target pose, G renders the subject in that pose while preserving identity.
