During training, we freeze the base weights of G and optimize a low-rank LoRA injected into its DiT attention blocks. Each training step draws a two-frame pair from an in-domain video: one frame serves as the reference, and G must reconstruct the second frame from its 2D pose. The optimizer, schedule, and trained layers are in Appendix A.

    Pose-targeted synthesis. From the driving sequence ℙ we select K key poses ℙ_K⊂ℙ by farthest-point sampling in keypoint space, anchored at the reference pose. This concentrates the supervision on the hard poses the video model F_θ must render and spans the range of motion. For each key pose pₖ∈ℙ_K the generator must produce one frame that is faithful to the subject and of sufficient quality to supervise appearance.

    Reward-guided sampling. Rather than draw N independent candidates and keep the best (best-of-N), we sample the N candidates as an interacting particle system and steer them while they denoise. We adapt inference-time particle steering [36, 28] to our task with two novel changes specific to the single-reference setting. First, every reward is derived from the reference image alone. No ground-truth target frame exists, so the guidance signal is self-supervised. Second, we split the reward by role.

    An in-loop steering reward Rₛ(x)=w_b DINO(x,x_ref)+w_σ sharp(x) combines body and appearance similarity to the reference, read from a DINOv2 encoder [32], with an image-sharpness term. At scheduled denoising steps, the particles are resampled in proportion to \exp(λRₛ), so sampling compute concentrates on the trajectories that already resemble the subject (Algorithm1). We resample only in the back half of denoising. Early, high-noise particles lack the structure for the reward to be informative, so the first half runs as a plain deterministic ODE, and steering it would only collapse diversity. After each resampling, a churn step re-noises the particles at strength η, so that duplicated high-reward particles diverge rather than remaining identical under the deterministic dynamics.

    A final selection reward R_f(x)=ArcFace(x,x_ref)[8] then picks the surviving candidate with the highest face identity. We steer in-loop with the dense, inexpensive DINO signal and reserve the sharper but detector-sensitive ArcFace score for the single final choice, where it is most reliable. At an equal sampling budget, the reward-guided sampler improves identity and video quality over best-of-N (the no-steering rows of Tab.7).

    The selected pair (xₖ^*,pₖ) enters the pseudo-supervision set D_pseudo={(xₖ^*,pₖ)}ₖ₌₁^K. Each selected frame captures a single pose. Replicated into a static clip for adaptation (Sec.3.3), it carries no inter-frame motion, unlike real video frames captured from a subject in motion. Reward-guided sampling and DINO- or identity-based rewards are each established [36, 47, 35]. Unlike reward fine-tuning against ground-truth video [35, 54], ours is training-free, uses only the reference image as its target, and acts at the pseudo-supervision stage. The novelty in our setting is that these frames are pose-targeted to the test subject’s driving sequence, then reward-steered against the reference before they supervise.

    3.3 Test-time adaptation

    Static-clip adaptation. We adapt only a low-rank update Δθ (LoRA [13]) of rank r on F_θ, and keep θ frozen. We train Δθ by minimizing an adaptation loss L_adapt on D_pseudo. Each adaptation step uses one selected frame xₖ^*. We replicate xₖ^* into a clip and hold the pose pₖ constant across every frame of that clip, then train F_θ+Δθ to reconstruct it. The static clip carries no motion. Writing clip(x)=[x,…,x] for the T-frame replication and z_τᵏ for the noised latent of 𝔼(clip(xₖ^*)),

    L_adapt(Δθ)=∑ₖ₌₁^K𝔼_τ,ε\lVertε-ε_θ+Δθ(z_τᵏ,τ,(x_ref,pₖ))\rVert₂²,

    		(3)

    so the pose pₖ stays fixed across the clip and the temporal pathway sees no motion during adaptation.

    A multi-frame clip of distinct pseudo poses would re-introduce motion into the temporal pathways of the unified self-attention DiT. That motion reproduces the canonical motion-prior damage seen in video personalization [4, 61, 23, 22]. The static clip removes that signal, so adaptation updates appearance only. Prior fixes that decouple spatial parameters from temporal parameters [29] do not transfer to unified-attention DiTs, where one attention operation mixes both. We therefore control motion through the data rather than the parameterization. Removing the static clip drops identity below the base model and worsens temporal consistency, as we report in Tab.4. At inference, the adapted model F_θ+Δθ renders x_ref along the full driving sequence ℙ to produce V̂.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Datasets. For in-domain training and evaluation we use the TikTok [16] and UBC Fashion [56] benchmarks with their standard train and test splits. To probe cross-domain transfer, we additionally evaluate zero-shot on Unseen100-Val, a set of 100 in-the-wild videos spanning diverse subjects, motion, lighting, and backgrounds (Tab.2). Full dataset details are in Appendix D.

    Evaluation. We follow the evaluation protocol of RealisDance-DiT [62] for all comparisons, covering reconstruction, perceptual, identity, and video-quality metrics. Metric definitions are in Appendix B, and the full protocol in Appendix D.2.

    4.2 Implementation details

    Base animator. The base animator F_θ is UniAnimate-DiT [45], a pose-driven human video DiT built on Wan2.1-I2V (14B) [43]. It uses a single unified 3D self-attention stack that models space and time jointly. Reference conditioning enters through dual cross-attention with dedicated image-token projections, and the target pose is injected as a residual at the latent entry. We keep θ frozen and adapt only the low-rank update Δθ of rank r.

    Generator. We build the pose-conditioned generator G on FLUX.1 Kontext [21] with a pose ControlNet [57] and freeze its base. We train a low-rank LoRA on its DiT attention blocks ourselves, on the in-domain training split of each benchmark, with the two-frame reconstruction objective of Sec.3.2. We optimize with AdamW at a constant learning rate for 4,000 steps on a single H100 GPU. The LoRA rank, schedule, and trained layers are in Appendix A.

    Adaptation. By default we synthesize K=5 pseudo frames, each selected from N=8 reward-guided particles, and train the rank-r LoRA on static clips of these frames. The K target poses, and the K real frames of the Real-5 baseline, are the same indices, chosen by farthest-point sampling over the driving poses and seeded at the reference frame, so they span the pose range rather than the timeline. We study how cost and quality scale with the number of fine-tuning steps in Appendix C.1. Full hyperparameters are in Appendix A.

    Test-time cost.Table8 reports the wall-clock and peak GPU memory of each stage on a single H100. The method has two distinct costs, with different hardware requirements. Generation and adaptation run once per reference image and take 9.3 minutes together, peaking at 62.1 GiB. That peak is dominated by the frozen base model, which accounts for 70% of it, against 15% for the low-rank update and its optimizer state (Tab.18). Inference is the recurring cost. It is unchanged by adaptation, since merging the update adds no parameters at inference, and it peaks at 21.6 GiB, within a 24 GB card. The two costs separate in deployment: the one-time stage runs server-side and produces a 1.1 GiB adapter, after which inference proceeds at base cost. Appendix F gives the measurement protocol and the full breakdown.

    4.3 Comparison with the state of the art

    In-domain.Table1 compares against eight pose-driven animators on TikTok and Fashion dataset. Our test-time adaptation improves the UniAnimate-DiT base on every metric and gives the best result on most metrics. The largest gain is on video quality: FVD on TikTok falls below every prior method. Three aspects of this result are worth mentioning: the gain lands on the metric that personalization usually degrades, it requires no subject video, and reconstruction and identity improve in step rather than trading against video quality. Figure4 shows the effect on hard poses, where the base and competing animators reconstruct identity inconsistently while our adapted model preserves the face and garment. Additional qualitative results are in Appendix E.

    Out-of-domain. Trained on TikTok and evaluated on the out-of-domain Unseen100-Val set (Tab.2), the adaptation transfers. It leads all methods and improves over the base on every metric, cutting FVD by roughly a quarter, with the prior animators further behind. The advantage holds under domain shift because the supervision is generated for the test subject rather than learned from the training distribution, so it does not inherit a dataset-specific prior.

    Cross-reenactment. When one subject is driven by another subject’s motion, no aligned ground truth exists, so we measure identity against the reference (Tab.3). Adaptation improves appearance fidelity (FaceID, BodySIM) while pose obedience (PoseAcc) is essentially unchanged, since the pose-conditioning pathway stays frozen. The adaptation thus binds appearance without disturbing the motion pathway, the asymmetry the static-clip recipe is designed to produce.

    4.4 Ablations and analysis

    Contribution of each component.Table4 removes one component at a time. Removing the reward-guided frame selection raises FVD as lower-quality pseudo frames enter adaptation. Dropping the static clip is the most damaging: identity falls and temporal consistency degrades past the base itself (dtSSD 369.0→416.3). This confirms that multi-pose clips push motion back into the temporal pathway.

    The full system also improves on adaptation on five real subject frames (Real-5) in FVD while using none, and matches it on identity, inverting the usual trade-off. The standalone generator G attains the highest per-frame identity but has no temporal model and cannot produce coherent video.

    Supervision source. Holding the adaptation fixed and varying only the supervision source isolates what drives the gain (Tab.5). Self-distillation adapts the base on its own outputs. It does not improve reconstruction and worsens temporal consistency, pushing dtSSD above the base, and scarcely improves identity, since those outputs carry the motion artifacts of a video model. Real frames help more, and our clean, static pseudo-GT from G helps most, cutting FVD to 133.5. Figure5(b) summarizes this across all seven metrics.

    Number of pseudo frames. FVD is lowest at K=5, our default, and both FVD and identity degrade at K=9 as extra frames expose generator artifacts (Fig.5(a), Tab.6). A larger K=21 reaches the highest full-video FaceID (0.626) but trades away the balanced result, while a small K under-covers the motion the model must render. The fine-tuning-time and generator ablations are in Appendix C.

    Steering and selection rewards. The reward-guided sampler reads two reference-only rewards in distinct roles, and Tab.7 shows both assignments matter. Its no-steering (i.i.d.) rows are the best-of-N baseline, which in-loop steering improves on at an equal budget. The dense but coarse DINO reward steers the particle population best. The sharp but detector-sensitive ArcFace reward is unreliable as an in-loop signal on the occluded, fast-moving faces typical of dance, but is decisive as the final selection. Steering with DINO and selecting with ArcFace is therefore our default.

    Temporal stability. The gains do not come at the cost of motion. Figure3 shows that adaptation confines inter-frame residual to true motion boundaries rather than spreading it across the face and torso. Identity improves without the flicker that personalization usually introduces.

    5 Conclusion

    We personalize a pose-driven human video model to a subject from a single reference image, with no subject video and no ground truth. A pose-conditioned generator synthesizes pseudo-ground-truth frames at the poses the driving sequence requires, steered and selected by reference-only rewards, and a per-subject LoRA adapts the base animator on static clips of them. The static clip, which we adopt from prior work, supplies subject appearance while carrying no motion, so the adaptation binds identity without disturbing the temporal prior. Personalization then improves identity and reconstruction and even improves video quality (FVD), the metric it usually degrades, and the gains transfer to out-of-domain subjects because the supervision is generated for the test subject rather than learned from a training distribution. The adapted model surpasses its non-personalized base on every metric and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real subject frames despite using none, inverting the trade-off personalization usually incurs.

    Limitations and future work. The method inherits the quality of its generator G, since a degraded pseudo frame weakens the adaptation, so rejecting blurred or occluded frames is a simple safeguard (App. G). The reference-only rewards are fixed and hand-weighted, and learning them would raise the ceiling G imposes. The adapted model’s own outputs could re-supervise G in a closed loop. Because the adaptation never touches the backbone, it should carry over to stronger animators as they appear.

    One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for
    Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time
    Supplementary Material

    Table of Contents

    Appendix A Further Implementation Details

    A.1 Base Model and Generator Architectures

    The base animator F_θ is UniAnimate-DiT [45], a pose-driven human video diffusion transformer built on the Wan2.1-I2V (14B) backbone [43]. It operates in the compressed latent space of a frozen video VAE and conditions on three streams: a reference-appearance stream, in which the source image is encoded by the frozen VAE encoder and concatenated with the noisy video latents to preserve high-frequency detail; a target-pose stream, which injects the driving skeleton as a residual at the latent entry; and dual cross-attention with dedicated image-token projections for reference alignment. The backbone uses a single unified 3D self-attention stack that models space and time jointly. We keep all pre-trained parameters frozen and adapt only a per-subject low-rank update Δθ.

    The generator G is built on FLUX.1 Kontext [21], a FLUX.1 [20] variant chosen for its strong reference and prior preservation, paired with a pose ControlNet [57] (Fig.6). We freeze the base and train a low-rank LoRA [13] on its DiT attention blocks with the two-frame reconstruction objective of the main paper, so that G renders the reference subject under a target pose while preserving identity.

    A.2 Key-pose and frame selection

    Which poses are supervised. We do not generate a frame for every pose in ℙ; we supervise only a small set of K key poses. The key poses are chosen by greedy farthest-point sampling in 2D keypoint space, initialized at the reference pose and adding, at each step, the pose whose minimum keypoint distance to the already-selected set is largest. This spreads the key poses across the range of motion and concentrates supervision on the poses farthest from the reference, which the base animator renders worst. The keypoint distance is the mean per-joint Euclidean distance between the normalized 2D whole-body keypoints (extracted by DWPose [55]) of the two frames. By default K=5: the reference pose plus the four farthest poses. For example, on TikTok sequence 07 the selected key frames are {0, 38, 53, 57, 71} of the 305-frame clip.

    Which frame is kept. For each key pose, the reward-guided sampler (Algorithm1) produces a single frame: N particles denoise under in-loop DINO steering toward x_ref, and the surviving candidate with the highest ArcFace identity is kept. There is no post-hoc filtering of a larger pool; selection is the in-loop steering followed by the final ArcFace pick. We use N=8 particles and resample at |ℝ|=3 points evenly spaced over the back half of the 30-step denoising schedule (start fraction 0.5; resample steps {18,22,25}), injecting churn η=0.5 so cloned winners diverge under the otherwise-deterministic dynamics. The in-loop steering reward weights a DINOv2 body-similarity term (w_b=1.0) and a Laplacian sharpness term (w_σ=0.5); the surviving per-pose candidate is then chosen by maximum ArcFace identity to x_ref.

    A.3 Efficient Adaptation via LoRA

    We inject LoRA [13] into the query, key, value, and output projections of the attention blocks and the two feed-forward layers (ffn.0,ffn.2) of every transformer block, with rank r and scaling α=r following standard convention. Freezing the backbone and adapting only these low-rank factors keeps the trainable parameter count a small fraction of the backbone and the adaptation fast. Concretely, the animator F uses r=128 (α=128) on {q,k,v,o,ffn.0,ffn.2} of each DiT block (≈ 0.61B trainable parameters, ∼ 4% of the frozen 14B backbone), and the generator G uses r=64 on its DiT attention, feed-forward, and modulation projections (≈ 0.31B trainable parameters).

    A.4 Training Details

    Generator training. We optimize G with AdamW at a constant learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴ for 4,000 steps on a single H100 GPU, on the in-domain training split of each benchmark. We train at LoRA rank r=64 with one (reference, target) frame pair per step and gradient checkpointing; supervision is real frame pairs, so no photometric augmentation is applied. The cross-frame pairing itself supplies the pose variation.

    Per-subject adaptation. At test time we synthesize K pseudo frames, replicate each into a static clip, and adapt Δθ on these clips. Adaptation is a one-time per-subject cost; once Δθ is obtained, inference along an arbitrary driving sequence requires no further optimization. Adaptation uses AdamW at learning rate 1×10⁻⁴ for 5 steps by default (Tab.10 sweeps 5–400).

    Appendix B Evaluation Metrics

    We provide the formulations of every metric used in our experiments. Let Iₜ and Îₜ denote the ground-truth and generated frames at time t, with spatial size H×W, C channels, and T total frames.

    PSNR. From the per-frame mean squared error MSE=\tfrac1HWC∑_x,y,c(Iₜ(x,y,c)-Îₜ(x,y,c))²,

    PSNR=20\log₁₀ ((255)/(√MSE)),

    		(4)

    averaged over frames. Higher is better.

    SSIM. Structural similarity [46] compares local luminance, contrast, and structure between Iₜ and Îₜ. We report the mean over all frames and channels. Higher is better.

    LPIPS. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity [58] measures the distance between deep features of Iₜ and Îₜ from a pre-trained backbone, averaged over frames. Lower is better.

    FID. Fréchet Inception Distance [12] compares Gaussian statistics (μᵣ,Σᵣ) and (μ_f,Σ_f) of real and generated frame features from a pre-trained Inception network,

    FID=\lVertμᵣ-μ_f\rVert₂²+Tr (Σᵣ+Σ_f-2(ΣᵣΣ_f)^1/2).

    		(5)

    FVD. Fréchet Video Distance [42] applies the same form to spatiotemporal features extracted by an Inflated 3D ConvNet [3] from fixed-length video segments, capturing temporal realism. Lower is better.

    FID-VID. A video-level variant [2] that aggregates clip embeddings into a single descriptor per sequence before computing the Fréchet distance, capturing long-range temporal consistency. Lower is better.

    FaceID. Facial identity preservation is the cosine similarity between ArcFace [8] embeddings of the generated and reference faces, averaged over frames. Higher is better.

    BodySIM. Body-appearance similarity is the cosine similarity between DINOv2 [32] embeddings of the generated and reference subject crops. Higher is better.

    dtSSD. Temporal consistency is measured on inter-frame differences: we compare the temporal gradient of the generated video, Îₜ₊₁-Îₜ, against that of the reference video, Iₜ₊₁-Iₜ, and report the mean squared deviation over time. Lower indicates motion closer to the ground truth without added flicker.

    PoseAcc. Pose-following accuracy compares the skeleton extracted from the generated frame against the driving skeleton, reporting keypoint agreement. Poses are extracted with DWPose [55] from both the generated and the ground-truth frame, and agreement is the percentage of correct keypoints (PCK@0.2): a predicted joint is counted correct when its distance to the corresponding ground-truth joint is within 0.2 of the person bounding-box size. Higher indicates closer adherence to the target motion.

    We follow the overall evaluation protocol of RealisDance-DiT [62] (see Sec.D.2).

    B.1 Identity under independent recognizers

    FaceID is ArcFace cosine and BodySIM is DINOv2 cosine, and those same two networks drive the pipeline: candidates are selected by ArcFace similarity to the reference and sampling is steered by DINOv2 body similarity. To verify that an identity gain measured with them reflects identity rather than the selection reward, Table9 re-scores the same rendered videos with recognizers that are not used at any stage of the pipeline. Two controls ensure a fair comparison: faces are detected and aligned once and every recognizer embeds the identical crop, so detector disagreement cannot appear as a difference between recognizers, and the scored set is fixed across arms, so no arm benefits from being evaluated on the frames on which its own faces are detectable.

    The gain persists and is larger under FaceNet512 (+0.059) and SFace (+0.067) than under ArcFace (+0.035). Exploiting ArcFace-specific artifacts would produce the opposite ordering. We also run the test in reverse, rebuilding the per-subject dataset by ranking the same candidate pool with FaceNet512 instead of ArcFace (Ours-FN in Tab.9). The two recognizers disagree on 7 of 12 selections, so the two training sets differ substantially. Scored with ArcFace, which it never optimized, Ours-FN gains +0.034 over the base. Although Ours-FN optimizes FaceNet512, it does not lead on FaceNet512: selection does not inflate the score of the network doing the selecting. Appearance evidence that does not depend on either reward is provided by LPIPS, which is computed on VGG features and improves substantially (0.177 vs 0.283, Tab.12). PSNR, SSIM and FVD are likewise reward-independent and all improve (Tab.1).

    B.2 Human preference study

    Every metric above is automatic, and two of them (FaceID, BodySIM) share their networks with the reward used to select pseudo-frames (Sec.B.1). We therefore also conducted a human study, which depends on neither.

    Thirty-four respondents rated clips from each method on a 1–5 scale along four axes: human appearance alignment, pose alignment, background alignment, and overall quality. Clips were drawn from the TikTok test split, method identities were hidden, and the presentation order of the four methods was shuffled per clip so that no position was systematically associated with one method. Each respondent saw the reference image alongside the clip, since appearance alignment is only meaningful relative to it. This yields 180 ratings per method per axis.

    Figure7 shows the resulting distributions. Ours places 93% of appearance-alignment ratings at 4–5 against 38% for the unadapted base, and leads on all four axes. The base model in turn leads both prior animators, which is consistent with the automatic metrics in Tab.1, and corroborates the perceptual metrics with judgments that depend on neither reward.

    Appendix C Further Ablation

    C.1 Additional Quantitative Results

    Quality versus fine-tuning time.Table10 studies how reconstruction, identity, and video quality scale with the number of per-subject fine-tuning steps and the corresponding wall-clock time on a single H100. Quality saturates by five steps, our default, and is flat over the rest of the sweep: five steps already match or exceed every larger budget on reconstruction and video quality, since the static clip presents the same target at every step and the low-rank update converges to it within a few updates. Longer budgets improve only identity, and not monotonically, so we adapt for five steps, at 5.8 s per subject. This sweep varies the step budget only. Peak GPU memory, the hardware requirement, and the cost of the other pipeline stages are reported separately in AppendixF.

    Per-subject LoRA rank.Table11 sweeps the rank r of the per-subject update on a tuning subset. Quality improves with adapter capacity up to r=128, our default. At r=256 the adapter over-fits the handful of pseudo-frames and quality regresses, marking 128 as a clear optimum.

    C.2 Generator and Reward-Guided Sampling

    Our pipeline contains a second trained model, the pose-conditioned generator G, and a reference-only reward-guided sampler. We ablate their components here.

    How much domain tuning does G need?G’s LoRA is trained on the in-domain split of each benchmark, so the pipeline assumes access to a human-video corpus before test time, even though no video of the test subject is ever used. Table12 quantifies the effect of that assumption by sweeping the amount of tuning G receives, from none to our default. Two conclusions follow. First, the dependence is present but bounded: with an entirely untuned generator the adapted model still improves over the base on every metric (21.88 vs 20.33 PSNR, 0.184 vs 0.283 LPIPS). Second, the benefit of tuning depends on the metric. Pixel and perceptual quality saturate early: 500 steps, one eighth of the default, already recovers 95% of the PSNR gain over base, and LPIPS, SSIM and BodySIM are flat from there on. Identity does not: FaceID continues to increase to 4,000 (0.699→0.714→0.720→0.764), so 500 steps recovers only 66% of that gain. Domain tuning of G therefore primarily improves identity fidelity, as expected of a LoRA that teaches G the appearance statistics of the domain. Reconstruction quality requires only light tuning on a human-video corpus rather than close matching to the benchmark. Consistent with this, the G used for Unseen100-Val is tuned on TikTok yet leads on in-the-wild subjects (Tab.2). The gains concentrate on the sequence where the base model performs worst, where PSNR rises from 12.12 (base) to 17.39 (untuned G) to 20.50 (default). On sequences where the base already performs well, the tuning levels are indistinguishable.

    Particle count N.Table13 sweeps the number of particles N in the reward-guided sampler, reporting the fidelity of the selected pseudo-frame to the real frame. Frame quality is already largely saturated by our default N=8, while per-frame sampling time grows roughly linearly, so larger populations cost compute without further gain. The value of in-loop steering over best-of-N selection at a matched budget is established separately in Tab.7.

    Resampling schedule.Table14 varies the denoising window over which particles are resampled and the churn strength η. Pseudo-frame fidelity is largely insensitive to the schedule. We default to resampling only the back half with churn for its downstream stability, since steering early, high-noise particles collapses diversity before subject structure emerges and the churn step keeps duplicated high-reward particles from remaining identical under the deterministic dynamics.

    Key-pose selection.Table15 compares strategies for choosing the K supervised poses from the driving sequence. At fixed K, farthest-point sampling in keypoint space (ours), random, and uniform-in-time selection are within noise of one another, indicating the gain comes from supervising diverse poses at all rather than from the specific selection rule. We use farthest-point sampling as a principled default.

    Appendix D Dataset Curation & Evaluation Protocol

    D.1 Datasets

    For in-domain training and evaluation we use the TikTok [16] and UBC Fashion [56] benchmarks with their standard train and test splits. To probe cross-domain transfer, we additionally evaluate zero-shot on Unseen100-Val, a set of 100 in-the-wild videos spanning diverse subjects, motion, lighting, and backgrounds.

    Motivation. Both standard benchmarks are limited for evaluating modern video diffusion models. The TikTok test set contains only 10 videos, too few for fine-grained comparison, while UBC Fashion, though larger, consists of simple catwalk sequences with uniform lighting and minimal background variation, so scores saturate across methods (Tab.1). Neither covers the diversity of real-world deployment, including varied skin tones, challenging lighting, and non-photorealistic subjects. We therefore curate Unseen100-Val, a 100-video zero-shot evaluation set designed to (a) better represent the visual diversity of real-world data and (b) stress-test models in challenging settings they were not trained on, such as difficult lighting, complex backgrounds, and animated characters.

    Collection and eligibility. Videos are sourced from a mix of TikTok and stock footage. Each clip features a single person or character performing a dancing motion, with no heavy occlusion of any body part (slight tolerance is allowed for an arm briefly disappearing during fast motion), and the pose skeleton must remain fully visible throughout, ensuring reliable pose extraction for both adaptation and evaluation.

    Composition and diversity.Table16 summarizes the dataset composition across several axes; each attribute group independently covers all 100 videos. We deliberately balance real and animated subjects and ensure broad coverage of appearance, motion complexity, and environmental conditions. Among the 80 real-human videos, skin tones span East Asian, South Asian, Caucasian, and darker-skinned appearances to promote evaluation fairness; the 20 animated videos split evenly between 2D (anime, cartoon) and 3D (rendered, stylized) characters, testing generalization beyond photorealistic subjects.

    Preprocessing and statistics. All clips are center-cropped and resized to a common resolution, with driving poses extracted by a 2D keypoint detector consistent with our training pipeline. The detector is DWPose [55], the same whole-body extractor used to render the training pose maps; keypoints are extracted at the clip’s native resolution and rendered as skeleton maps at the model input resolution of 832×480. The average clip duration is 14.4 seconds (±3.2 s), ranging from 8 to 24 s. At 100 videos, Unseen100-Val matches the test-set size of UBC Fashion while being 10× larger than TikTok’s test split; because it targets zero-shot cross-domain evaluation rather than statistical power over a narrow domain, 100 diverse videos provide sufficient coverage to surface meaningful failure modes and performance differences across methods.

    D.2 Evaluation Protocol

    We follow the evaluation settings of RealisDance-DiT [62]. All generated videos are center-cropped and resized to a common resolution for metric computation, ensuring a fair comparison across methods that train at different native resolutions. For competing methods we use officially released checkpoints and evaluation code where available, and directly report published numbers where applicable. Our base animator and adapted model are sampled with the Wan2.1 flow-matching solver for 50 steps at classifier-free guidance scale 1.0, and metrics are computed at a common 832×480 resolution (image metrics on the trimmed window, video metrics over full clips). Pseudo-frames are generated with the fixed prompt “The person is dancing.” We do not re-train any competing method: their scores come from official checkpoints and evaluation code, or from the published papers where applicable. All baselines in Tab.1, including the UniAnimate-DiT base, are quoted from MTVCraft [9]; the base rows of Tabs.4 and 5 re-evaluate it under our protocol, so its numbers there differ.

    Appendix E Additional Qualitative Results

    We provide extended visual comparisons across subjects, motion types, and visual domains, including cross-domain subjects unseen during training. Figures8 and 9 give in-domain comparisons spanning diverse motions, backgrounds, appearance, and illumination, and Fig.10 shows cross-domain results on animated characters. Across all examples, the adapted model preserves the subject’s appearance while maintaining temporal coherence under challenging lighting and complex motion.

    Appendix F Test-Time Cost

    This section reports the cost of serving one reference image on a single H100: the wall-clock and peak GPU memory of every stage, how that memory is allocated, how it amortizes over repeated use, and the implications for deployment.

    F.1 Measurement protocol

    All numbers are measured on one NVIDIA H100 80 GB (driver 580.173) on a single TikTok test subject, with adaptation and inference at 832×480 and pseudo-frame generation at the generator’s native 576×1024, using the default recipe of Sec.4.2 (K=5 pseudo frames from N=8 reward-guided particles, rank-128 adapter, 5 adaptation steps). Peak memory is the maximum device memory sampled every 250 ms for the lifetime of the stage, cross-checked against the per-process figure. We report the device-level number because it includes the CUDA context and allocator reserve and is therefore what a deployment must provision. For the inference rows we also report the torch allocator peak: it runs ∼ 1 GiB lower, and quoting only the allocator figure would understate the requirement. Inference times exclude the one-off model load, which a deployment pays once rather than per video.

    F.2 Composition of the memory peak

    Table18 decomposes the adaptation peak. The frozen base model accounts for 70% of it, the video DiT contributing 49% and the text encoder, image encoder and VAE a further 21% between them. The per-subject update accounts for 15%, and is dominated not by the adapter weights (613M parameters, ≈ 4% of the backbone) but by the optimizer state they require, since the low-rank tensors are upcast to fp32 and AdamW keeps two moments per parameter. The remaining 15% is activations, workspace and allocator reserve.

    The adaptation requirement is therefore a property of fine-tuning this animator rather than of the supervision we propose. The Real-5 and reference-only arms of Tab.5 run the identical trainer at the identical rank and differ only in which frames they consume, so they occupy the same footprint, as would any adapter-based personalization of a backbone this size.

    Minimum GPU. The minimum GPU is therefore set by the frozen base model, not by our update: adaptation needs an 80 GB card, while inference needs only 24 GB, the same requirement as running the base animator unadapted.

    Inference requires far less memory despite using the same backbone, because it streams the DiT: only a 6B-parameter working set is resident and the remaining blocks are fetched layer-by-layer during the forward pass.

    F.3 Deployment and amortization

    The two costs are distinct. Adaptation is a one-time, server-side job of 9.3 minutes whose entire output is a 1.1 GiB adapter file. The 2.3 GiB training checkpoint additionally carries optimizer state, which is not part of the deployment payload. Once obtained, the adapter is reused for every video generated from that reference. Inference is the recurring cost and is unchanged from the base model, at identical peak memory and the same generation time to within run-to-run variance, so a user never requires training-grade hardware: the adapter is downloaded and inference runs at base cost.

    Table19 quantifies the benefit of repeated use. Because adaptation is paid per reference image and not per video, the average cost per video falls as 1/n: a reference animated 25 times costs 1.05× what the unadapted base would cost for the same 25 videos, and approaches parity beyond that. The regime where the overhead dominates is the single-video case, where the one-time stage is 1.25× the inference it enables. Adaptation is thus better characterized as a provisioning cost, paid once when a reference is enrolled, than as a per-request cost.

    Appendix G Limitations

    The method inherits the quality of its generator: when the generator produces weak pseudo-ground-truth for a subject (for example under heavy occlusion, motion blur, or strong out-of-domain appearance), the downstream per-subject adaptation is correspondingly weaker, since adaptation can only bind the appearance that the pseudo-ground-truth actually exposes. This motivates both the reference-only selection that curates high-quality pseudo frames and the closed-loop direction discussed in the conclusion, where the adapted model’s own outputs re-supervise the generator. A complementary safeguard is an automatic frame-quality filter that rejects blurred or occluded pseudo frames before adaptation. Figure11 illustrates how the adapted output tracks the quality of the pseudo-supervision.

    Appendix H Ethical Considerations & Broader Impact

    Our method lowers the cost of personalizing a human video model to a new subject: it needs a single reference image, no subject video, and no manual labels. This benefits creative content production, accessibility, and avatar applications, but the same capability warrants a discussion of misuse.

    Risk of misuse. The ease of synthesizing realistic video of a person from one image raises the risk of non-consensual or deceptive media, such as impersonation or misinformation. We condemn any use that depicts an individual without their explicit consent, and we intend any release to be governed by terms that prohibit such use.

    Data bias. Like all generative models, ours can inherit biases in its training data. If the underlying datasets underrepresent particular skin tones, body types, ages, or styles of dress, personalization quality may be uneven across groups. We encourage evaluation across diverse subjects, and our Unseen100-Val set is curated to include a broad range of appearances and conditions toward this end.

    Mitigation strategies. To navigate these risks responsibly, we support provenance and detection measures, including digital watermarking of generated video and research on deepfake-detection methods that distinguish authentic from synthesized motion. Because our pipeline selects supervision by reference identity, it is also compatible with consent-based safeguards that verify the subject of the reference image before adaptation.

item.title: 世界模型别只在 2D 里预测：混合粒子-体素表示同时出外观、几何与触觉，跨视角一致才成立 ｜ Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
item.description:
一句话：只在图像/视频空间预测未来，会丢掉底层 3D 结构，长时程与跨视角一致性都难保证。

要点：

  • 问题定位：很多动作条件世界模型直接在 2D 图像或视频空间预测，没有显式建模底层 3D 场景，于是跨视角一致性与长时程交互都难以维持
  • 作者提出「3D World Simulator」：在一个统一的 3D 表示上**联合预测外观、几何与触觉**三种观测
  • 表示采用混合粒子-体素动力学，兼顾自由运动（粒子）与稠密场（体素）两类动态

为什么值得看：「触觉」这一维进入世界模型，说明仿真侧对多模态反馈的需求在上升；而把预测锚回 3D 表示，是解决「走远就不一致」的根本做法，比在视频空间打补丁更彻底。

中文摘要：预测世界如何随动作演化，是策略学习、评估与规划的核心；但不少动作条件世界模型直接在 2D 图像或视频空间预测未来观测，没有显式建模底层 3D 场景，于是跨视角一致性与长时程交互都很脆弱。这篇提出「3D World Simulator」：在一个统一的 3D 表示上联合预测外观、几何与触觉三类观测，并用混合粒子—体素动力学同时刻画自由运动（粒子）与稠密场（体素）两类演化。把预测锚回 3D 表示，是解决「走远之后世界就对不上」的根本做法，也让触觉这类非视觉反馈有地方可挂。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-01

本期推送：2026-11-05

[Submitted on 3 Nov 2026]

Title:Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation

Authors:Jimmy Wang, Yifan Chou, Kaifeng Zhang, Yixuan Wang, Binghao Huang, Tao Yu, Saleh Nabi, Yunzhu LiView PDF
Abstract:Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.
Subjects:Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

item.title: CAD 生成该被按「画工程图」考：Parametric CAD Bench v3 加工程图输入，专测 agentic 参数化建模 ｜ Parametric CAD Bench v3: Evaluating Agentic Parametric CAD Authoring from Text and Engineering Drawings
item.description:
一句话：从文字和工程图生成参数化 CAD，是 agent 造资产最像真实工作的形态。

要点：

  • 任务设定贴近工业：从文本与工程图两种输入出发，让 agent 产出参数化 CAD 模型
  • v3 的定位是系统性评测「agentic 参数化 CAD 创作」——不是单轮生成一个形状，而是按参数化约束把模型建出来
  • 作为 benchmark，它补齐了此前多考「图像→网格」、少考「工程约束→参数化模型」的空白

为什么值得看：AI 造资产在工业侧真正的验收是「参数化正确、可改」，而不是「渲染像」。这个基准把评测口径从外观挪到参数化正确性，对做 CAD/工业资产 agent 的团队是现在最贴近的考卷。

中文摘要：Parametric CAD Bench v3 把评测对象定为「agentic 参数化 CAD 创作」：输入既可以是文本，也可以是工程图，要求 agent 产出符合参数化约束的 CAD 模型。这与此前大量「图像到网格」类基准不同——后者主要看外观是否相似，而工业侧真正关心的是参数化是否正确、后续能否被工程修改。v3 因此把工程图纳入输入模态，并按参数化正确性来评判，对正在做 CAD、工业资产或程序化建模 agent 的团队，这是目前最贴近真实工作形态的一份考卷。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-05

Parametric CAD Bench v3:
Evaluating Agentic Parametric CAD Authoring
from Text and Engineering Drawings

Results snapshot: September 24, 2026

Abstract

Producing an executable CAD script is not sufficient to establish that an agent has satisfied an engineering design request. Evaluation must also consider the resulting geometry, specified dimensions, and native CAD modeling history. We present Parametric CAD Bench v3, a 100-task benchmark comprising 30 text-to-CAD creation tasks, 30 text-to-CAD create-and-edit tasks, and 40 tasks that reconstruct mechanical parts from engineering drawings. Agents operate in a pinned FreeCAD environment and submit native CAD artifacts to a separate programmatic verifier. The primary metric is mean continuous task reward, combining geometry similarity and specification consistency rather than binary task success. A September 24, 2026 snapshot covers 13 model–agent systems; Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest overall point estimate, 61.03%, and an image-to-CAD mean reward of 84.66%. These measurements describe complete systems, not isolated model capabilities. We release versioned tasks, evaluation configurations, and inspectable result artifacts.

1 Introduction

Computer-aided design (CAD) systems represent engineering intent as editable digital models. In a parametric CAD system, the artifact contains more than final geometry: a geometry kernel represents and manipulates curves, surfaces, topology, and solids; constraint solvers enforce dimensional and geometric relationships; and feature histories and dependency graphs record modeling steps so that changes to upstream parameters or features propagate to downstream geometry. These capabilities are fundamental to both professional CAD systems such as Siemens NX, CATIA, Creo, and SolidWorks, and open-source systems such as FreeCAD, which uses Open CASCADE Technology (OCCT) as its geometry kernel. By contrast, CadQuery is a code-centric parametric CAD library built on OCCT. Our benchmark instead requires native FreeCAD documents with an application-managed feature tree and document dependencies, rather than a CadQuery program or exported B-rep alone.

This distinction matters for evaluating CAD agents in real engineering workflows, where parametric CAD systems underpin modern mechanical design and manufacturing. An output can resemble the requested part while containing incorrect dimensions, missing features, broken dependencies, or a static shape in place of the required native feature structure. Conversely, alternative feature constructions can satisfy the same engineering requirements. Evaluating CAD agents therefore requires more than testing whether generated code executes or whether the resulting geometry is visually or geometrically similar.

Our central question is whether general-purpose AI agents can produce geometrically correct, specification-consistent, parametric CAD artifacts across three workflows.

The benchmark has evolved through three releases. We released Parametric CAD Bench v1 in May 2026 to evaluate text-based creation of native parametric FreeCAD models [11]. In September 2026, v2 retained the 100-task creation format while tightening validation and evaluation isolation: it upgraded the validator and FreeCAD runtime, moved held-out assets into a separate verifier image, and standardized reward reporting and failure handling [12]. V3 broadened the suite to include editing and reconstruction from engineering drawings [13]; the September 24 update added evaluations of Claude Opus 5.5 with two agent frameworks [14].

This paper focuses on v3; v1 and v2 provide historical context rather than additional evaluation cohorts.

Parametric CAD Bench v3 evaluates three workflows: text-to-CAD creation, text-to-CAD create-and-edit (two-stage creation and editing), and image-to-CAD (reconstruction from engineering drawings); we refer to the first two as creation and create-and-edit. Its native FreeCAD output contract permits inspection beyond a rendered image, while its grader combines geometric and task-specific specification checks. These checks are proxies for the intended engineering requirements; they do not by themselves certify manufacturing readiness or functional editability under arbitrary future modifications.

The contribution of this work is threefold:

  • 1.

    A versioned 100-task evaluation suite spanning three CAD workflows with native parametric output requirements.

  • 2.

    An isolated execution and programmatic scoring protocol, with frozen configurations and per-task diagnostic artifacts.

  • 3.

    A dated evaluation of complete model–agent systems, exposing differences across workflows and observed failure modes.

    • 2 Related Work

    CADGenBench: artifact-centered CAD evaluation.

    CADGenBench evaluates CAD generation and editing through tool-agnostic STEP/BREP submissions [19, 4]. Its public leaderboard accepts a ZIP archive of candidate artifacts; the hosted Hugging Face Space runs evaluation, and maintainers separately review methodology evidence before marking a submission validated [19, 5]. This is an artifact-submission protocol rather than a requirement to run a submitted agent inside a common task environment. However, it is not restricted to single-shot generation: its reference baseline is iterative, and evaluation tools are also available locally [19, 4]. Our emphasis is instead on evaluating complete agent executions in a versioned FreeCAD environment and requiring native parametric documents.

    CADBench: multimodal CAD-program reconstruction.

    MIT’s CADBench evaluates reconstruction of executable, editable CAD programs from meshes and rendered images [7]. Its released evaluation pipeline currently accepts generated programs as CadQuery Python code; supporting other CAD programming languages would require adapting the pipeline [3]. It contains 18,000 samples across six benchmark families and five input modalities, with complexity-stratified STEP-based splits and diversity-aware sampling. Its six metrics cover volumetric IoU, surface IoU, Chamfer distance, valid-shape rate, token count, and operation count. Like Parametric CAD Bench v3, it evaluates executable CAD geometry rather than rendered appearance alone. However, its reported general-purpose VLM evaluation uses direct generation without tool use, self-correction, or multi-turn refinement; we evaluate complete interactive agent workflows in FreeCAD. CADBench emphasizes reconstruction from 3D observations and object renders, whereas our suite combines text-based creation, create-and-edit, and reconstruction from dimensioned engineering drawings. Its paper also distinguishes code editability from recovering the original feature tree, sketch constraints, or design intent, which it does not require. Our tasks instead require native FreeCAD documents with task-specific parametric structure and specification checks, without requiring exact reproduction of the reference construction history. The benchmarks are complementary: CADBench provides broad reconstruction and modality-shift diagnostics, while our smaller suite studies end-to-end CAD task completion by model–agent systems.

    BenchCAD: programmatic CAD over CadQuery.

    BenchCAD 1.0 contains 17,900 execution-verified CadQuery programs across 106 industrial part families, with image-to-code, instruction-guided code editing, and visual/code question-answering tasks [21]. Its generation evaluation compares the executed geometry with a reference; the current website also reports agentic runs with rendering, measurement, and iterative tool use [2]. BenchCAD 2.0, released on October 12, 2026, after our September 24 snapshot, adds part and assembly construction from dimensioned engineering drawings, reverse engineering from rendered views, and agentic evaluation in an offline sandbox, all scored against reference geometry [1]. Its drawing-based part tasks are the closest counterpart to our image-to-CAD workflow. The distinction from Parametric CAD Bench v3 is therefore not whether agents can use tools, but the modeling interface and required output representation. CadQuery is a high-level parametric CAD library built on Python bindings to Open CASCADE Technology (OCCT), not the geometry kernel itself [6]. FreeCAD also uses OCCT, but provides a CAD application with native model history, geometry-constrained sketches, and a Python API [8]. BenchCAD’s CadQuery tasks emphasize parametric program synthesis, whereas our tasks require agents to construct and save native FreeCAD documents with the specified feature structure. Both are CAD workflows; our setting additionally exercises the application-level document and feature system.

    CAD-bench: functional CAD generation.

    CAD-bench, presented at an ICML 2026 workshop, executes generated CAD code or agent-produced STEP files and checks the exported geometry with task-specific tests, including dimensional and pose verification, thread-profile analysis, and rigid-body simulation in Blender [20]. Its 17 tasks span four difficulty tiers, from basic solids to threaded mating pairs and gear trains. It therefore tests whether generated parts function together, whereas Parametric CAD Bench v3 requires native parametric FreeCAD documents across 100 tasks and scores their geometric similarity and compliance with named dimensions without simulating mechanisms. Despite the similar name, it is a separate benchmark with a different evaluation target.

    3DCodeBench: mesh-based procedural 3D authoring.

    3DCodeBench evaluates Blender Python scripts generated from text and images, including iterative execution and visual feedback [9]. Its evaluated outputs are meshes, assessed through executability, geometric and perceptual similarity, and pairwise human preferences. In contrast, Parametric CAD Bench v3 targets engineering-oriented mechanical CAD: native parametric FreeCAD documents with boundary-representation (B-rep) geometry and task-specific dimensional and structural checks. B-rep geometry represents surfaces and their topological relationships, rather than only a polygonal surface approximation [18]. Thus the distinction is between procedural mesh assets and dimensionally specified, editable CAD models, not between imprecise and precise software. 3DCodeBench includes manufactured objects, but its evaluation does not require native mechanical-CAD feature histories or engineering-dimension compliance. Likewise, our checks do not certify complete manufacturability.

    Terminal-Bench and Harbor: agent evaluation infrastructure.

    Terminal-Bench provides complementary methodology for evaluating agents on difficult terminal workflows [17]. Our benchmark is built on Harbor, a framework for specifying and evaluating agent tasks in sandboxed environments [16]. We also contributed three FreeCAD tasks to Terminal-Bench 3.0/4.0: two create-and-edit tasks (freecad-impeller and freecad-spring-clip) and one image-to-CAD task (freecad-platform-drawing) [15]. These tasks follow the same create-and-edit and engineering-drawing reconstruction workflow types evaluated in Parametric CAD Bench v3.

    3 Tasks and Dataset Construction

    3.1 Task workflows

    Table 1 describes the released task composition.

    In create-and-edit, the agent first constructs the base from text and then produces the edited model; both artifacts are graded. The task does not provide an externally authored starting FCStd. Scoring the two artifacts does not establish that the agent actually reused the base or preserved its feature history. Image-to-CAD tasks provide engineering drawings rather than the held-back dimensional specification.

    3.2 Example tasks

    Text-to-CAD creation examples.

    Two creation tasks illustrate the range of specifications. Figure 1 shows freecad-2002df3ce7, a trussed upper plate: a thin planar frame whose outline is the union of three rectangular sections with rounded corner chamfers, with mirrored trapezoidal recesses on the sides of the largest section. Diagonal truss webs separate seventeen triangular openings and one central six-sided opening, forming 18 internal loops; peripheral mounting holes and a center bore complete the part. Its 86 key parameters fall into five groups (Table 2). The description fixes the conventions needed to place them, including a sketch frame rotated about global +X so that layout +y points along global -Z, and centroid, base-length, and base-angle definitions for each isosceles opening. The grader reference builds the plate from one sketch and one pad; it is one solid with 203 faces, 280 mm wide, 549 mm tall, and 8 mm thick.

    Figure 2 shows freecad-fa0a1abef3, an asymmetric clevis joint connector: a rectangular central body with a large split-ring clevis at its +X end, a smaller fork at its -X end, and a long rounded side arm with three relief slots. The description states that the two ends are not mirror images and fixes global axes along, across, and through the connector. Its 44 key parameters fall into eight groups. The grader reference uses eight sketches, four pads, and four pockets; it is one solid with 31 faces, measuring 157 mm by 45 mm by 50 mm. Appendix B reproduces both complete descriptions and parameter lists as given to the agent.

    The held-back grader specification also states how each parameter is checked. Only 8 of the plate’s 86 parameters and 7 of the connector’s 44 are bound to witnesses on the final geometry; the task’s param_check.py measures the rest from native sketch and feature geometry. Neither task uses task-specific bindings. A candidate therefore earns specification credit only when its model exposes the named dimensions in a form these checks can measure. Section 5.5 reports how the evaluated systems fared on both tasks.

    Text-to-CAD create-and-edit example.

    Figure 3 illustrates freecad-ff7883ab0c. The agent first builds an axisymmetric flanged inlet housing: a continuous 50.8 mm central bore, a tapered inlet rim, a tubular middle body, a tapered rear hub, and a plain 152.4 mm rear flange disk. The edit adds a fourfold-symmetric front plate, 16.51 mm thick, whose outline joins side, corner, and transition arcs with short tangent connectors. It also adds four 13.34 mm through bolt holes in the plate and four 19.05 mm openings cut 34.54 mm deep from the rear flange face, each pattern placed from a signed seed center at uniform angular spacing. The tubular body, inlet rim, rear hub, rear disk envelope, and central passage must remain unchanged. Fifteen base parameters and 14 additional target parameters specify diameters, axial positions, arc radii, hole sizes and counts, and seed-center offsets. The complete supplied base description, edit instruction, and parameter lists appear in Appendix C.

    This task couples an axisymmetric base with a non-circular, arc-bounded plate and two four-hole patterns on opposite faces. The script must save both answer_base.FCStd and answer_edit.FCStd, each as an editable single-body PartDesign model. Both stages are evaluated; a plausible final silhouette alone does not demonstrate correct base construction or compliance with the plate-outline and hole requirements. As with the other create-and-edit tasks, the two saved artifacts do not by themselves prove that the target reused the base feature history.

    Image-to-CAD example.

    Figure 4 shows the input drawing and trusted reference for freecad-9749149002. The drawing combines orthographic, section, and isometric views of a linkage arm with two eye ends, angled transitions, and ribbed connecting beams. Dimension labels specify its 56 mm overall length, 19.5 mm depth, unequal 3 mm and 2 mm eye holes, and local radii and offsets. The agent must reconcile these views and dimensions to construct an editable single-solid PartDesign model.

    Unlike the text-based examples, the agent receives no separate prose description or key-parameter list: the drawing is its only geometry input. It must write /app/answer.py and save /app/answer.FCStd under FreeCAD 1.1.0. The reference shown here is held back during evaluation; it illustrates the intended output, not an additional agent input.

    3.3 Reference-model statistics

    We count solid-modeling steps using FreeCAD’s native feature type hierarchy: objects derived from Part::Feature, excluding body containers, sketches, and datum helpers. Intermediate and hidden feature-history objects are included; a pattern counts as one feature regardless of instance count. Generic Part::Feature objects count too, so this statistic alone does not certify parametric editability. Sketch counts are reported separately. The main distribution gives each task one observation, using the target reference for create-and-edit rather than counting both stages as separate tasks. The 100 final reference models contain 687 solid-modeling feature objects in total, with a mean of 6.87, a median of 6, and a range of 1–20 features per task. For the 30 create-and-edit pairs, the base and target means are 2.47 and 5.60, respectively. These describe the provided reference constructions; they do not establish a minimum number of features required for a valid alternative solution or a calibrated measure of task difficulty.

    Figure 5 shows unit-bin histograms for the full benchmark and each workflow. Supplementary figures show feature-type composition, sketch counts, and base/target distributions for the 30 edit pairs.

    4 Execution and Evaluation

    4.1 Pinned runtime and isolation

    The runtime uses FreeCAD 1.1.0, Harbor 0.23.0, and task schema 1.3. The verifier pins gnucleus-freecad-validator 0.6.0 with its v2 scorer. The benchmark version, validator package version, and scorer version are distinct identifiers. Reference geometry and task-specific grader assets are placed in a separate verifier environment rather than the agent environment. Each public job records its agent version and concurrency.

    4.2 Programmatic scoring

    The verifier computes two independent axes, geometry_similarity and cad_spec_consistency, using the default v2 scorer in gnucleus-freecad-validator 0.6.0 [10].

    Geometric similarity.

    The scorer compares the candidate and reference solids using surface-type areas, volume, total surface area, normalized principal moments of inertia, and face-center iterative closest point (ICP) alignment. Let q_surf,qᵥₒₗ,qₐᵣₑₐ,qₘₒₘ and q_ICP denote their respective subscores in [0,1]. After the gates below pass, the geometric score is

    p=(0.05q_surf+0.175qᵥₒₗ+0.175qₐᵣₑₐ+0.10qₘₒₘ)/(0.50),(1)
    g=p(0.50+0.50q_ICP).(2)

    Volume receives full credit at relative error at most 0.1% and zero subscore at 1% or more; the corresponding thresholds for surface-type areas, total surface area, and normalized principal moments are 1% and 10%. Intermediate errors receive logarithmically interpolated credit. Surface-type comparison uses the largest per-type relative area error, with a denominator floor of 1% of the larger total surface area. An independently measured OCCT oriented bounding box is a gate, not an additional weighted subscore: maximum relative error across sorted extents of 10% or more sets g=0. Structural gates also require one non-empty PartDesign::Body producing one solid through allowed native features rather than baked shape holders. Candidates with more than 5,000 faces, or face/vertex counts differing from the reference by more than 50% of the larger count, are rejected. Gate failures override the spatial multiplier’s nonzero floor. Face-center alignment depends on face decomposition, so congruent geometry built through a different feature history need not receive g=1.

    CAD specification consistency.

    The scorer parses the task’s held-back specification and checks its parameters against measurements extracted from the candidate document. CAD engineers wrote the parameter-checking logic shipped in each task’s tests/grader/param_check.py. Most tasks share a workflow-level implementation, and a subset adds case-specific checks. These checks encode ways to measure the dimensions, the correct placement of dimensions on the CAD part, feature relationships, and derived quantities required by the task’s specification. They supplement generic measurements with engineering-specific checks beyond global shape similarity. The v2 path honors trusted geometry bindings and case-local param_check.py refinements where supplied; remaining checks use generic per-kind measurements. The default scalar relative tolerance is 1%, with case-specific measurement logic and binding tolerances where applicable. Let n be the number of parsed specification parameters and f the number classified as inconsistent or not found. The default v2 failure budget is 10:

    s=\begincases0,&n=0, [2.0pt] \max (0,1-\dfracf\min(n,10)),&n>0.\endcases

    		(3)

    For n≥10, each failed or unmeasurable parameter costs 0.1, preventing large specifications from diluting failures. This score measures the encoded checks, not every possible engineering requirement or functional editability under arbitrary future changes.

    Combined task reward.

    Let g,s∈[0,1] denote geometry and specification scores. Define

    H(g,s)=\begincases0,&g=0 or s=0, [2.0pt] \dfrac2gsg+s,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(4)

    For creation and image-to-CAD, the task reward is r=H(g,s). For create-and-edit, each output is scored separately, then combined:

    r_edit=H (H(g_base,s_base),H(g_target,s_target)).

    		(5)

    Thus a zero score on a required axis or deliverable cannot be rescued by another axis. The wrappers clamp rewards to [0,1]; text reward files use six decimal places, and the image-to-CAD wrapper also rounds its JSON reward to six decimal places.

    The reported overall percentage is

    S=100/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nrᵢ, N=100.

    		(6)

    Final exception outcomes contribute zero. Workflow percentages are computed within each cohort, so S=0.30S_create+0.30S_edit+0.40S_image.

    This continuous reward is not Pass@1. We additionally report the fraction of final rewards exactly equal to 1.0 as the operational perfect-task rate. A scored trial is one without a final exception; scored count and positive-reward count are different quantities.

    5 Results and Analysis

    5.1 Dated leaderboard snapshot

    Figures 9–12 visualize the 13-row September 24, 2026 snapshot. The plots are generated from the published leaderboard rows. The overall chart shows 95% intervals computed as the mean reward ±1.96 s/√100, where s is the sample standard deviation of a system’s 100 per-task rewards. They describe uncertainty over the task sample, given one final trial per task, not variability across repeated runs of a system. Workflow charts show point estimates only.

    Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest overall point estimate, 61.03%, followed by mini-swe-agent with the same model at 57.96%, Codex with GPT-6 Astra at 56.87%, and Claude Code with Claude Fable 5.1 at 56.75%. Point-estimate ordering alone does not demonstrate a statistically decisive ranking.

    The workflow leaders differ: Fable 5.1 with Claude Code has the highest creation point estimate (55.48%), Astra with Codex leads create-and-edit (44.37%), and Opus 5.5 with Claude Code leads image-to-CAD (84.66%). Because workflows use different task populations, these differences cannot be attributed solely to input modality.

    5.2 Same-model and same-agent comparisons

    We pair final rewards by task ID, rather than comparing only cohort means. For the following descriptive counts, two outcomes are similar when their rewards differ by at most 0.05 (5 percentage points); a higher outcome must exceed this tolerance. Similarity is not a statistical equivalence claim, nor does it imply success: two zero-reward outcomes also count as similar. Final exception outcomes retain their zero rewards.

    Opus 5.5 versus Opus 5 with Claude Code.

    Within Claude Code, the overall point estimate rises from 50.86% for Opus 5 to 61.03% for Opus 5.5, a 10.18 percentage-point increase. The release analysis reports a paired 95% confidence interval of 5.22–15.13 points for this improvement [14]. It is a normal approximation over the 100 per-task reward differences: their mean ±1.96 s_d/√100, where s_d is their sample standard deviation. Table 4 shows that this is not a uniform improvement across workflows. For creation, Opus 5.5 is higher on 8 tasks, similar on 18, and lower on 4; for create-and-edit, the corresponding counts are 4, 23, and 3. Image-to-CAD shows the broadest improvement: Opus 5.5 is higher on 22 of 40 tasks, similar on 15, and lower on only 3. Its median paired drawing-task gain is 7.62 points, and all five drawings receiving zero reward under Opus 5 receive positive reward under Opus 5.5. The 22.02-point image-to-CAD mean gain accounts for approximately 87% of the overall improvement after applying the benchmark’s 30/30/40 workflow weights.

    Claude Code versus mini-swe-agent with Opus 5.5.

    To support multimodal tasks, we add an explicit system prompt to the mini-swe-agent run: when a task references an image, the agent must first send that image through its multimodal observation channel, inspect the resulting visual input, and only then proceed with the task. This is paired with a configured bridge that converts marked, base64-encoded shell output into image content for the model; the prompt alone does not enable image transport. The Opus 5.5 configuration uses mini-swe-agent 2.4.6, preserves complete image payloads, and leaves malformed image output as text.

    With Opus 5.5 held constant, Claude Code exceeds mini-swe-agent by 3.08 points. However, the paired interval computed the same way is [-1.15,7.31] points, so these results do not establish an overall advantage for either agent. The workflow-level comparison in Table 5 is more informative than the overall ordering. Claude Code leads creation by 8.07 points, with 9 higher outcomes, 20 similar outcomes, and 1 lower outcome. mini-swe-agent leads create-and-edit by 1.68 points: Claude Code is higher on 2 tasks, similar on 24, and lower on 4. For image-to-CAD, 30 of 40 outcomes are similar, and each agent is higher on 5 tasks. Claude Code’s 2.90-point mean advantage there therefore reflects the magnitudes of the differing outcomes, rather than a greater number of task-level wins. Both systems exceed 80% mean reward on drawing reconstruction with direct image input. These comparisons remain conditional on the evaluated configurations and dates, including different Claude Code versions; they are not completely controlled model or agent ablations.

    Initial takeaway.

    The clearest observed gain is in engineering-drawing reconstruction: Opus 5.5 improves Claude Code’s image-to-CAD score by 22.02 points, versus 1.39 points for creation and 3.17 points for create-and-edit. Both Opus 5.5 systems exceed 80% on image-to-CAD (84.66% and 81.77%), so the strong drawing results are not confined to one agent implementation [14]. This suggests substantial progress in drawing-to-CAD task completion, but not uniformly reliable CAD authoring: the same systems reach only 39.69% and 41.38% on create-and-edit. These are distinct task cohorts, not a controlled test of modality alone. Together with the launch post’s Gemini comparison across two agents, the results also indicate that model capability and agent interface both matter; they do not identify a universally superior agent [13].

    5.3 Multimodal CAD performance

    Image-to-CAD produces the largest separation between the evaluated model–agent systems. Across the 13 rows, its mean reward ranges from 8.18% to 84.66%, a 76.49-point spread. By comparison, creation ranges from 23.32% to 55.48% (32.16 points), and create-and-edit from 23.23% to 44.37% (21.14 points). The five highest image-to-CAD systems achieve 62.64–84.66%, whereas the remaining eight achieve only 8.18–31.10%. Drawing reconstruction therefore distinguishes these systems much more sharply than either text-based workflow.

    This pattern is also visible within a single agent family. Across the three Claude Code rows, image-to-CAD ranges from 62.64% with Opus 5 to 84.66% with Opus 5.5, a 22.02-point difference. The corresponding spreads are only 6.00 points for creation and 3.17 points for create-and-edit. Agent configuration matters as well: Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves 31.10% on image-to-CAD with mini-swe-agent’s multimodal bridge, versus 17.45% with Antigravity, a 13.65-point difference. Its creation and create-and-edit differences between these agents are smaller, at 4.66 and 5.90 points, respectively.

    These results suggest that multimodal CAD task completion is a major differentiator among the evaluated systems. Strong drawing performance requires interpreting views, dimensions, and geometric relationships and translating them into a valid parametric model. However, these scores measure that entire workflow, not visual perception in isolation: CAD construction, tool use, image transport, and failure recovery can all affect the outcome. The larger score spread does not by itself establish which of these factors causes the gap, particularly because the workflows contain different tasks.

    5.4 Efficiency

    Cost per score point.

    We divide the known API cost of the complete 100-task run by its overall score on the 0–100 scale. API costs come from the usage recorded in each job’s artifacts. For Grok Build with Grok 4.7 and for mini-swe-agent with Kimi K3, Muse Spark 1.3, and Claude Opus 5.5, whose artifacts record no or incomplete cost, they come from our audits, which price the token usage in the saved trajectories at standard API rates. This descriptive ratio measures expenditure per achieved score point, not the marginal cost of improving a system by one point. Codex with GPT-6 Astra has the lowest ratio among all 13 systems: $317.81 divided by 56.87 points, or $5.59 per point. Its total spend is not the lowest, but the additional expenditure buys substantially higher reward: compared with GPT-5.6 Sol using Codex, Astra costs only $25.82 more while scoring 26.89 points higher.

    Per-task speed.

    Astra also has the shortest mean elapsed trial duration, 14.42 minutes, compared with 16.58 minutes for Sol, 31.11 for Claude Code with Fable 5.1, and 32.51 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5. These are final-trial elapsed times, including setup, agent execution, and verification, rather than isolated model inference latency. We do not use whole-job wall time to rank speed, because concurrency, pauses, retries, and scheduling differ between runs.

    Reward–cost trade-off.

    Astra’s 56.87% mean reward is close to Fable 5.1’s 56.75%, but its known API cost is approximately 70% lower and its mean trial duration is less than half as long. The higher-scoring Claude Code–Opus 5.5 system improves the point estimate by 4.17 points over Astra, at 1.81 times the API cost and 2.25 times the mean trial duration. Astra therefore offers a favorable observed balance of reward, cost, and per-task speed, rather than the highest reward at any price. These comparisons describe the evaluated configurations and their audited API accounting; they exclude some compute and hosting costs and do not establish why one system requires less time or expenditure.

    5.5 Observed task difficulty

    Across the 1,300 selected final trials from the 13 evaluated systems, 393 (30.23%) earn zero reward. Table 6 summarizes the pattern by workflow. Create-and-edit has the largest zero-outcome rate, 41.54%, compared with 22.56% for creation and 27.50% for image-to-CAD. These counts use the official final outcomes, including zero-valued final exceptions and reruns of provider or platform failures that produced no model outcome, rather than the superseded attempts.

    Difficulty is concentrated in a subset of tasks. Twenty-four tasks receive zero reward from at least 7 of the 13 systems: 5 creation tasks, 11 create-and-edit tasks, and 8 image-to-CAD tasks. Five tasks receive zero from every system, all in create-and-edit. On 26 tasks, no system reaches 0.5: 9 creation, 16 create-and-edit, and 1 image-to-CAD. At the other end, 15 tasks earn a perfect reward of exactly 1.0 from at least one system (6 creation, 3 create-and-edit, and 6 image-to-CAD). Thus, strong aggregate drawing performance coexists with substantial remaining difficulty, especially in two-stage CAD construction. These are descriptive outcomes for the evaluated systems and configurations, not estimates of a task’s inherent solvability.

    The saved diagnostics also show that zero reward is usually associated with the CAD scoring criteria rather than a final execution exception. Of the 393 zeros, 326 involve a zero geometry component, including 50 that also have a zero specification component. Another 33 fail only specification consistency; the remainder comprise 23 final exceptions, 7 missing outputs, and 4 scorer crashes. This breakdown describes observed failure surfaces, not independently adjudicated root causes.

    Example task outcomes.

    The two creation examples fail in different ways. The trussed plate (Figure 1) is one of the 24 tasks with zero reward from at least 7 systems: 9 of the 13 systems receive zero (Table 7). Eight of these zeros come from the specification axis alone. These outcomes have geometry similarity between 0.126 and 0.445, but 12 to 80 of the 86 parameters are inconsistent or not found, which exhausts the failure budget of 10 in Equation 3. The ninth zero is a final exception. Among the four positive outcomes, Claude Fable 5.1 with Claude Code is nearly exact (0.999, with every parameter consistent); the others miss 1, 7, and 9 parameters. Codex with GPT-5.6 Terra earns 0.140 with lower geometry similarity (0.232) than five zero-reward attempts, because it stays within the failure budget. On this task, specification consistency rather than overall shape separates the rewarded attempts.

    The clevis connector (Figure 2) shows the opposite pattern (Table 8). Twelve of the 13 systems earn positive reward, and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code earns 1.000 to three decimals, with every parameter consistent. Only Codex with GPT-5.6 Terra receives zero, on both axes. The other eleven positive outcomes miss at most 7 of the 44 parameters, but their geometry similarity ranges only from 0.175 to 0.500. Two of them, Claude Fable 5.1 with Claude Code and Gemini 3.8 Flash with mini-swe-agent, pass every parameter check yet earn 0.419 because their geometry similarity is 0.265. Here, geometry rather than the named dimensions limits most rewards.

    6 Discussion and Limitations

    The benchmark is a curated 100-task FreeCAD evaluation, not a representative sample of all engineering CAD. Family dependencies and selection choices limit generalization. Native single-body PartDesign requirements do not cover general assembly mating, FEM/FEA, manufacturing qualification, or broad organic-surface modeling.

    Create-and-edit measures two-stage construction, not maintenance of an externally authored document. Grader rewards are heuristic proxies: geometric similarity and checked parameters do not certify all future edits, design intent, or engineering validity. Alternative valid constructions may challenge reference-based comparisons.

    Public assets, providers’ undisclosed training data, and changing provider implementations limit contamination claims and reproducibility. Agent tools, prompts, serving paths, and budgets confound model-only comparisons. Single official attempts do not establish run-to-run robustness. Known API costs exclude some compute and hosting costs.

    7 Conclusion

    Parametric CAD Bench v3 evaluates agentic CAD authoring across text-based creation, create-and-edit, and engineering-drawing reconstruction. Its 100 tasks require native parametric FreeCAD models, evaluated through geometric similarity and CAD-engineer-curated specification checks.

    Across 13 evaluated model–agent systems, the largest performance differences occur in image-to-CAD. Opus 5.5’s improvement over Opus 5 is concentrated in drawing reconstruction, while agent comparisons reveal workflow-dependent strengths rather than a universally superior interface. Create-and-edit remains challenging: five tasks receive zero reward from every evaluated system. Cost and speed also distinguish systems; Codex with GPT-6 Astra offers the lowest observed API cost per score point and the shortest mean trial duration.

    These results highlight substantial progress alongside remaining limitations in reliable parametric CAD construction. By releasing versioned tasks, execution configurations, scoring code, and inspectable run artifacts, Parametric CAD Bench provides a versioned, inspectable foundation for measuring progress in engineering-oriented CAD agents.
